translations.text: Nisibis I
To the tune of “I will open my mouth with knowledge.”
God of mercies, you who gave Noah rest, he too gave rest to your mercies. He offered sacrifices and checked the flood; he gave offerings
and received a promise. With prayer and incense he appeased you; with oaths and a rainbow you showed him favor. Wherever the flood rushes to harm the earth,
the bow is stretched out against it, to drive it away and reassure the earth, so that your oaths may preserve peace and your bow wage war against wrath.
Refrain: Stretch out your bow against the flood, for look, it has raised its waves against our walls!
Thunder openly, my Lord, for the weak blood that Noah sprinkled restrained wrath entirely, in every generation, from everyone. How much more powerful is the blood of your Only Begotten, that

its sprinkling should restrain our flood! For it was through the mystery of that blood that the weak sacrifices Noah offered gained strength and restrained wrath. Be appeased by the offering on my altar, and hold back from me
the flood of living men. Let your two signs protect us: your cross for me, and your bow for Noah. May your cross break the [sea] of waters; may your bow restrain the flood of rain.
Look, storms of every kind have shaken me, and I have called the ark blessed, for waves alone surrounded it, while mounds, arrows, and waves have surrounded me.
It was a storehouse of treasures for you, but I have become a storehouse of sins. Through your love it trod upon the waves, but through your wrath I was blinded among arrows.
Its scent [?] the flood; the river has shaken me. Be my pilot on dry land, as you were the sailor of that ark. You gave it rest in the mountain’s harbor; give me rest in the harbor of my walls.
Righteous One, discipline me with floods, but cherish the ark among the waves. Because Noah overcame the waves of desire that drowned the children of Seth in his generation, because he subdued
his flesh concerning the daughters of Cain, his vessel subdued the crests of the waves. Because women had not defiled him, he kept the animals chaste—all the pairs within that ark. The married man
kept marriage chaste. The olive, whose oil makes faces cheerful, made their faces cheerful with its leaf. But for me, my Lord, the river whose irrigation brings joy—look, its flood brings me sorrow.
Your justice saw the filth of my sins, and your pure eyes turned away from me. You gathered waters by means of an unclean man, to bring about the cleansing of my own sins—not that

you would immerse me in them and cleanse me, but that through them you would frighten and discipline me, so that the waves might awaken me to prayer that would wash away my sins. The sight of them, filled with repentance, became for me
a baptism. My Lord, let your mercies drown sins in the sea that came to drown me. In the Red Sea you drowned bodies; in this sea drown sins instead of bodies.
In mercy you prepared the ark, to preserve every remnant in it. So that the earth would not be emptied in wrath, your compassion made an earth of wood. You emptied them, one
into the other; you returned them, one to the other. My own lands have been filled and emptied three times, and now waves rush against me to wipe out the remnant

that escaped within me. You preserved a remnant in the ark; my Lord, preserve within me too a portion of leaven. The ark gave birth on the mountain; let me give birth in my lands to those confined within me.

My Lord, gladden within me those confined in fortresses, for you gladdened those confined in the ark with an olive leaf. Through the dove you sent a physician to the weakened people who had suffered in all the waves. He entered
and drove away all their pains, for his joy swallowed up sorrow, and mourning vanished through his comfort. Like a commander, he gave courage to the frightened; he sowed companionship

among the desolate. He gave their eyes a taste of the sight of peace, and quickly opened their mouths to praise you. Preserve me among the waves like the olive, so that through me you may gladden those confined in fortresses.

The flood rushed forward and battered our wall. May the power that sustains everything hold it firm, so that it does not fall like a building of sand. For I have not built my teaching on sand. Let the rock be my
foundation, for I have built my faith on your rock. May the hidden foundation of my trust support my walls. For the walls of Jericho fell, because on sand
she had built her trust. Moses built a wall in the sea, because he had built his mind on the rock. Noah’s foundation was on the rock; it supported wooden dwellings in the water.
Compare the souls within me with the animals in the ark. In place of Noah, who mourned and humbled himself, [?] women, and kept himself chaste in it, here are my virgins who have not
married. In place of Ham, who went out exposing his father’s shame, here are those who give alms, who have modestly clothed the naked. In my sufferings

I lost my senses and spoke. My Lord, do not reproach me because my words provoked anger. You silenced the diligent workers who grumbled; show mercy to me as you did to the last workers, who were silent.
Before the wrath came, you made a refuge, and every species was tamed within it. Noah was at ease in a house of rest, which gave rest to its inhabitant, as his name implies. You shut the doors
to protect the righteous man; you opened the floodgates to sweep away the unclean. Noah stood between the dreadful waves outside and the destructive mouths within. They carried him—
the waves—and troubled him—the mouths. You made those within peaceful toward him; you subdued those outside before him. You quickly changed his hardships, for difficulties are easy for you, my Lord.
Hear and weigh my comparison with Noah. Although my suffering is less than his, may your mercy make our deliverances equal. For here my children stand, like him, between furious men and destroyers.

My Lord, make those within peaceful toward me, and subdue those outside before me. Double my victory. The one whose wrath has killed three times—may your third [?] triple his mercy. Let the evil one not defeat those who love you,

for you have defeated him twice and three times. May my victory spread throughout the world, so that I may gain glory for you throughout the world. You who brought three people back to life, do not put me to death on the third occasion.
Nisibis II
On the Deliverance of the City. To the tune of: “[?] in the Promise.”
On this day mouths were opened to give thanks. The openings of the breaches opened the mouths of my children. Give thanks to the Merciful One, who delivered our humanity
and did not look for an opportunity then to repay us. The destroyers who lay in wait for us, who rose up to take us captive—the nations tasted your grace through our deliverance.
Refrain: From everyone who has a mouth, glory to your grace!
He delivered us without a wall and taught us that he is our wall. He delivered us without a king and made known that he is our king. He delivered us in every way from everything and showed that he is
everything. He delivered us by his grace and revealed again that he shows mercy freely and gives life. From everyone who boasts, he took away boasting and gave it to his grace.
The thunder of all mouths is too little to give you thanks. For at the moment when our light flickered and was about to go out, because everything is easy for you, it suddenly flared up
and shone brightly. Who has seen two such wonders? Just as hope came to an end, hope followed close behind and grew abundant. The hour of lamentation turned into good news.

This is a festival day on which the other festivals depend. For if wrath had taken us captive, our festivals too would have ceased. Because our peace triumphed and prevailed, now our festivals resound—
our feasts! This blessed day supports everything. On it the city depends; on the city the people depend; on the people peace depends; on peace everything depends.
From the breaches themselves you multiplied victories. Glory rose to the Triune One from our three breaches, for he came down and fenced them around with mercies that held back
wrath. He struck what cannot learn in order to teach us. He taught those within that he is just: he broke open the walls. He taught those outside that he is good: he fenced them around.
Speak and give praise on this day, you whom I have redeemed: old people and troops, young men and young women, children and innocent ones, and the mother Church.
For the procession. For the old were spared captivity, the young men torture, the infants being dashed to pieces, the women exposure, and the Church humiliation.
He came to us with hardships, and we feared for an instant. He came with comforts, and we behaved well for an hour. He left us alone and withdrew a little, and we strayed without
limit, like a beast with teeth that learns through coaxing and intimidation. But if it is neglected, it rebels, goes astray, and becomes vicious in a time of peace.

He punished us, but we did not fear; he rescued us, but we felt no shame. He pressed us, and vows multiplied; he relaxed his grip, and sins multiplied. When he oppressed us, there were my promises; when he gave relief, there was my straying.
He pledged himself [?], knowing us, to release us. In the evening we made a pledge to him; in the morning we went back on it. Compulsion passed from us, and faithfulness passed from us.

He laid us low through breaches, so that we would pay our debts. He raised siege mounds so that through them he might humble our arrogance. He broke open seas so that through them he might wash away our filth.
He confined us so that we would gather in his temple. He confined us, and we grew weary; he opened the way for us, and we became distracted. We resemble wool, which takes on every color.
Let us recognize that the people of Nineveh were blessed when they repented. They did not repent because of siege mounds, nor through seas, nor because of breaches, nor because of bows.
It was not the sound of a bowstring that frightened them into repentance. They heard a lowly voice and made their infants fast. They made their young men chaste and humbled their kings.

You struck us, and we acknowledged that you were not acting tyrannically. You rescued us, and we confessed that it was not [?] because we were worthy. You showed us mercy, not because you were mistaken and supposed that we had repented

on our own. It is clear to you that whenever you show us mercy, we stray. You knew that we had sinned, and you knew that we were sinning. You were aware of the wrongdoing that had happened and was happening when you showed us mercy.
Compare our repentance, to see whether it outweighs our debts. The measure did not even come out equal, one against the other: our wrongdoing weighed heavily, while our repentance was light.
He had ordered that we be sold for our debt. His mercy became our advocate. Principal and interest we paid with a small coin, which our repentance had stamped.
He forgave us ten thousand talents for a small payment of debt. It was entirely fitting that he should demand payment, to satisfy his justice. That he should forgive was necessary
too, to gladden his grace. We give him eyes full of tears [?]. He troubled his justice: instead of demanding payment, he forgave much.
The ten thousand debts he forgave us—even ten thousand tongues of ours cannot make an adequate return for his grace. He forgave us, but we did not forgive; we repaid him with the opposite.

We wrote down anew the wrongdoing of the sinner. “Forgive, my Lord!” we cry; “Exact payment, my Lord!” we pray. “Forgive us for having offended,” we say; “Exact payment from whoever offends against us,” we say.
We did not even labor for ourselves as the outsiders did. They raised siege mounds, but we did not even raise our voices. They dismantled a wall, but we did not even
untie the slight knots within our hearts. He wronged the diligent because of the lazy. He wronged the labor outside while he himself was being wronged within.
He spared those who speak and struck the silent things. The wall was being scourged, and the people were being taught wisdom. He had compassion on those who can feel; he struck what does not
feel. For instead of living beings that have sensation, he struck stone, which has no sensation, to discipline us. In his love he spared our bodies and hurried to strike our wall.
Who has ever seen a breach become like a mirror? Two sides looked into it; it served those outside and those within. In it they saw, as though with their own eyes, the power that shattered

and bound up. They saw him who had made a breach and then fenced it up again. Those outside saw his might and departed without spending the night. Those within saw his help and gave thanks, but did not make an adequate return.
On the day of your deliverance, let us recall your flooding: when the wall was breached and the elephants were pressing forward, when arrows were raining down and men were attacking fiercely
—it became a spectacle for the heavenly beings. The infant fought there; mercy triumphed there. Compassion prevailed below; the Watchers cried out above.
Your enemy struggled to damage by his devices the wall that surrounded you, the refuge of your inhabitants. He struggled and could not succeed; and so that he would not

suppose that, if he breached it, he would also enter and take us captive, he breached it—not just once—and was put to shame. Yet that was not enough: it happened three times, so that he would be put to shame three times over.
May blessedness increase for me too within you, through grace. Since my sins have multiplied in you, may my fruits multiply in you. Since my youth sinned in you, may mercy be shown in you to

my old age. Through the mouths of your children, plead for your son. For I sinned beyond my strength, but repented with less than my strength. I scattered without measure, but gathered less than a measure.
Nisibis III
2. To the same tune.
Fix our attention firmly, so that it does not break loose and wander, for it wanders into investigating who he is and whom he resembles. For how can we depict his likeness

within ourselves? That self-existent Being resembles the mind: there is nothing closed off in him; with his whole being he sees and hears. His whole being is, as it were, speech; his whole being possesses every sense.
Refrain: Glory to the one self-existent Being, whom we cannot search out.
His appearance cannot be grasped so as to be pictured in our minds. He hears without ears, speaks without a mouth, acts without hands, and sees without eyes.
Our soul does not gather itself and rest with one who is like this. In his grace he clothed himself in human forms and gathered us through his likenesses.
Let us learn that, just as he is a spiritual being and appeared as a bodily being, so too he is serene and appeared as one who is angry. These things are

for our help. The self-existent Being resembles us through our likenesses, so that we may resemble him. There is only one who resembles him: the Offspring who came forth from him, who is stamped with his likenesses.
Nisibis, hear these things, for on your account these things were written and spoken, both for you and for others. You became an occasion throughout the world for verses [?] and expositions.
Mouths lamented over you because you were besieged; mouths sang over you because you triumphed and were delivered. Because of you, mouths were opened for lamentation and for praise.
The prayer of your inhabitants was enough for your deliverance—not because they are righteous, but because they repent. As much as they act shamefully, so much do they run beneath the rod.
They are a mixture of sins and victories. Since their sins have grown strong, may their fruits grow strong. Since they triumphed in their sackcloth, may their crowns also triumph.
The day of your deliverance is king of all days. The Sabbath brought down your walls; it brought down the unbelievers. The day of the Son’s resurrection raised up
your fallen ruins. The day of resurrection raised you up, true to its name; praise it for its title. The Sabbath broke its own observance; through the toil over its breaches, it rebuked itself.
In Samaria famine grew severe, but in you abundance grew great. Plenty burst into Samaria suddenly; but into you a sea roared and entered
suddenly. In that city an infant was eaten and kept it alive; in you the living Body that gives life to all was eaten. Suddenly the one who was eaten delivered those who ate.
It is known that the Good One did not desire the afflictions that occurred in every generation, although he brought them about. Our sins are the cause

of devastation. No one has a grievance against him who created us; he has a grievance against us, because we sinned and forced him to become angry when he did not wish to, and to strike when he did not desire to.
The earth, the vineyard, and the olive tree need discipline. When the olive tree is beaten, its branches become abundant; when the vineyard is pruned, its fruit becomes fine.
When the soil is cultivated, its crops flourish. When the sea is disciplined, they drink it from vessels. When bronze, silver, and gold are polished, they shine.

If a human being disciplines everything, he improves it; but if he despises and neglects it, everything becomes ugly and unruly. From what he disciplines, let him learn about the one who disciplines him.
When he himself disciplines, it is for his own benefit, for whenever he disciplines his servants, it is to profit from them. The Good One disciplines his servants so that they themselves may benefit.
Let your afflictions be scribes to record your memories. For three sieges are enough to serve you as books, whose accounts you should ponder at every moment.
You scorned to read about your life in the two Testaments. Therefore he wrote you three harsh books in which to read about your punishments.
Let what has happened put an end to what might happen again. Let us be disciplined by what has come, so that we may avert what is coming. Let us remember what has passed, so that we may dismiss what
is yet to come. We forgot the first blow, and the second overwhelmed us. We forgot the second, and the third wore us down. Who will forget again?
Nisibis IV
To the tune of “The Gathering of My Afflictions.”
My God, I will knock at the door of your house without tiring. Though I have denied every kindness, I will ask boldly, so that I may receive through shameless persistence.
Refrain: Our hope, be our wall.
For, my Lord, if the earth, bribed with a grain of wheat, enriches it with many grains, how much more will my prayers be enriched by your grace!
At the tender and resounding voices of my children, open the door of your mercy to me. Let me gladden the mourning of their sackcloth with their voices.
Firstborn, who became [?] and joined the children, the accursed sons of Nazareth, answer my lambs, who have seen wolves and are now bleating.
My Lord, if a sheep in the wilderness sees wolves, it clings to its owner and takes refuge in his staff, which drives away those that would devour it.
Your flock has seen wolves and is now crying out loudly. Come to its aid, for it is terrified. Let your cross be a staff that drives away those that would swallow it.
Accept the cry of my little children, who are pure in everything. The one who is young in days can, my Lord, appease the Ancient of Days.
On the very day when the infant lay in the manger, the watchers came down and proclaimed peace. May that peace be in my streets for all my little children.
Seventy-two elders, the elders of that people, were not enough to bring reconciliation. It was the infant, the son of Mary, who brought peace to every region.
Have mercy, my Lord, on my children. In my children remember your own birth, when you became a child, so that those who resemble you in your childhood may live by your grace.
Within your flock mingle the bleating of the innocent and the voices of the ewes, calling to the Shepherd of all to deliver them from everything.

I will weave together all our voices and make a crown of voices. I will offer it to your Father; I will buy [?]. [?]
a.
Woe to me! What a neighbor I have, so close to me, whose feet never tire

at his post! At all times he stands constantly over my head.
b.
Woe to me! What a guest I have, who wants to eat both me and my bread! My Lord, let him be restrained by

justice. Starve his greed!
c.
Woe to me! What an enemy I have, so close to me! Blessed am I! What a Lord and Savior I have, who has rebuked him and restrained him!
Joy that harms has sorrow hidden within it; sorrow that helps is a fountain of joys in that new world.
The prosperity my persecutor has acquired has woes hidden within it. Therefore I rejoice, for the sorrow I have received from him has blessedness hidden within it for me.
Who would not give thanks to the one who gave us birth and can again bring forth voices of good news from the reports we hear?
You are the healer of all; you visited me in my illnesses. I could not pay the price of your medicines, for they have no price.
Your abundant mercies surpass your medicines. They cannot be bought; they are given freely and received with tears.
How long, my Master, can a forsaken city stand without mercy, when her king's son is far away and her enemy is near?
You are a harbor and a place of refuge at all times. When the seas covered me, your mercies descended and lifted me up. May your help reach me again.
Apply the medicine of your salvation to my wounds. The suffering through which you help can, by your will, become a medicine that heals all.
I am deeply distressed and eager to complain against the one who has troubled me. May your compassion, my Lord, dilute the cup my sins have mixed.
I looked in every direction and wept because I had been forsaken. Although my leaders and rescuers were very many, only one rescued me.
My Lord, my children flew away and departed, like chicks pursued by an eagle. Look, they are hiding in shelter. May your peace bring them back.
My ears now miss the sound of my vineyards, whose voices have been cut off. Let the news of your salvation thunder with glad tidings.
I heard a sound of terror upon my towers, where my rescuers cried out as they guarded my walls. Silence it with the sound of your peace.
Let the clamor of my workers grow quiet outside my wall; let the uproar of my inhabitants grow quiet inside my wall, so that I may give thanks outside and inside.
End, my Lord, the mourning of your pure altar and of your chaste priest, who stands clothed in mourning, with sackcloth wrapped over him.
May the church and her ministers give thanks for your salvation, together with the city and her inhabitants. My Lord, let the sound of peace be the reward for their voices.
Nisibis V
To the tune: “Your flock, plaintively.”
In your grace, let the news of salvation be heard, for reports of terror have made our hearing a passageway into our minds.
Refrain: Praises to your victory! Glory to your lordship!
Comfort with small and modest gains those who have traded their labor for loss. At the time of profit, they have inherited loss.
It is clear that wrath itself took its stand in the midst of the land, angrily distributing loss and gain. Some it suddenly ruined, and others it suddenly enriched.
To teach that it can chastise by every means, when it saw that persecutors were terrifying in my eyes, it stripped me before my children, and my loved ones scourged me.
See, he taught me to fear him and not any human being. When there was no one striking us, his wrath suddenly gave the command, and everyone stretched himself out and scourged himself.
Even the Babylonian, who scourged all kings, when he grew confident and thought no one could harm him, he made him scourge himself with his own hands.

His appearance and his mind suddenly changed together. He tore his clothes to shreds, threw them off, and went out wandering in the wilderness. First he chased himself, and then his servants chased him.
He showed all the kings whom he had taken captive and brought low that he had not been able to conquer by his own strength. The power that scourged him was the very power that had disciplined them.
I bore and endured, my Lord, the lashes of my rescuers. In your grace you can do good through those who cause harm; in your justice you can discipline through those who help.
On the day when the army advanced and came up against Samaria, her persecutors abandoned abundance and luxury, treasures and possessions, and fled. He crowned her with the spoils of her persecutors.
My loved ones crowned me, and my rescuers visited me. Because of the wrongdoing of my inhabitants, my helpers scourged me. Give me a cup of consolation to drink from my vines.
Preserve the ear of grain and the vine, my Lord, in your grace. May the vineyard's vine console the farmer; may the farmer's ear of grain gladden the laborer.
The ear of grain and the vine accompany one another. In the field, wine can gladden the reapers; in the vineyard, bread in turn strengthens the workers.
Both of them can console me in my troubles. A third thing can console me still more: that I give thanks because I suddenly escaped through grace.
But anyone whose life is preserved through grace, if he goes on to complain about the loss of his possessions, denies the grace of the one who had pity on him.
He deliberately chose to destroy one thing in place of another. He destroyed possessions and spared possessions; he destroyed our plants in exchange for our lives.
Let us be afraid to complain, lest wrath awaken, spare the possessions, and strike their owners, so that at the end we learn the mercy shown at the beginning.
Let us learn whom it is right to complain against. Learn to complain, not against the one who disciplines you, but against your own will, because you sinned and were scourged.
Let us abandon complaining and turn to prayer. For if the owner dies, his possessions also come to nothing; but as long as he remains alive, he can recover his losses.
In mercy, let consolations increase for my inhabitants. May what survived and what remains console them amid wrath, and through what is left may I forget the grief of destruction.
Tend and bring to maturity, my Lord, the fruits that wrath left behind. They seem to me like sick people who escaped the pestilence. Through the few, make me forget my grief for the many.
As I spoke, my Lord, I remembered that it is already a month since the vine blossom became ill and fell sick. May it return to health and become a consolation.
For they escaped the pestilence that carried off their brothers. The vines weep without a sound, for before them their beloved trees lie cut down and cast aside.
Look, the earth longs for the company of its plants. The roots weep for the farmers and make them weep as well. Beauty spread out and gave shade, but in a single hour they folded it away.
The axe approached and cut, and its cutting cut the farmer too: cutting for the trees, and grief for the farmer. Every axe blow they struck—he tasted its pain.
Nisibis VI
2. To the same tune.
In my afflictions I will run to the physician who heals freely, who healed my first wounds and my second ones. May he who restored the third to health heal the fourth.
Refrain: Heal me, firstborn Son.

My sons, my Lord, drank and became drunk on the good drink that wrath mixed. They seized my adornments, stripped them off, and threw away my ornaments. It mercilessly tore my clothes and my crowns to shreds.
They stripped me, and I was exposed—I who had felt a little shame at that first exposure and the second. I who was ashamed at the third—look, they have exposed me a fourth time.

They folded up and took away my garments, my ornaments, and my gardens. Look, my Lord, at my altar wrapped in sackcloth, and clothe me modestly. Let its sackcloth become for me, my Lord, a covering of salvation.
See, it was not through a chaste man that you chastised me, Rabbula [?]. His shame goes before him, and his disgrace follows behind him. His marriage is adultery, openly committed by him.

See, his wife is his daughter, and his partner is his sister. The mother from whom he came forth—he returned and married her again. The heavens were astonished at how greatly he provoked anger, yet see, he prospers!
Even if, my Lord, my wrongdoings have multiplied and my sins have grown so strong, would you hand over the chaste woman, the mother of chaste women, to defiled Assyria, the mother of filthy women?

Rebuke him, so that he does not come and shake his head at me, stamp his heel upon me, and rejoice at the sound of his own fame. He has thrown the world into such turmoil; will he now be exalted a little more?

My Lord, my own children have seen my exposure; even though they exposed me, they weep. Expose me before my children, who suffer because of my suffering, and do not let the merciless accursed ones exult over me.
My lands were laden and standing full of fruit and delicacies: good things in the vineyard, abundance in the fields. While I was at ease, wrath suddenly swept down.

The farmers are cheated; the plunderers are satisfied. What they borrowed and sowed they have lost; along with his debt comes his hunger [?]. Perhaps he even spends the night fasting, because his bread has been snatched from him.
The farmer has been cheated, my Lord: he was the one who lent to the earth. It took his deposit and gave it to a stranger. It repaid the farmer’s loan to the plunderer.

Be jealous for me, for I am yours, and to you, my Lord, I am betrothed. The apostle who betrothed me to you told me that you are jealous. The jealousy of their husbands is a wall protecting chaste women.
For days Samson caused turmoil, so greatly jealous was he for his wife, although she was utterly defiled and unfaithful to him. Protect your church, who has no other besides you.
If anyone is not jealous for his betrothed, she is held in contempt. Jealousy can reveal the love between them. You were called jealous so that you might show me your love.
This is a woman’s nature: weak and bold. Jealousy keeps her in fear at all times. They counted you among the jealous, so that you might make your care known.
Everyone became master of what was not his. Everyone went out and gathered what he had not scattered. Through my sins I have appointed a day of turmoil for myself.

How much suffering must the toilers and farmers endure? Before the farmer’s eyes they cut down and carried away the fruits of his work. They reaped and carried away the farmer’s crops, the fruits of his toil.
They yoked their oxen, sowed, hoed, and cultivated; they planted and tended. They stood facing it and wept, and went away empty of everything. Toil fell to the farmers, the harvest to the plunderers.

The leaders did not establish order amid the wrath, my Lord. Had they wished, they could have restored order, but our wrongdoing did not allow it. Though the wrath was very mild, wrath was stirred up to plunder [?].
To which of all my sides shall I look for comfort? To my plantings, condemned to ruin? To my buildings, destroyed? Let the welcome sound of peace soothe my sorrow.
Do not hand me over, lest I think that you have given me a certificate of divorce, dissolved our bond, and cast me away. Do not let them call me abandoned and disgraced, my Lord.
I have nothing by which I may be remembered before your eyes, for I am altogether contemptible. Remember this alone for me, my God: I have set no other beside you.
Who would not weep for me with cries and lamentation? A few days before the cup, I was chaste and crowned; a few days after the cup, I am uncovered and exposed.

My chaste women of the inner chambers wander bewildered in the fields, for the wrath that makes everyone drunk has reached my honored women. May your mercy, which brings peace to all, restore modest covering to my beloved women.
See, my old women and my mothers cry out before you: the young women with their voices, the old women with their tears, my virgins with their fasts, and my chaste women with their sackcloth.

I raised my eyes toward all the streets, and look, they are deserted. Ten remain out of a hundred, and a thousand out of ten thousand. Bring peace; fill my streets with the multitudes of my inhabitants.
Bring back those outside and gladden those within. Look, your grace is great enough to spread within and without. Let the wings of your grace gather my chicks.

May the prayer of my righteous people protect my fugitives. Those who do not believe have broken me, and those who believe have supported me. Through the believers, put those who did not believe to shame.
Two feasts came together as one on a single day: the feast of your ascension and the feast of your champions, the feast when your crown was bound on, and the commemoration of your servants’ crown.
Have mercy, for our feasts had been doubled on a single day; and in their place two feasts were doubled for us together: suffering instead of glad tidings, and mourning instead of destruction.
Bring peace to my festivals, for my two feasts have ceased. Instead of the delights of my festive banquets [?], groans and pains have met me everywhere.
Bring back those of mine who are far away; gladden those of mine who are near. Let joyful news be proclaimed throughout our land, and in return for peace I will offer praise through every mouth.
Nisibis VII
3. To the same tune.

Wrath came to rebuke the greedy who, during peace, trafficked, oppressed, and plundered. During wrath the greedy grew rich. Look, their own possessions have been scattered—the possessions of those who gathered what was not theirs.
Refrain: Son, bring peace to our land.

For ten years my afflictions resembled branches, my Savior, which are compressed during winter and sprout when the weather grows mild. My afflictions sprouted; along with our fruit, our heart ripened.
Nisan is the season of shoots; good things spring up in it. When my proud deeds multiply, then my calamities multiply. At the time for winnowing wheat, there was a winnowing of heaps [?].
For the three brothers in Babylon did not flee from the fire that men kindled; therefore they were valiant. They had fled from lust; therefore they were perfect.
The fire of the victorious can whiten black kids within it. The fire of fools can turn lambs into a leopard with its spots.
How many must my laments be, that I should wail amid every bewilderment? How many must my livers be, to cook in every [?]? How many must my harvests be, to perish every month?
For my children’s sins he scourged me; through their struggle he rescued me. The people who rescue me are themselves the ones who scourge me. Stop the sins, and look, the scourges will stop.
In prosperity they are afflicted; in wrath they are crucified. In peace they are worn down, while everyone else finds relief. They denied grace; they repaid it on everyone’s behalf.

Their sackcloth is humble on my behalf; their ashes are scattered in my distress. Their prayer is for my victory; their fasting is for my deliverance. Look, the debt of my lowly people hangs upon my honored ones.
The fool in every generation is the master of the wise. The scribes and elders, in their zeal, killed the Master who taught all nations the law of Moses.
Wisdom in this age is material for loss. Someone who is a little ignorant has very little guilt; but someone who is a little cunning has guilt exceeding his measure.
They build with words and tear down with their conduct. Those who teach have multiplied and become insipid. It is the judge’s mouth that, in both cases, is judge and accuser.
Woe to us, for justice at the gate of the house of—[?]
Nisibis IX
[2. To the same tune.]
[Line missing] My afflictions [?]. As your righteousness delivered Job, may your grace have mercy on me.
There is a twofold benefit: that the righteous should not grow weary of asking, and that the rebellious should not increase their sinning.
You labored over the children, disciplining and helping them; and so that our fathers would not grieve at the sound of your scourge, they left me in peace.
Look, my Lord, at my outer bosoms, which have been cut off. See, my Lord, my inner bosoms, which are too weak to carry my beloved ones.
With swords they cut off my outer wings; fire also blazed in my inner bosoms—the frankincense of an old woman.
In the countryside the sun worshipers slaughtered my children; in the fortress the worshipers of Baal sacrificed my oxen, my sheep together with my children.
In my fields there is wailing; in my courtyards, dancing; in my vineyards, terror; in my streets, confusion. Who can meet my need?
The Evil One acted cunningly and stirred up confusion with his words. He caused bewilderment within, so that my entire inner condition would resemble my outer condition.
With what face, my Lord, can I call on you to send an army of holy ones to guard my bosoms, which are full of uncleanness?
With your new leaven you drew creation to yourself. The old leaven, which seduces and makes people shameless, resembles your leaven.
Let your power triumph in an open contest, lest my error should crown your athletes, for it depends on deception.
If we rust in our own time, this accords with our falseness, for in the years of the True One we practiced divination; we ourselves made invocations in secret.
When I look at the time, it provokes us and brings hidden things into the open, so that our falseness, which had been wrapped in truth, may be put to shame.
Truth truly exists and conquers everything. The sea, with all its bitterness, cannot cloud it, for it is clear by nature.
You acted wisely, my Lord: you disguised its terrors so that the child would not lose heart; and so that he would not grow overconfident, you concealed the crown.
On the trembling walls through which you had made me victorious, the ungrateful repaid you with sacrifice and libation that openly provoke your anger.
If sacrifices had been offered to my false gods at that time, there would have been grounds for thinking that I had been delivered through them.
Through the many deliverances I exposed both my error concerning carved idols and the teaching of the Magi, for it was through you, my Lord, that I was delivered.
Nisibis X
3. On the fortress of Enzit. To the same tune.
My children and my daughters outside me were killed. Their walls are uprooted, their children scattered, and their elders trampled underfoot.
Refrain: Blessed is your discipline.
The hunters drove my doves from my fortresses. They left their nests and fled to the sheltered places; there they caught them with a net.
Like wax melting before fire, the bodies of my children wasted away and melted from the heat and thirst in the fortresses.
Instead of the springs of milk that used to flow for my children and my little ones, milk failed the infants, and water failed the grown children.
The infant fell and writhed away from his mother; he could not groan, nor could she drink. They breathed their last and died.
How was your grace able to shut the channels of its springs, whose gushing streams cannot be restrained?
And how indeed did your grace shut off its compassion and withhold its springs from the people crying out to moisten their tongue?
There was a chasm between them and their brothers, like the rich man who cries out, with no one answering to moisten his tongue.
The weak lay as though thrown into a fire. The heat breathed fire within the thirsty and burned inside them.
Their bodies wasted away and melted from the heat. The thirsty turned to give the earth a drink with the moisture of their bodies.
The fortress that had killed its inhabitants with thirst turned to drink the discharge of the corpses that had wasted away from thirst.
Who has ever seen a people parched with thirst, surrounded by a wall of water, yet unable to moisten their tongue?
Was it with Sodom’s judgment that my beloved were judged, and were my children tormented with Sodom’s torment, which lasted only a single day?
Her torment by fire lasted only one hour, my Lord; with prolonged thirst came prolonged death and lingering torture.
After my mourning and my bitter sufferings, my Lord, is this another consolation with which you have comforted me—that you have increased my sorrow?
The medicine I awaited is certain pain; the bandage I looked to wants to cause me a bitter fracture.
And when I hoped to come up out of the storm, the harbor’s own storm was [?] for me than the one at sea.
In my misery I thought I had taken hold and climbed up out of the pit, but my sins threw me back into it again.
Look, my Lord, at my limbs: swords are crowded into me and lodged in my arms, and the marks of arrows are planted on my sides.
Tears are in the eyes, reports in the hearing ears, cries in the mouth, and mourning in the heart. Do not add to my suffering, my Lord.
Nisibis XI
4. To the same tune.
Your discipline is the mother of our childhood. Its rebuke is that of a compassionate mother who kept the children from playing, and they became wise.
Refrain: Glory to your justice!
Let us examine your justice—but who is equal to it?—and measure its benefits, for through it the shameless have become exceedingly modest.
Its hand has greatly cared for the sick, my Lord, for it is the hidden physician of their pains and the spring of their life.
The finger of your justice is very gentle; with love and compassion it touches the wounds of the one being healed.
Its incision is very gentle and welcome to the wise. Its sharp medicine, in his mighty love, consumed corruption.
His wrath is very fitting to the discerning. Its medicines are hateful to the fool who takes pleasure in the decay of his limbs.
Her bandaging closely follows her cutting. When she strikes, she shows compassion, so that through both she may bring about healing.
How fitting is his anger, and how pleasant her wrath! How sweet is her bitterness, which sweetens the bitter so that they become pleasant!
Your respite gives the slack a reason for idleness; your rod gives the sluggish a reason to seek profit, so that they become merchants.
Your justice is the reason for our diligence; your grace is the reason for our slackness, because our understanding is foolish.
Pharaoh became hardened because of your grace: whenever his punishments grew mild, his offenses grew severe, and he broke his promises.
Justice exacted payment from him, because he had repeatedly dealt falsely with her. Her freeborn sister, in turn, spared him, so that he would not rage again.
My Lord, rebuke my deceitful ways, for I am false like Egypt. My prayers plead that I have not become like her, because I have not abandoned your door.
My Lord, let your cross, which stood in my visible breaches, also fence off the hidden ones, lest enemies within breach me in place of those outside.
The sea burst forth and threw up a siege tower, over which I triumphed. Injustice surged and erected a shrine, through which I was put to shame; its libation choked me.
My persecutors heard my prayers upon my walls. The sun was put to shame in its magi and its worshipers, because I triumphed through your cross.
The creatures cried out when they saw the contest: truth fought against my error upon the trembling walls and was crowned.
The force of truth scourged my error. Through its scourging I became aware of it, and through its defeats I learned its victory.
It is a great terror to me that, after deliverance, the glorious and mighty ones who hovered over my altar built high places within me.
My Lord, even if my seven senses were springs of weeping, my tears would be too few to weep over our ruin.
The streets that once cried out in sackcloth and ashes are now in an uproar with revelry like that which took place in the wilderness before the calf.
The beauty of the lilies borrowed sackcloth and put it on. And the more their deceptive shoots were covered, the more it exposed their [?].
Nisibis XII
5. To the same tune.
In my afflictions I will call upon the power that conquers everything, for he can overcome the captor of wrath, just as he subdued Legion.
Refrain: Glory to his grace!
My brothers, the Evil One repaid me debts he had not borrowed from me; the Good One also repaid me mercies I had not lent him. Come, marvel at both!
The Good One divided and assigned my sins to his grace and my wrongdoing to his justice. His compassion blotted out my sins; his judgment exacted payment for my wrongdoing.
Sin became very angry and spent the night in turmoil, because it saw that grace had strengthened free will to overcome its stumbling.
Rage, my Lord, and pour out your love; be reconciled, and let your wrath overflow—your wrath to destroy, your love to take the captive away from the captor.
In the very days when the Evil One threatened to hurl me into destruction as though with a sling, the Good One bound up my soul and kept it in the bundle of life.
Let the rational beings who never cease giving thanks at all times, who guarded me amid the waves and supported me so that I would not fall, give thanks on my behalf, my Lord.
For who has ever been capable of giving thanks for the mercies surrounding him, that I should be capable of giving thanks for the mercies surrounding me?
Nisibis XIII
On Mar Jacob and his companions. To the tune of: “Wondrous, my Lord, is all that she endured.”

Three illustrious priests, patterned after the two lights, passed on and handed over to one another the throne, the hand, and the flock. Though our mourning for the two is great, the last is entirely a consolation.
Refrain: Glory to you, who chose them!
He who created the two lights chose three lights for himself and set them amid three dense periods of darkness that arose. Though the pair of lights went out, the remaining one is entirely radiant.
Our three priests are treasurers who faithfully hold the key of the Trinity. They opened three doors for us; each of them, with his own key, opened his door in his own time.

Through the first, he opened a door for the chastisement that came upon us. Through the middle one, he opened a door for the kingdom that came down to us. Through the last, he opened a door for the good news that comes up to us.

Through the first, he opened a door for the warfare of both armies. Through the middle one, he opened doors for kings of both spirits. Through the third, he opened a door for the envoys of both sides.
Through the first, he opened a door for war because of sins. Through the middle one, he opened a door for kings because of conflict. Through the last, he opened a door for envoys because of mercy.

See, in our three successive periods, as in a mystery and a symbol, wrath resembled the sun: it began in the time of the first, grew strong in the time of the middle one, and set and disappeared in the time of the last.

The sun, too, displays three patterns in three regions: its beginning is keen and bright, its middle is fierce and harsh, and its end is gentle and pleasant toward creation, which has been brought to completion.
Its beginning is light and bright, for it comes to awaken those who sleep. Its middle is hot and harsh, for it comes to ripen the fruit. Its end is lovely and pleasant, for it has reached completion.

Who is this daughter, this daughter of vows, envied by all women, whose successive generations have advanced so, whose orders have multiplied so, whose ranks have risen so, and whose teachers have excelled so?
Did these likenesses belong only to Abraham’s daughter, or to you, daughter of vows, whose adornment matches her beauty? For her help matched her time, and her minister matched her help.

To meet the lack caused by her need, the fulfillment of her need came to her. Her fathers matched her births, and her teachers matched her stages of understanding; her nurture matched her growth, and her garments matched her stature.

Grace weighed and gave all these things as though on a balance. She set them in due proportion so that help would come from them. She arranged them in succession so that completion would come from them.

In the days of the first, peace abounded, and peace came to an end. In the days of the middle one, kings came down and kings went up. In the days of the last, armies came in succession, and armies ceased.

Under the first, the orders entered; they entered with him and departed with him. Under the middle one, the crown that surrounded our churches drew near and withdrew. But under the last, grace that cannot be repaid came down to us.
Against the first wrath, the first offered his toil. Against the midday heat, the shade of the middle one stood firm. Against deceptive peace, the last increased his vigilance.
The first and victorious priest met the first siege; the second, merciful priest met the second siege. But the prayers of the last secretly fenced in our breaches.
Nisibis is planted beside waters, waters hidden and visible: living springs within her, a mighty river outside her. The river outside betrayed her; the spring within protected her.

The first priest, her cultivator, made her branches grow up into heaven. Now he has died and lies buried within her; he became fruit in her bosom. So when the woodcutters came, the fruit within her protected her.

The time for cutting her down had arrived; the one who had taken away her cultivator came. To keep him from bringing a charge against her, she hurried in her cunning: she placed her cultivator in her bosom, so that through her cultivator she might be delivered.

You daughters of Nisibis, endowed with speech, resemble Nisibis: she placed a body within her, and it became a wall outside her. A living body is placed within you, to become a wall protecting your lives.
Nisibis XIV
2. To the same tune.
The three shepherds had many concerns. The one mother in the city had daughters in every region. Wrath destroyed her monasteries; may peace rebuild her churches.
Response: Blessed is he who chose all three of them!

The good labor of the first bound up the land in its distress. The bread and wine of the middle one bandaged the city in its brokenness. The sweet speech of the last sweetened our bitterness in distress.

The first worked the land with toil, uprooting its brushwood and thorns. The middle one surrounded and fenced it in; he made the redeemed its hedge. The last opened his Lord’s treasury and sowed in it the words of its Lord.
Through fasting, the first priest closed the gates of mouths. For captives, the second priest opened the mouths of purses. But the last pierced ears and placed in them ornaments of life.
Aaron stripped ears of their earrings and made a calf. The dead calf secretly stabbed the camp and killed it. Those who fashioned its horns—it tore them apart with its horns.

But our third priest pierced the ears of the heart and put in them earrings that he fashioned from the nails that had been driven into the cross on which his Lord was crucified and brought his fellow servants to life.
Fire bore a son to Death; Death feeds on all bodies. The mortal who overcame death shepherded human souls. The calf left grass alone; thoughts became its pasture.
Grace bore a son to the first, murderous tree. O true offspring of the tree, who fought against its parent! The tree became a fountain of death; the cross became a fountain of life.
The son that Death had—all mouths are open to curse him. He swallowed bodies and souls and greatly increased his father’s disgrace. But the cross removed the shame of its father, the first tree.
Both sons resembled the mothers who bore them. The calf that fire bore increased fire among the people. The cross, the offspring of grace, distributed blessings to creation.
O my tongue, be still and leave unspoken the pressing accounts of the cross, which the mind suddenly conceived! Now their birth pangs strike it. It conceived them last, but they want to be firstborn.

The infants fought within the womb. The elder hurried to come out, and the younger, who loved the birthright, laid his hand on his heel. What he did not obtain by birth, he obtained through a cooked meal.

In the same way, the later accounts now clamor against the earlier ones, seeking to come out and take the birthright. Let us bring forth the account of our fathers, for the accounts of the cross are the firstborn of creation.

For if he who has no beginning is the firstborn of all creatures, his histories too are firstborn, older than created things. My Lord, let your histories make room for us to speak about your ministers.

The first was at the rank of a disciple, and his speech matched his rank. The middle one was at the second rank, but his teaching rose above his rank. The last, in the third generation, had speech that grew great like himself.
The first, through simple teachings, gave milk to his infancy. The middle one, through easy teachings, gave a taste to his childhood. The third, through mature teachings, gave food to his maturity.
She too, the daughter they raised, ascended step by step with her teachers and fathers. She was a little child with the first; she was simple with the middle one; she reached maturity with the third.

The first treated her like a little girl, showing her affection and making her afraid. The middle one treated her like a young girl, rebuking her and gladdening her. The last was gentle and kind to her, as to an educated woman.

The Most High too gave Jacob’s daughter persuasion and the rod in her childhood. For her boldness and youth he joined the sword with the law. Then he came to her gently and kindly, as to one trained and instructed.

The first, who fathered the flock, carried her infancy in his embrace. The middle one, cheerful in countenance, guarded her childhood and made it joyful. The last, grave in countenance, now instills modesty in her youth.
The first priest, who fathered her, gave milk to her infancy. The middle priest explained and gave a taste to her childhood. The third priest nourished her and gave food for her strength.

The diligent first father laid up treasures for her childhood. The middle one increased provisions for her journey toward maturity. The third, a magnificent olive tree, filled her vessels with abundant oil.

When she reaches the Rich One, she shows the treasure of the first. When she reaches the Savior, she shows those redeemed by the middle one. When she goes out to meet the Bridegroom, she shows the oil in her lamps.

Before him who rewards the weary, she presents the labor of the first. Before him who loves givers, she presents the almsgiving of the middle one. Before him who judges teachings, she presents the instruction of the last.

And as for the sinner who has labored, who was raised by all three of them: when they see the third one, whom the door of his bridal chamber has shut out, let all three plead for me, that he may open his door a little for me.
Let the sinner press in and enter, rejoicing and fearing for tomorrow. Let our three teachers graciously call one disciple, so that I may gather beneath the tables the crumbs that are full of life.
Nisibis XV
To the tune of “God, whom you have loved.”
Had the head not been upright, the members might have grumbled, for a crooked head throws the movement of the members into confusion. They would have laid the blame on the head.
Refrain: Blessed is he who chose you, the pride of our people.
If now, when he is entirely excellent, we pin our ugly deeds on him, how much more would we do so if he were ugly! Even God, though he is kind, has been assailed by bitter people.
The members became like the head. They acquired tranquility through his serenity, kindness through his gentleness, purity through his holiness, and learning through his wisdom.
They acquired good judgment through his meekness, modesty through his dignity, and harmony through his poverty. Since he is excellent in every respect, let us all be excellent with him in everything.
See how his words and deeds have measure and weight. Notice that even his steps have a quiet rhythm. He holds all the reins of his whole being.
He became master of his youth and yoked it under the yoke of chastity. His members did not grow unruly, for they were placed under the rod. His will was a stern master over him.
His rank ripened early, for his conduct had ripened early. Because he laid his foundations properly, he became a leader while still young, and they made him a herald to the people.
He was distinguished among the heralds and learned among the readers. He was eloquent among the wise, modest among his brothers, and honored among his friends.
In both dwellings he was a solitary throughout his days: he was holy within his body and solitary within his house. In private and in public he was chaste.
But although we, my brothers, have confused the measures and lost our sense of taste, we have become our own teachers in the perfection that has called us.
Yet the measure of truth preserves itself in his vessel. It chose him because it saw that he had chosen it; in him it preserved its fragrance and flavor from beginning to end.
A leader, modest and honorable, he did not grow angry and harsh. He did not become undisciplined like us. He set limits and kept his proper measures, and placed bridles on his thoughts.

He provided an example in his own person: just as he observed the measure proper to his time of life, we ought to have recognized our own time. We ourselves have become strangers to our time, for we have become tasteless at the season for flavor.
At first the blowing wind disciplines the fruit in its unripeness, and in the middle comes the sun’s fierce heat. When its harshness has passed, its final stage gathers it into sweetness.
The first disciplined us, and those in the middle also rebuked us; the last added sweetness to us. Yet when our flavor ripened, our tastelessness increased.
For we came to maturity to stop children from playing and bring them to seriousness. Yet our old age has come to need people to rebuke us as though we were children.
Therefore, gentle one, be firm, but do not resort to compulsion. Let us honor our old age all the more; and if it does not recognize its rank, let the one who knows its proper season grow greater.
And if someone says that compulsion and the rod govern the little one, fear governs the thief, threats govern the plunderer, and public exposure governs the contemptuous—
If the members of the second rank had run with the head of the first rank, they would have drawn along the third, and the entire body would have followed them.

Those of the second rank despised those of the first, and those of the third despised those of the second. The ranks were held in contempt by one another. Because those within despised one another, those outside also trampled on them.
Nisibis XVI
2. To the same tune.
In this respect the mirror is blameworthy: if its clarity is dimmed because there are stains on its surface, the dirt upon it becomes a covering before those who look into it.
Refrain: Blessed is he who polished our mirror.
No beauty is adorned in it, and no blemish is shown as ugly in it. It is nothing but disappointment for the beautiful, whose beauties gain no adornments as profits.
Blemishes are not removed in it, nor do adornments increase in it. A blemish that remains is a disappointment; an adornment that does not come into being is a loss. Disappointment has met with loss.
If our mirror is dark, it is nothing but joy for the ugly, because their blemishes are not reproved. But if it is polished and bright, it is our free will that must adorn itself.
Disappointment joined with loss has been doubled for the ugly and the beautiful: neither have the beautiful been crowned, nor have the ugly been adorned. The mirror has distributed disappointment.
The mirror has never compelled anyone who looks into it. Nor does the grace that came after the justice of the law possess the law’s compulsion.
Justice was an adorner of childhood through compulsion. For humanity was a child, and justice adorned it through compulsion, without depriving it of its freedom.
Justice held persuasion and the rod ready for childhood. Whenever its blows disturbed childhood, its rod restrained insolence, while its persuasion soothed minds.
[?] that we may be adorned today, my brothers. With another way of thinking, he is a child at the time of mature understanding; he becomes a person without understanding.
For at the stage of maturity he has descended into infancy. He loves that law for slaves, which strikes him when he grows bold and beats him when he grows merry.
All adornment imposed by force is not genuine, for it is borrowed. This is great in God's eyes: that a person should adorn himself of his own accord. Therefore he removed compulsion.
For just as he wisely gave compulsion at its proper time, so he wisely removed it at the time when humility was required in its place.
For as fitting as it is for childhood to run beneath the rod, it is utterly unfitting for wisdom to be enslaved beneath the rod, with compulsion as its master.
Look, then, at how God also ordered the stages of my life through the shepherds I had, the teachers he gave me, and the fathers he appointed for me.
The benefits of their different ways were measured to suit their times: when fear was right, when encouragement was suitable, and when gentleness was fitting.
He guided the stages of my life in due measure. To my childhood he granted dread, and to my youth, fear. To my wisdom and discernment he granted and gave gentleness.
In the insolence and stage of childhood, I had a stern guardian. His rod kept me from captivity, his severity from wrongdoing, and the fear of him from pampering.
He gave another father to my youth. Where something of childhood remained in me, there was something of severity in him; where something of old age was in me, there was humility in him.
When I rose beyond the stages of childhood and youth, the first dread passed away, and the second fear passed away. He gave me a gentle shepherd.
Here is his nourishment for my maturity, his explanations for my wisdom, his humility for my quietness, his gentleness for my tranquility, and his dignity for my modesty.
Blessed is he who weighed out fathers for me as though on a balance and gave them to me: my helpers suited to my times, my medicines suited to my pains, and my adornments suited to my beauties.
It is we, then, who have disturbed the succession and its beautiful order, since at a time for gentleness we now seek severity to rebuke us as though we were children.
Nisibis XVII
On Abraham, bishop of Nisibis. To the tune of “The Infants Were Slain.”
Allow my lowliness too, my Lord, to cast its small coin into your treasury, like the merchant of our flock who increased the talent of your teaching, set sail, and departed for your harbor.
I will speak about his entry into office, when he became head of the flock. He was the disciple of three; he became the fourth teacher. Blessed is he who made him our consolation.
With one love I will blend them together, and weave them into a crown—the splendid flowers and fragrant blossoms of that teacher and his disciple.
He remained after him like Elisha. The horn of his election overflowed; he was consecrated and became head. He was exalted and became a teacher. Blessed is he who made him chief.
The honored members of the flock rejoiced in the shepherd who tends those who tended him. The fold of rams rejoiced when they saw the succession of their ranks. He took his place like the mind
within the great body of the church. Its members surround him to draw life from him—teaching, fresh bread. Blessed is he who made him their storehouse.

He chose him from the multitude of rams, for he had given proof of his faithfulness. Time examined him within the flock, and long years tested him like a furnace, for he had given proof in his own person.
He made him a wall for many. May your fasting be a weapon for our land, your prayer a barrier for our city. May your censer obtain reconciliation. Blessed is he who sanctified your sacrifices.
The shepherd who departed from his flock pastured it in spiritual meadows, and with his victorious staff guarded it from hidden wolves. May you fill your master's place for it,
which thirsts for the sound of his songs. He established you like a pillar in the city of the trembling people. May we be supported by your prayers. Blessed is he who made you our pillar.
His hand handed over to his disciple the throne, to the one worthy of it; the key, to the one entrusted with it; the axe, to the one who proved victorious. The hovering of your hand is fitting,

and forgiveness for your offering, and consolation for your tongue. May peace adorn your authority: the angels within and the congregations outside. Blessed is he who chose you for joyful celebrations.
May your teaching excel in deeds far more than in words. You sow few words; cultivate our land with deeds, so that through abundant cultivation
the scanty seed may become plentiful. [?] May the old seed yield thirtyfold among us, and your new seed sixtyfold. Blessed is he who multiplies a hundredfold.
Anger is idle in your presence, for peace is imprinted upon your whole being. The jealous person is quenched in your presence, for your love is always ablaze. You have broken the sting of envy,
so that it may not strike anyone in secret. Your hearing does not turn toward slander that causes confusion, for open truth delights you. Blessed is he who adorned your members.
May you give counsel among your people: there is a Jethro among the Hebrews. May you go wholeheartedly with whoever counsels you for your benefit. May you flee wholeheartedly from whoever
counsels you otherwise. Let Rehoboam be an example to you: choose counsels that help, and reject counsels born of envy. Blessed is he who counseled understanding.
The gift given to you flew down from on high. Do not call it by a human name; do not attribute it to another power, for no one could reach its dwelling place.
Crafty Satan suggests that human beings gave it to you, so that this freeborn gift might serve human beings in slavery. Blessed is he who sent his gift down.
Your master was portrayed in your person: look, his likenesses are upon your whole being. One has departed from us; one is with us. In you may we see all three victorious men who departed
from us. Be a wall for us like Jacob, full of mercy like Babu, and a treasury of words like Vologeses. Blessed is he who portrayed them in one.
I too, the weakling of the flock, do not shirk my duty. I painted a portrait of both of them with the colors of both, so that the sheep might see their adornments,
and the flock their beauties. Because I have become a speaking lamb, I will give thanks to you, the God of Abraham, in Abram's presence. Blessed is he who made me his lyre.
Nisibis XVIII
To the same tune.

O you who ministered as priest after your master, the pure one after the victorious one, the chaste one after the honored one, the watchful one after the fasting one: your master has not departed from you. In the living man

we have seen the departed one, for his likenesses are portrayed in you and his footprints are marked in you. His whole being has shone out from your whole being. Blessed is he who gave you to us in his place.
O fruit in which its tree is portrayed, proclaiming its root! The tastes of his sweetness have not yet been scraped away from us. You showed his words in bodily form,
for you fulfilled them in deeds. His teaching is portrayed in your conduct, its explanation in your actions, and its interpretation in your perfection. Blessed is he who made your purity triumphant.
O late-born one who grew great and became the head of his members, the younger one who received the birthright—not for a price like Jacob, nor through zeal like Aaron, whom they envied.
In him, his brothers the Levites [?]. In love he bore it like Moses, though he was older than Aaron. Your brothers rejoiced in you as he did. Blessed is he who chose you in concord!
There is no envy or jealousy among the limbs of the body. They obey the head in love and are cared for by it with compassion. The head is the guardian of the limbs,
looking in every direction. It is exalted, yet humble in its compassion: it lowers itself even to the heels to remove harm from them. Blessed is he who mingled your love within us!
This would have been a small thing: for paganism to be defeated through an old man. Old age lay down in its wisdom; youth triumphed in its season. The young athlete
bore the hateful contest of the raging storm, full of paganism, which rose fiercely like smoke and passed away. Its end came with its beginning. Blessed is he who blew upon it, and it vanished!
Suddenly the sound of the horn startled you and called you to battle. You entered like David once more, and a second Goliath was defeated by you. Your combat was no ordinary one,
for every day you drew up your ranks against the Evil One in a hidden battle. Hidden training is accustomed to bring a visible crown. Blessed is he who chose you, our boast!
Before his trial, Job trained his body and mind, and in his trial he triumphed. Joseph conquered in the bedchamber; Hananiah and his companions in the furnace;
and Daniel in the pit. Satan acted foolishly: after testing the strength of their victory in secret, he went on to be defeated openly. Blessed is he who increased his disgrace!
The farmer who turned to paganism kept sowing thorns with his left hand. The righteous farmer was stirred to zeal against him and lopped off his left hand. He filled his right hand and sowed
living words in the heart. See, our mind is cultivated by his prophets and also by his apostles. May our souls be cultivated through you. Blessed is he who chose you as our farmer!
Even if your words are few, cultivate our soil through deeds, so that through abundant cultivation the stalk and root may grow strong. A good deed is better than
hearing ten thousand words. May your seed yield a hundredfold, the late-sown crop sixtyfold, and the aftergrowth thirtyfold. Blessed is he who increased your harvests!
It is not fitting for light to grow dim, nor right for salt to lose its flavor. A stain does not suit the head, nor dirt a mirror. For if medicines lose their potency,
illnesses are not healed. And if the lamp is dim, occasions for stumbling multiply. May your light drive away our darkness. Blessed is he who made you our lamp!
Appoint scribes and judges for yourself, collectors and distributors, stewards and caretakers. Entrust each one with his task, lest a morsel corrupt
it and a thought defile it—the [?], together with the tongue with which you offer supplication for the forgiveness of all the people. Blessed is he who makes your ministry pure!
However clear the mind becomes, and however pure the tongue; however thoroughly the hands are cleansed and the whole body purified—it is little for the priest and his title,
for he offers the living body. Let him be wholly pure at all times, since he stands as a mediator between God and humanity. Blessed is he who purified his ministers!
Nisibis XIX
By the same author. To the same tune.
You have fulfilled the name Abraham, for you have become a father to many. Yet you have no wife like Sarah was to Abraham. See, your flock is your wife. Raise
her children in your truth. May they be children of the Spirit to you, sons who are children of the promise, so that in due time they may become heirs. Blessed is he who portrayed you in Abraham!
Beautiful fruit of chastity, the priesthood has adorned itself with you! Youngest of his brothers, like the son of Jesse, the horn brimmed over and anointed you; the hand hovered and chose you.
The Church has longed for you and loved you: a pure altar for your ministry, a great throne for your honor, and all of them together for your crown. Blessed is he who has made your crowning glorious.
Here is your flock, blessed one! Rise and visit it, diligent one. Jacob used to arrange flocks; arrange the sheep endowed with speech, and guide the male virgins in purity,
and the female virgins in chastity. Appoint priests in purity, leaders in humility, and the common people in righteousness. Blessed is he who has filled you with understanding.
Protect the healthy sheep, visit the sick one, bind up the broken one, and seek out the lost one. Shepherd it in the pastures of the Scriptures,
and give it the springs of instruction to drink. May truth be your wall; may the cross be your staff; and may righteousness be your peace. Blessed is he who has multiplied your victories.
May the strength that was with David be with you among your flock. For if he snatched a passing lamb from the lion’s mouth, how much more ought you, victorious one,
to act zealously and rescue from the evil one a soul more precious than everything, which cannot be bought with anything except the blood of Christ! Blessed is he who was sold and purchased everyone.
Joshua served Moses, and as the reward for his service he received his right hand. Because you served the venerable elder, he too gave you his right hand. Moses entrusted to Joshua
a flock half of which were wolves; but to you has been entrusted a flock whose quarter and third are holy. Blessed is he who has adorned your flock.
May the love of Moses dwell in you, for his love was a discerning love, and his zeal an understanding zeal. When Korah and Dathan caused division, he split the earth beneath them.
With a split he put an end to division. Through Eldad and Medad he made known that his whole desire was this: that all the people should prophesy. Blessed is he who was pleased with his desire.
Elisha loved Elijah’s poverty more than wealth. The poor man gave the poor man a gift greater than everything. Because you loved the neediness of your master,
who was rich in secret, may you pour forth the fountain of his words. May you become a lyre for the Spirit, and may she sing her wishes to you through you. Blessed is he who made you his treasurer.
No one envies your election, because your leadership is humble. No one is angered by your rebuke, because your word sows peace. No one fears your voice, because gentle
is your authority. No one complains about your yoke, because it labors on behalf of our necks and lightens the burden of our souls. Blessed is he who chose you for our rest.
Do not behave lightly toward the great; do not neglect the weak. Persuade and instruct the rich; encourage and win over the poor. Pair a gentle person with a harsh one, and a patient
person with an angry one. Catch the wicked through the good, plunderers through the generous, and the impure through the holy. Blessed is he who chose you as our fisherman.
Take countless medicines with you, rise, and walk among the illnesses. Administer medicine to the sick and protection to the healthy. Do not administer just one medicine
for an ailment, lest it prove unsuitable. Offer many remedies so that the ailment may be healed and you too may gain experience. Blessed is he who has labored over our wounds.
May we be soil for your will; may we be a vineyard for your labor. May we be a flock within your fold, and healthy sheep beneath your staff. May you be a great head,

and we the jewels of your crown. May we be beautiful through you, and you beautiful through us, for people and priest adorn one another when they are in harmony. Blessed is he who sowed harmony among us.

Listen to the apostle as he speaks to this virgin whom he had betrothed: “I am jealous for you with a jealousy—the jealousy of God,” he says. Be zealous not with the zeal of the flesh, but with that of the Spirit.
In her, you too, purely [?], so that she may know that she is from me and whose she is. Through you may she love and cherish Jesus, her true bridegroom. Blessed is he whose zeal is holy!
Her conduct follows that of her leaders: with a lax leader she is lax, and with one who is radiant she is glorious. The Church resembles a mirror: just like the face of the one looking into it,
so she wears his likeness. As the king is, so is his army; as the priest is, so is his flock. Through them she is stamped with their likeness. Blessed is he who stamped her with his likeness!
Those three glorious priests died without a will, though they meditated on these two Testaments of God. They left us a great benefit: that
example of poverty. Because those blessed men acquired nothing, they made us their possessions. Their church became their treasure. Blessed is he who acquired his possessions through them!
With the glorious priest Jacob she became glorious like him. Because he joined his love to his zeal, she clothed herself in reverence and love. Under Babu, who loved charitable giving, with silver
she redeemed captives. Under Vologeses, the teacher of the Law, she opened her heart to the Scriptures. But through you may her benefits increase! Blessed is he who made her merchants great!
Nisibis XX
To the same tune.
O virgin who has become a bridegroom, turn your thoughts with a little zeal toward the wife of your youth. Cut off the attachments she formed in her childhood toward many others.

Rebuke her and gather her thoughts, so that she may know who she is and whose she is. Through you may she be zealous and love Christ, the true bridegroom. Blessed is he who betrothed her to his Only Begotten!
Farmer, be zealous against the weeds that have branched out and become entangled among the wheat. The thicket is easy to uproot, for its growth comes from neglect. If the seed receives a little air,
it grows bold and overcomes it. Since three farmers sowed it, may it yield in three measures: thirty, sixty, and a hundredfold. Blessed is he who enriches your harvests!
A new shepherd ought to inspect the flock afresh, know its number, and see what it needs—the flock purchased with the blood of that
chief of shepherds. Call each sheep by name and have it pass before you, from that flock whose name and number are written in the book of life. Blessed is he who requires an account of its number!

Look, your Lord’s betrothed is with you. Guard her from every harm and from people who have corrupted congregations and called them by their own names. Place upon her the name of her betrothed, so that she may not

commit adultery with another name. For she was not baptized in the name of a human being. Let her confess the names in which she was baptized: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Blessed is he by whose name she was called!
The apostle who betrothed her was jealous for her, lest she be corrupted by names—not merely false names, but not even true ones: neither by Peter’s nor by his own,
for they were faithful agents of betrothal. They placed upon her the name of her betrothed. The false ones, like adulterers, placed their own names upon the flock. Glory to your name, our Creator!
My brothers, no one openly tampers with the brand on livestock, and no one adds or changes a name in a sealed document. Whoever damages a brand is a thief,

and whoever changes a name is a forger. Christ’s name has been replaced: look, false names have been placed upon the congregations that have been corrupted. Blessed is he who called his flock by his own name!
Look at the prophets and the apostles, how closely they resemble one another. The prophets placed God’s name upon God’s flock, and the apostles placed Christ’s name
upon Christ’s Church. The false ones resemble one another: the congregations that have committed adultery with them are called by their names. Blessed is he in whose name we have been sanctified!
Nisibis XXI
To the same tune.
