John, who was a lamp, exposed and rebuked the shameless. They hurried to extinguish the lamp, wanting to pour out their lust. Be a brightly shining torch,
and put an end to the deeds of darkness. For as long as your teaching shines, no one dares to serve the desire of darkness in its light. Blessed is he who made you our torch!
A great blessing lay hidden in Elijah’s rebuke. Elisha served him and asked for a double reward for his service. It gave him a double measure of beauty,
so that he was clothed twofold in its victories. Because you loved his poverty, [?] your rich master, you will inherit the treasury of his wisdom. Blessed is he who enriches your teaching!
May gluttony be defeated by your fasting, as it was by Daniel’s fasting. May lust be put to shame before your body, as it was put to shame before Joseph. May the desire for money be defeated by you,
as it was defeated before Simon. May you bind on earth as he did, and loose in heaven as he did, for your faith is like his. Blessed is he who entrusted his ministry to you!
Your chastity is like Elisha’s, and your virginity like Elijah’s. You have a covenant with your eyes like Job’s, compassion like David’s, and freedom from envy like Jonathan’s.

Your firmness is Jeremiah’s; your gentleness is that of the apostles. Yours are the old things of the prophets; yours are the new things of the apostles. Blessed is he who filled you from their treasuries!
May you be a crown for the priesthood, and may the ministry shine through you. May you be a brother to the priests and an overseer of the deacons. May you be a teacher to children, a staff

and a helping hand to the elderly. May you be a wall for chaste women. May the covenant community flourish through your standing, and may the church be adorned with your beauty. Blessed is he who chose you to serve as priest!

Through your poverty may the hateful custom of Gehazi’s household be abolished. Through your severity may the unclean custom of Eli’s household disappear. Through your harmony may the greeting also lose its force—
the deceitful greeting of our lips, that of the treacherous Iscariot. Melt down all our thinking and shape it anew from the beginning. Blessed is he who refines us in your furnace!

May Mammon, who became master over our freedom, be put to shame through your standing. May the sickness that has become habitual among us, and that we find pleasant, be removed from us. Remove the causes that have taken hold of habits
full of harm. Habit has gained us for evil; establish us in goodness through habit. My lord, be the cause of our help. Blessed is he who chose you for our life!
Let evil customs be cut off. Let the church acquire no possessions, so that it may be free to gain souls—and if it is free, that is a marvel! Let the dead [?] not be buried
in hopelessness, in pagan fashion, with garments, lamentation, and dancing: the living person wears a tunic, while the dead person is a whole cloud. Blessed is he who returns us to our dust!

Desire, the cause of evil, and the gluttony of Eli’s household, the thievery of Gehazi’s household, and the insulting behavior of Nabal’s household—stop up these hateful springs, so that there may not
be a great outpouring and turmoil arise from it, so that even you are reached by its spray. May our Lord stop up their springs. Blessed is he who dried up their sources!
Entrust speech to the old man; assign silence to the young man, so that a stranger who comes to you may learn about you from your orderly conduct: who speaks first,
and who second and third, whether everyone guards his mouth, and whether everyone knows his rank. They will call you blessed. May our Lord fulfill your desire!
Let the voice of your truth be one, but your borrowed voices beyond number. Let the image of truth be upon your heart, and every likeness upon your face: sorrowful, cheerful, and feeble.
Show the one who has done wrong that you are angry; show the modest person that you are glad. Be one toward God, and many toward humanity. Blessed is he who became all things with everyone!
If you hear bad news from trustworthy people who do not mislead, pour out tears; extinguish the fire that has broken out among others. Let discerning people pray with you.
And prescribe a fast for those who understand. Let your monastery mourn for the one who has been lost through sin, so that he may return in repentance. Blessed is he who found the lost sheep.
Do not lend your ear to everyone, lest liars mislead you. Do not lend your feet to everyone, lest frivolous people distract you. Do not entrust yourself to everyone, lest
the insolent trample you. Keep your hand away from the deceitful person, lest he gather thorns with your hand. Be distant and near. Blessed is he who is near even when distant.

Look, news of the new king comes thundering through the world. It has become encouragement to the plundered and terror to the plunderers. The time for the greedy to disgorge has arrived, so that they may give back

everything they swallowed. Let them also tremble before you, those of the priest's household [?] the righteous king. At the remembrance of former things [?], let them choke. Blessed is he who became angry and then showed mercy again.

One person found an opportunity and acted recklessly; another struggled and restrained his inclination. One considers that judgment is reserved for him, while another thinks that it will not even happen. One stole and quenched his thirst, and another
stole and thirsted to steal. The rich stole, and so did the poor; but the hungry stole in measure, while those who were full stole without measure. Blessed is he who examines every will.

But now he has given an opportunity, and everyone has shown his will: what it is like, whom he resembles, and what he chose for himself in preference to what. He obtained proof from everyone, so that [?]

he might deny that he had not even been hateful [?]. He gave us an opportunity to recognize that restraint is far more helpful than this freedom of action. Blessed is he who rebukes us for our benefit.
For he does not wish to put his yoke on our necks by force. He gave us freedom, and we grew arrogant, so that [?], when we rebelled and suffered harm, we might love his light yoke
and choose his gentle rod. Our ease has wearied us greatly, for in his constraint there is rest, and in his yoke there is lightness. Blessed is he whose labor is delight.
The whole world, like a body, had fallen gravely ill. Through the fever of paganism it grew hot, became sick, and collapsed. The right hand of mercy felt it
and gently massaged its soul. Paganism, which was the cause of its illness, quickly ceased. It shook itself, sweated, and recovered. Glory to the hand that cared for it.
May the earth have peace in your days, for it has seen that you are full of peace. Through you may churches be built and clothed in their adornments, and may their books be opened within them,
and their tables be set in order. May their ministers shine, and may thanksgiving rise from them as firstfruits to the Lord of peace. Blessed is he who revives our [?].
May your prayer rise to heaven, and may reconciliation rise with it. May the Lord of heaven rain down his good gifts upon our wickedness, and his consolations upon our afflictions,

and his gathering upon our scattering. May he stir up his zeal together with his love. May his justice call our disgrace to account; may his grace blot out our wrongdoing. Blessed is he who blesses his flock.

For the former priest and king were portrayed as resembling one another, and Vologases and the king's son were likewise balanced as though in the pans of a scale, because they were humble. And in these things
may their successors resemble one another. May the priests be luminous, and those who walk [?] be rays of light, and the judges shining beams. Blessed is he who has enlightened our souls.
From kingship come laws, and from priesthood forgiveness. For both to yield is undesirable; for both to be stern is harsh. Let one be stern and the other
be gentle, with understanding and discernment. Let fear be mingled with mercy. May our priesthood be gentle, and our kingship strong. Blessed is he who blends together the things that help us.
Let the priests pray for kings, that they may be a wall protecting humanity. From kings comes victory, and from priests, faith. Through victory let bodies be protected, and through faith—
souls. Let kings put an end to fighting, and priests put an end to disputes, so that contention and strife may cease. Blessed is the birth of him who brings peace to all! Glory to you for your gift!
Nisibis XXV
[To the tune of “The heavenly King calmed its turmoil.”
Your parable persuades you, my Lord—the one you told about the widow. She pressed the judge, that merciless rock; she coaxed and softened that unyielding iron.
He is good: he goes out to meet whoever seeks him. Before anyone looks toward him, he has turned wholly toward that person; before anyone reaches his door, he has opened his treasury for them.]
Nisibis XXVI
[II. To the same tune.]
[?] / [?] / Through you they provoked me to anger; through you they can also reconcile me.
May I be crowned, modest and fostering modesty, with my children within my embrace and my enemies outside me. Let whoever is sick recover, and cleanse them of weeds.
O Physician, show your wisdom in my limbs. Fit together and firmly attach those that have been cut off from my body, so that to those who see them they may seem never to have been severed.
The evil one rejoiced in my defects and gloated over my limbs. Add to them a beauty that torments his ugliness. Let him regret the trouble he took when he sees how beautiful I have become.
Suffering befell me through his temptation, so that we might not repeat it. I was hurt when I was cut apart and they were severed. Let us take care in our final recovery not to fall sick again.
I and they will give you thanks every day, because you let us go and taught me suffering through trial, and you gathered us together and gave me love through testing.
Pray also for me, the weak one, O Church. As I suffered at your division, may I rejoice at your reunion, and with you may I enter the kingdom under your protection.
Nisibis XXVII
III. To the same tune.
My Lord, it is easy for a physician to cut off a limb, but it is not easy for him to attach it again in its place. Both are easy for you, my Lord, because you are God.
Refrain: Hear the cry of my children.

For twelve years the physicians exposed that woman, whose bleeding they exposed without helping her. Even if they had healed her, it would have been a disgrace; how much more so, since they did not heal her!

As much as they exposed her, you preserved her modesty and healed her. Keeping herself concealed, she approached your garment, not your body. A garment that preserves everyone's modesty became her physician.

How much more, my Lord, should you preserve the modesty of your Church, now that she has been disgraced! Even passersby have turned aside to look at her shame. You preserved the modesty of a passing woman, but exposed your own betrothed.
The duration of my wound does not even compare with hers. It is six years old, half the years of that woman's affliction. Heal this new pain, you who healed the old one.

If you have let me go and abandoned me because I have become a little ugly, how hateful to you, my Lord, is the man who despises his wife because she is ugly! Love me in my ugliness, and teach him to love his wife.
It was you who made Leah beautiful when she was ugly. Her eyes were weak, but her children were very beautiful. As for me, my Lord, although you are beautiful, my children make me ugly.
You alone and your mother are more beautiful than all others. There is no blemish in you, my Lord, and no stain in your mother. Which of these two beauties do my children resemble?

When your Father took the hateful congregation, which prostituted itself with that calf, that hateful one went in and fathered her offspring; that is, they bear the imprint of the stranger’s likeness.
For look, it is through his symbol that they stab the faithful—Moses and the prophets, whom they stabbed in every age. You, my Lord, know what they did to you.
The apostle betrothed me to you, my Lord, as a pure virgin. I hated the calf of my ancestors, my Lord, and loved you. Let my children, the sheep, not stab their brothers.

They come from the Lamb who was tried and did not speak, who was slaughtered and did not protest, who was crucified and did not complain, and who returned alive and labored to give life to his killers.
It was not Adam who fathered you, who acted presumptuously and unjustly, and whose son killed his brother without judgment or cause. You are children of the Spirit, children born of water.

I will also tell you what happened to me: they stoned me, and I did not become angry; they crucified me, and I did not revile them; they burned me, and I did not curse them. Resemble your Lord, and take after your mother.
Human beings were called offspring of vipers, not because of their natures but because of their deeds, for the bitterness of free choice surpasses that of a viper.
Likewise, human beings were called gods, not by their essential being but by grace. But for you I established kinship with him.
It is a wonder that God himself became your kinsman, yet you have cut yourselves off from kinship with him. For if he is a creature, then you have become kin to a slave.
Praise to you, my God, for you did not establish our kinship with created things, but with your very self. Lord of all creatures, glory to your union with us!
For it is no wonder if we become kin to created things, since we share the same servitude. Blessed is the Lord who wished his servants to become his kin!
Nisibis XXVIII
To the same tune.
If natural things, my Lord, are ugly in their diseases, hideous in their afflictions, and repulsive in their defects, yet desirable in their fruit and lovely in their beauty—
Refrain: Bring my children to peace quickly.
How much more, then, should human beings feel their pains, grieve over their sorrows, and be ashamed of their blemishes, since their sins have become the cause of their scourges!
Branches that have split have ugly scars, and cracks are ugly even when thoroughly filled. How much more repulsive, my Lord, if they remain like this!

The garment tore itself, and you returned and mended it. It went back and repeated its tears, and once more you repaired it. It was soaked in your blood, my Lord, and healed, yet it rebelled against you.
Is there still hope that my cracks will be filled? Although they are blind, my Lord, they grope for you and seek you. Although they stumbled and fell, they thought they had remained close to you.

Show yourself to them, our Light, for they seek you. Those who stumbled fell while thinking that they were standing firm. Bend down and show, my Lord, that it was toward the fallen that you bent down.

For [?] years my children have been separated from me and are no more. Women have buried their children and forgotten their mourning for them. My children have not been forgotten, because my dead have not been buried.
Do not let your zealous servants rebuke me, my Lord. Let them not reproach me for weeping over my dead while they are alive. If only they had departed from me in death rather than in life!

If only I had tended them, laid my hands over their eyes, accompanied them with psalms, and entrusted myself to the Giver of life to all, so that at the resurrection he would return them to me and I would see them!
But no, my Lord: look, I mourn for them on both counts. Whoever died on the road was buried in a foreign land, while those who died in their dwellings became outcasts in their [?].
Grant, my Lord, the living among them the resurrection of repentance, and multiply songs of praise for their dead. Let us rejoice over their living and accompany their bodies in procession.
Let us learn to mourn from the cry of the cow and the ewe, which bellow because their lost young are no longer there, as though they themselves, my Lord, were lost with the lost.

And if their young are found and return, they rejoice and exult again, as though they themselves, my Lord, had been found and returned. How afraid I am that you may put me to shame through the animals!
You greatly reproached the foolish synagogue, my Lord, through the locust and the swallow, which observe their appointed seasons. To put free will to shame, you praised the bird.
Nisibis 29
5. To the same tune.
Our Lord, you wept with tears over Jerusalem, the mother of crucifiers, whose children were united within her. Have mercy on your church, whose children are divided within her. Refrain:
Have mercy on me, for I have become a disgrace before the outsider.
Those who would have benefited from being divided against one another were united in purpose. But my children, who ought to have agreed in one love, have divided the one truth.
The serpents that devour their brothers united and loved their companions. But my lambs became wolves toward their brothers and attacked the shepherd within.
You said that you would gather Jerusalem, using the image of a mother gathering her chicks beneath her wings. May your truth, my Lord, gather my children beneath my wings.
You comforted Samuel when the fools rejected him, because in him the people rejected you. Your church, my Lord, is represented in you: when they rejected your priest, my children hated me in him.
Because you knew that it was a time of abuse, you did not give me a young shepherd, tall and handsome, since such abuse would readily attach itself to youth.
Through an old man they insult me; through a chaste man they disgrace me. Yet nature itself, my Lord, does not allow an abusive accusation to be readily brought against old age.
They cannot fast with him or keep vigil with him—that old man whose wakefulness exhausts the young. My prayer, my Lord, is that they come to be compared with him.

He is poor, but they are rich; he is peaceable, but they are quarrelsome; he is gentle, but they are violent; he is humble, but they are unjust. Perhaps through his humility they became insolent and exalted themselves.
Toward a man full of mercy they were merciless, my Lord. They dishonored their father and disgraced their mother. Through that old man they made me an old woman subjected to insults.
Who would not weep at what my end has become? My youth was honored, but my old age has been dishonored. My children have cheapened me, and I have become a disgrace before the crucifiers.
My upright ones departed and went away, leaving me to mockery. Because of them the pagans danced before my face. Today everyone points a finger at me.
Look, my champions have been taken away, my perfect and victorious ones, who made me crowned and envied throughout the world. I who was renowned have become an object of reproach.
Each one, through his conduct, honored me with victories. Pagans and outsiders honored me because of them. But today, my Lord, look: even my own people despise me.
Where have my chaste ones gone, those victorious in their fasts, constant in good works, diligent in their deeds? That flavor is gone, because that salt is gone.
Through one of them a king could be appeased, and through two the King of kings could be comforted and rejoice. You chose them and took them, one by one, for your offering.
My workers gathered my fruit, perfect and delicious. Its flavor was truth, and its sweetness was love. Today my fruit has become tasteless, because winter has lingered over me.
A hidden and hateful winter, with its snows and its frosts, blighted the blossom from the moment it sprouted. It is sick in its teaching and diseased from its beginning.
The beauty of the leaves of that time has surpassed and outdone today’s fruits. The unripe fruit of those earlier times is far dearer than today’s harvest.
The winters became summers and lost their proper order. The fruits stood bewildered, and their flavor was spoiled by worms. What grew plump ripened rotten; what ripened early was utterly tasteless.
The late fruit, the last to come, winter’s kinsman, surpasses and outdoes in fragrance and flavor this fruit of today that ripened in summer.
My winepresses are full, and wine overflows, but it does not ferment. Like wine that is not new, its love is quiet and feeble. Both new wine and old deceive me, my Lord.
New wine ferments, while aged wine is mellow. The wine of this generation deceives me in both respects: its love does not ferment, and its flavor is not mellow.
Instead of fermenting with sweetness, as it should, it boils only with fury, for anger turns it sour. You alone now know what the outcome will be.
I do not complain, my Lord, that winter has lasted so long. The north wind blew fiercely, and through it the south grew cold. The very north wind that brings clear weather made clouds gather over me.
Just as the disciples woke you in the midst of the sea, and you arose and stopped the storm with your voice, hear, my Lord, the voice of the tears that wake you every day.
It is written, my Lord, that you came from the south and melted the ice of the Egyptians, and the people budded and blossomed. Hurry and bring a joyful summer that will gladden us.
In it may my fruits ripen; in it may my seeds grow plump. In it may my days become fair; in it may my sufferings pass away. In it may my mourning end, and in it may my festivals resound.
May my fruits increase a hundredfold through your grace, so that this very gain may come as interest to the land whose harvest ceased during winter.
There was a hidden famine: the grain of truth dwindled, and the bread of love grew scarce. In their hunger, people were scattered in every direction and cast to every side.
For anyone who desires it, my Lord, your storehouse is full of abundance. If Joseph’s storehouse provided for the famine, your storehouse nourishes my faith a hundredfold.
Give us, and increase for us, the abundance of your teaching. May fasting yield thirtyfold and love sixtyfold; may your truth alone yield a hundredfold in every good thing.
You yourself said, ‘I will repay the years that the locust, the crawling locust, and the cricket have eaten.’ Repay me still more, my Lord, for a hidden locust is eating my faith and its seed.
The land of the disputants, the field of their [?], lay fallow under the spirit of error. Famine came upon the soul that did not hate falsehood, the apple of its eye.
My farmer, plow my lands; plow them a second and a third time, my Lord. For you baptized threefold and gave life to the soil of our souls and the church of our spirits.
The apostles plowed a second and a third time, sowed, and reaped. From that company it was handed on and came down, and the earth grew rich and was filled with the treasure of teaching.
Just as its root spread and reached us, so it will continue to spread until your coming. Kings with their swords could not cut it off.
However much I give you, my Lord, it is little to you; and however much you give me, my greed asks for more. Your love hungers for what is ours; my need thirsts for what is yours.

Let my mind be your land. Plow it in the name of your Father; plow it a second time in the name of your Son, and a third time through your Holy Spirit. May a heap of praise rise to the one who sent you.
For you have returned my children to me and gathered my loved ones around me. If a bird rejoices in her chicks, my Lord, who would not rejoice in the company of her loved ones?
By your grace, may they recognize their mother’s voice. May they hurry to me, return, and come back to me. Then they and I, my Lord, will give thanks in one truth.
Nisibis 30
6. To the same tune.

Just as wheat, my son, once it is ripe, is stripped of the worthless chaff that was mixed with it, so the righteous stripped off whatever was of no help.
Response: Glory to your lordship!
Moses and Daniel, skilled and wise, were doves who became shrewd among serpents. One was educated in Egypt, the other in Babylon.
One abandoned the wisdom of the weak, the other that of the Chaldeans. They joined natural wisdom to childlikeness, like light, which is akin to the pupils of the eyes.
They were clever and pure, shrewd and simple. They were serene and discerning, skilled and blameless. They saw goodness and clothed themselves in it; they saw evil and stripped it off.
Like someone who does not travel a road he does not know, they did not know the road of darkness. They were familiar with only one road: the road of light.
They were children toward evil, eunuchs toward desire, infants toward pride, mature in duty, novices in vanity, and chaste in purity.
Who has ever seen wolves become teachers of innocent lambs, serpents teachers of doves, and hawks teachers of birds, teaching them their ways?
It was the Evil One, my brothers, who mixed his gall with sweetness, his darkness with light, his falsehood with truth, his evil with kindness, and his injustice with righteousness.
He chose clean and holy vessels for himself and poured his dregs into them. He filled them with his mud: the teaching of sorcerers and the discourse of the Chaldeans.
He let his dregs linger and remain amid purity, so that perhaps truth would grow accustomed to darkness, and what is true would go astray and tread amid falsehood.
He thought that if it all came about, it would be to his advantage, although it was to his loss: he was stirring up the dregs, the mud of his teaching, in the mouths of the children of truth.
He thought that even if the pure rebelled and threw out the dregs the accursed one had poured into them, it was impossible for no taste or flavor of his teaching at all to remain in them.
Thus he cunningly defiled the vessels of service, so that once they were defiled they could not be cleansed, intending to cut off the people's hope so that they would not look for restoration.
He was put to shame on both counts. He could not defile the natural vessels, for their Master reclaimed them; that palm of a hand came and cleansed them.
Its writing was [?], and its interpretation too was a refiner in the furnace. At Daniel's hand they were polished and purified, made beautiful and washed clean.

Those that had gone out in contempt returned and entered in splendor. Those that had gone out amid blasphemy were brought together amid praise, for the children of error turned back and praised the Lord of all.
The vessels of nature exposed him as being without a nature. The vessels of freedom exposed him by their own choice. The vessels were filled with truth and poured forth their truths.
The vessels that, by their own choice, had been filled with falsehood were in turn overturned and emptied, poured out and drained. The Evil One labored to repair them and fill them again.
Moses overturned them ten times in Egypt, and Daniel also overturned them in Babylon. Our Lord broke them and made them chaff.
By force he filled the vessels, the children of truth, but they emptied themselves. In place of the gall he had poured out, they poured sweet love and truth back into themselves.
But as for us, into whom our Savior poured his truth and whom he filled—the vessel overturned itself and was poured out by its own choice. Then it filled its interior again with dregs and strife.
Blessed are you, our Maker, who became our potter! You made us vessels of understanding from dust. Let us not be filled with dust instead of the treasure of truth.
Nisibis 31

On Vitus, bishop of Harran.
To the tune of the preceding hymn.
Remember, my Lord, Abraham's prayers in Harran and Jacob's in Paddan, and comfort your worshiper, who in his love took your beloved ones and clothed himself in them.
Response: Praises to him who chose him.
He was beautiful in their adornments and victorious in their fasts. Whoever gazed into your mirror grew much more beautiful—the chaste man whose mouth abstained from everything of the vine.

Haran is accustomed, my Lord, to distressing the house of Jacob. She defrauded him of his labors, did wrong, and then stood in judgment. When she wished, she acted deceitfully and brought in one sister instead of the other.
“It is not done this way in our country,” said Laban. Your custom testifies against you: either you alone are deceitful and your country is innocent and truthful, or your country bears your stamp.
For you changed his wages ten times and tossed him this way and that. Is this also your country’s custom—not to pay wages, but to defraud and lie about what was agreed?
He abandoned his shearing and went up to fight against the man who had endured his ambushes and his stings. He deceived the truthful man and insulted the honorable one.
The Watcher stood on the road for the vigilant man, while in Haran Laban was defeated in his sleep: a dream overcame him and brought a crown to that vigilant man as the reward for his wakefulness.
He chose the spotted animals for himself, but lost and was defeated by the white ones. Laban was [?] in his changes—a cloud of alterations and a wheel of changes.
His Lord saw his labor, how he remained silent when defrauded, how he overlooked insults, and how he multiplied his prayers. The Hearer of prayers crowned him with victories.
The elderly Eliezer, who came down and arranged his sister’s betrothal, saw his cunning and buried him in every kind of gift, for Laban had taken possession of the house and its inhabitants.
He had loaded ten camels and brought every kind of good thing to satisfy every mouth. He purchased freedom and bribed Haran’s ravenous hunger with his offerings.

That dignified man also outwitted them with wisdom. For it is written that he gave to her father, and it is written that he gave to her mother. He piled gifts upon Laban and increased them, for he was their spokesman.

His customary greed came seeking something from that companion of the dust, who was stripped of possessions and carried a staff, a symbol of the cross. Because he was poor and innocent, he overwhelmed him with every kind of trickery.
His deceit was among the sheep, his ambushes at the banquet. A man without God—how could he make peace? He hated his own daughters; on whom, then, could he have compassion?
The innocent trusted the deceiver’s promises because he concealed himself behind Abraham’s name. At the time of the banquet, he deceitfully prepared the bridegroom’s bed.

Because he deceived people through his kinship with Abraham, Jacob became the furnace in which his base metal was exposed. Through his repeated changes, he was revealed as an enemy of Isaac’s household.
He seethed and did not conceal his wickedness to make himself look good. “It was compulsion,” he said, “that restrained me, not kindness.” He showed that his will was opposed to reconciliation.
Jacob, a man of peace, rejoiced in that peace. He bought off the greedy man with a feast, which delighted him. The Righteous One stood up for the righteous man, the Worshiped One for his worshiper.
He was bitterly envied and violently assailed. He was furiously pursued and prayed continually. He was wondrously delivered and filled with abundant joy.
Laban saw that whatever he did to you turned against him and in Jacob’s favor. He turned back to make peace, established a covenant with him, kissed him, let him go, and departed.
The wholly pure one shone out from the wholly troubled one. The Righteous One separated them; he parted them forever. The sediment sank to its depth, and the clear liquid returned to its height.
My prayer, my Lord, is that you will not do this in our days. For if the bitter root receives the sweet so that it may taste it within itself, we too long for it, though we are unworthy.
How easy it is, my Lord, for those who have freedom of action, whose natures are not bound, to turn back and become one! Let the one who has fallen seek help, and let the one who stands support him.
For even animals have received, loved, and nursed young that are very foreign to their own nature. And if they are separated, they proclaim their suffering with their cries.
Let us imitate the Watchers, my Lord, who rejoice over those who repent. For unless I mourn, I am greatly blameworthy: the Watchers consider me a mother without compassion.
How my inward parts ache for my children, who come from me! They are children of my nature and children of my truth. Let them sometimes appease with their fruits the farmer whom they have angered.
Comfort the farmer over his planting: hail, flood, and locusts consumed the new planting and damaged the old. Their deeds caused lamentation.
Comfort the farmer whose roots have collapsed: a worm is in the ground, and a weevil in the granary. It bored into what was inside and ate what was outside.
May he who suffered loss in both become rich in both. Bless the seed outside; fill the granaries within. May he bring forth new things and old in his teaching.
The new shepherd went out, and [?], frost and mist, met him. They confused the lambs, who loved the wolves and thought that the shepherd was a wolf.
The flock’s eye has grown dim in the darkness. Let their sight and understanding be put right by your light. Let them turn toward the shepherd and pasture his lambs.
Although lambs and wolves are alike in size, a sheep has gored its fellow. Rebuke Satan, my Lord, who has made innocent lambs into fearsome leopards.
Who could grant that shepherd of sheep the power to transform wolves? Who could grant the farmer the power to turn weeds into wheat?
Look, priests have the means to transform wolves, and weeds along with them. It is hard work: see how they labor over wolves, that they may become sheep, and over thorns, that they may become crops.
Help the farmer to plant the thirsty land with springs, with myrtle and cypress, with speaking box trees and Christian cedars.
Let their branches be a haven for weary birds coming from afar to sing David’s songs to you and praise you with melodies.

The lowly one, whose wing has grown heavy and who has grown weary, has closed his mouth to vigil and praise. With their lyres may those who keep watch, and with their harps the chaste, pray for me, our Lord.
Nisibis 32
To the same tune.
Rebekah, Laban’s sister, was not like him: hers was pure wisdom, his was hateful cunning. Through his cunning Rebekah lived; through her wisdom Laban perished.
Refrain: Praises to the one who knows all!
The pure woman accompanied the old man who had led her. The Most High saw that she was much on Abraham’s mind. He sent, betrothed her, led her, and brought her into his inheritance.
Wheat came out from among thorns and weeds, and from the pagans’ storehouse into the dwelling of the righteous. O [?]
Their master is hidden and crafty. They learned his craft and imitated his cunning, for he labored greatly over them so that they would become his partisans, his instruments, and his disciples.
From their own circumstances they could have discerned his: just as Leah does not resemble Rachel, so an idol does not resemble God.
If even a sister does not resemble her sister, though she shares her nature, how much more alien to God is error, which has been called by his name!
Though Jacob was deceived by their trickery, the righteous man acquired the land they entrusted to him and cast his seed into it, so that his seed would not remain in the land of weeds.
It is true that he was never deceived into joining his truth to paganism, his holiness to impurity, his garment to filth, or his robe to defilement.
Rebekah clothed herself in his craft to oppose him, and with his own cunning she entered the contest against him. She turned and put on the armor he had forged, and defeated him.
Although Esau was her firstborn son, she knew that he was a stranger to the offspring of the faithful—that is, he resembled Haran in his conduct.
The master of the people of Haran was dwelling within Esau. Rebekah acted shrewdly and defeated the one who had taught human beings to substitute one thing for another.
She called the innocent man, devised her scheme, and clothed him in skins, the confidants of Satan himself, so that he might be utterly defeated through everything that belonged to him.

She devised her scheme and plundered his treasury of blessings. She searched it out and emptied it, so that no portion would remain for her son of the left, whom she would leave empty-handed at his side.
And just as she had stripped him of the blessings, she sent the innocent man, the vessel of purity, down to plunder again and impoverish Haran.
Above and below, Rebekah defeated the deceiver. She deceived him with his own deception: she defeated him through the blessings; she defeated him through the captives he brought to his disciple.
She sent him hunting, and he worked for wages and [?] the two young women, a symbol of the congregations, for that patient endurance is fitting for both of them.
Nisibis 33
3. To the same tune.
The thorns, tares, and [?] of paganism, which grew drunk on libations so that my erring people might be caught in them, flourished within [?], in that shrine of demons.
Refrain: May my children be united in you.
If Adam caused natural thorns to spring up because, by his free choice, he crossed the boundary of the commandment, these people, by their own will, caused thorns to spring up within Haran.
The farmer came down to earth for the sake of human beings, who had become thorns, so that they might become wheat. The thorns wove thorns for the farmer’s head.
Yet the seed of that [?] which they traced was not lost. Look, the thorns have turned into roses and lilies, a crown for the laborer who endured a crown of thorns.
And for that farmer who labored in Haran among thorns so that they might become wheat, may they become, through your grace, cypress and myrtle, blossoms—a crown for your athlete.
Your champion resembles you in everything, my Lord. And just as his humiliation resembled your abasement, my Lord, may he resemble you in your exaltation, growing great upon his throne.
May a road of reconciliation and a path of joys stretch from Edessa into Haran, and may they travel from church to church in harmony.
May the old man from Edessa visit Haran, the citadel he had nurtured; and may the son of his [?] visit his mother, and then return again to his betrothed, Haran.
Fill with your grace the pit that the evil one made. He cut a great chasm to divide the two sides. Throw him into his own pit and make a road over him.
Let us give thanks to your grace, which made the road easy and [?] before the crowds coming to the festival. Since they traveled easily, let them give thanks abundantly.
And may Jacob, Isaac, and Abram give thanks on their behalf. For if their names helped those who worshiped the calf, may they rejoice with us in Paddan at their commemoration.
Just as all the fathers were drawn into our land through Abraham’s hidden leaven, so, through the apostles’ leaven, draw and bring the apostles, their companions.
Through the bones of John, some of which are in our land, prophets came to our land. Through Guria and Shmona, and through Habib, their beloved, martyrs came and visited us.
Nisibis 34
Again on Haran. To the tune of “The King’s Bride.”
The glorious physician Abram came to Harran, for she was sick. He examined her, was astonished, and turned toward the land of Canaan. He reached Egypt; the whole body
he visited as he went down. He bandaged and healed with the word of truth. If Abram was not enough for you, who will be enough for you, Harran, whose sickness gives her pleasure?
Refrain: Blessed is he who has never abandoned humanity, who in every generation has multiplied those who care for her.
The renowned physician Jacob came to Harran to examine her. He examined her, cast her aside, and left her, so that he would no longer concern himself with her. For twenty years he tended
her. When he saw that she had gone mad and was also raging against him, he left her and departed. Look, your waters are bitter, and your children are shriveled! Harran, be sweetened by the cross!
Babylon is the neighbor of that building whose builders stopped their work. Egypt is the neighbor of the Sodomites. But you, Harran, have been placed
in the neighborhood of glorious, beautiful Edessa. Daughter, resemble your mother, for she is salt within the world, and purify your mind through her teaching.
Anyone who looks into a mirror for a moment adorns himself by it. But you, filthy Harran—look, your mirror is glorious and clean! Adorn yourself by it,
by the blessed city set before you, so that you may please Jesus. Look at her and become beautiful through her, so that she may be a help to you, lest she become a reproach to you.
Look at sick Egypt, who was indeed healed by the healer of all! Yet the rust of idolatry has corroded Harran. Even when she has recovered, there is no confidence
in her health, for at every opportunity her wound breaks open. Babylon, Harran, and Egypt—all three of them! Be baptized and put on the threefold names.
How like the great statue that the tyrant saw is the world! Its head is Babylon; its middle is the land of Judah; Egypt is situated in the position of the feet.
It is a great body over which great physicians have labored. Through his servants, the Good One extended his care like a great physician to every region.
And just as Abraham the physician treated it from the head downward, Moses too treated it from the feet. Oh, the sick man whose physicians surround him on every
side! Yet he remains estranged from health. Heal him! Blessed is he who has never abandoned humanity, who in every generation has multiplied her [?].
And just as Joseph treated the land of Egypt like a sick heel, the prophets treated Zion like the heart. Daniel too tended Babylon
like the head, which went mad in the wilderness, recovered, and gave thanks. Egypt is a physician skilled in her medicines, yet her pains have grown severe through her own will.
All creation became sick, like a body, with the disease of error. Its attendants, the renowned physicians, came in succession so that it might be healed of the
hidden sickness of the soul, and rise and give thanks to the physician who showed it mercy. Glory to him who sent the righteous around to every region, so that he might care for the sick world!
But the physicians with their medicines were not sufficient for the world. The physician who is sufficient for everyone saw it and [?]. He cut from his own body and placed it upon its sore,
and healed our suffering with his body, and with his blood healed our wound. Glory to the medicine of life, who proved sufficient and healed the pain of souls through his teaching!
Jesus is our physician, and just as it was through him that we originally came into being, so it was by his hand that we were healed. As God, he knows the nature and the pain of the soul,
for he is both the maker and the one who binds wounds, the physician and the medicine. Glory to him who created what had not existed, and when it sinned and fell, raised it up again!
The physicians of the world can heal only through suffering; their hand is very frightening to the wounded. But to our wound, my Lord, its touch is very dear.
of your hand, for your finger too is a bridge of mercy. Blessed is he from whose blessed, soft garments power went out and gently healed.
Good One, who labored in the world so that the whole body might be healthy, my Lord, in your love do not despise one weak member. Into the body of the righteous
let it be joined, my Lord, and let its attachment to them last forever. Good One, who reattached the ear that had been cut off, do not cut me off from you because I have angered you.
Nisibis XXXV
On Our Lord, Death, and Satan. To the tune of “The Horn and the Trumpet.”

A voice proclaimed, and the forces of the Evil One gathered and came with his servants—the camp of weeds, the entire assembly—for they saw that Jesus had triumphed, a stumbling stone for the whole left side. For there was none

among them who had not been tormented. One by one they began to recount everything they had suffered. Sin and Sheol were alarmed; Death trembled because the dead had rebelled, and Satan because sinners had rebelled against him.
Refrain: Glory to you, whom the Evil One saw and was thrown into confusion.
Queen Sin called her children, the demons and evil spirits, and said to them, “Legion, the commander of your ranks, is no more, for
the sea swallowed him and his companions. You too, my children, if you treat this Jesus with contempt, he will destroy you. You who caught Solomon—it is a disgrace
indeed for you to be defeated by his disciples, fishermen and uneducated men. Look, they have caught the catcher of human beings who used to catch us!”
“This is greater than all our troubles,” said the Evil One about our Savior. “It was not enough for him to plunder us; he has also begun to take vengeance on us for Jonah son of Amittai. From Legion

he is surely exacting payment for taking him and throwing him into the sea. Jonah remained submerged for three days and came up, but Legion will not come up even after a long time, for at a command the depths of the sea closed over him.

“After his fast I tempted him with fine bread, but he was not tempted. To my sorrow I labored to learn a psalm, so that I might catch him with his own psalm. In vain I learned about the dragon, and he made

my dragon powerless. I took him up the mountain and showed him all our possessions. I offered them to him, but he was not enticed. How fortunate I was in Adam’s day, for he did not make me labor hard to instruct him!”

The Evil One gave up his efforts and said, “This Jesus is putting me out of work! Look, tax collectors and prostitutes have taken refuge in him. What occupation shall I seek for myself? I, who was everyone’s master—
whose disciple shall I become?” Sin spoke again: “It is right that I should now stop and change from what I am, for this son of Mary who has come has made humanity a new creation.”
Greedy Death wailed and said, “I have learned fasting, which I never knew before. Look, Jesus has held feasts, but in his feasting he proclaims a fast for me. One man has shut my mouth, though I shut

the mouths of many!” Sheol said, “I reproach myself for my greed; from now on there is famine! Look, he triumphed at the wedding feast. Just as he turned water into wine, he has turned the condition of the dead into life.
“God too brought a flood, washed the earth, and cleansed its sins. Again he brought fire and sulfur upon it, to whiten its stains with fire. He gave me the people of Sodom, and through the flood

the giants. He shut the mouth of Sennacherib’s household and opened Sheol’s. These things and things like them I loved. Instead of plagues inflicted in justice, through his Son he has brought the dead to life by grace.”
“Prophets and righteous men saw me,” said the Evil One to his followers, “and although their forces were very strong, there was in them an admixture of what is mine. For the nature of the children of

A human being—she is the mate of our leaven [?]. This one put on Adam’s body, yet he bewilders us, because our leaven has no power over him. Is he, then, both man and God, his humanity mingled with his divinity?
I have seen Adam, that fountain from which all our races flowed. His children have been examined by me and tested one by one, and I have never seen a human being with one part belonging to God

and his other half human. Moses, who shone with his radiance—I tested him too, and confounded him through his tongue. But this one I could not confound even in his thinking, for the fountain of his thoughts is exceedingly clear.

Bodily desire is present in all our bodies; even when they sleep, it is awake in them. Whoever has become pure while awake, I disturb through a dream. The body’s [?] stirs within him through the impulse
hidden inside him. I have disturbed both those awake and those asleep alike. This one alone remained pure: I did not bewilder him even in a dream, for even in his sleep he was serene and holy.
His childhood, too, was different from that of the children I had seen. For I saw no share of what belongs to me in him. From his childhood I was afraid; therefore I stirred up Herod

so that he would be killed along with the infants. The very fact that he escaped frightened me greatly: how had he become aware of our secret? He took the Magi’s offerings, mocked us, departed, and turned aside from our sword.
I have seen children of righteous men, and infants born to chaste women. I tested them one by one from the womb, and I saw our leaven in them: they were irritable and ill-tempered,

and also hot-tempered and pale. They were fruits that ripened and became sweet through instruction. But this one, from the womb, was good fruit possessing a sweetness through which sinners became sweet.
Even as an infant he was a teacher of human beings through the radiance upon him. The priest himself, when he carried him, marveled at him. In the wisdom
of elders he was clothed. Joseph stood in awe of him; his mother was radiant before him. In his childhood he was a help to all
who saw him, and a benefit to those who knew him. From the day he entered creation, he was humanity’s helper through his victories.
Where did Mary’s fruit spring up from against me—a cluster whose wine is not natural? Here I stand amid doubts. If I neglect
and leave him alone, I am afraid that through his teaching those who have acquired my bitterness will become sweet. And if I press and trample him, again
I am terrified that he may turn into new wine for sinners, and when they become drunk on him, they will forget their idols.
Look, I am afraid of both things: of his death and of his life.” But the Evil One’s servants answered him and advised him: “If
both are hard, a lighter burden is easier for us. Let us choose his death rather than his life. Let Death tell us whether anyone
among the righteous has ever come back to life. O mighty and victorious ones, no one has escaped from all-devouring Sheol.”
“Can anyone touch a gust of wind? And who can fathom Mary’s son? For when he wept, he deceived me with his tears.
And when I also told him to throw himself down from the holy temple, I thought that he did not fall because he was afraid. Yet when they threw him from a mountain, he flew
through the air. He entered the wilderness, grew tired, and sat down again. I could not understand his changes, for he walked both on dry land and on water.

I saw him hungry like a human being, but that was undone by the bread he multiplied. From the very beginning I tested him and came to him. He asked questions like someone who did not know, but this too was undone by what he revealed

He who knows hidden things also chose Iscariot, as though he did not know; then he turned and showed that he knew him. As he bound and as he released, he bewildered me: he plunged, emerged, and overwhelmed me.
But one sign that I saw in him encourages me more than anything. For I saw him praying and rejoiced: his color changed, and he became afraid. His sweat became drops of blood, because he realized
that his day had arrived. This sign pleased me more than anything—unless he has deceived me by it. But if he has indeed tricked me, woe both to me and to you, my servants!

The camp of demons raised an outcry and said, “The sign we see in you is dreadful! Nothing like this has ever happened to you. You used to triumph over crowned kings. The Son of Mary is capturing strongholds, while look at you—

fainthearted! Interpretation. Get up, go out, and let us fight him! It is a disgrace to us that so many should be defeated by one. If you are in pain or afraid, give us a king for the battle, and stay where you are.
“From this Jesus’ own words I can learn how to fight him. For he said that Satan is divided against himself and cannot stand. In wanting to fight us, he has given us

a weapon against himself. Go, divide his disciples for me! If they are divided, you will defeat them through one another. Through the serpent and feeble Eve, I defeated the first Adam by means of what was his own.”

Death answered the Evil One and said to him, “Who has discouraged you, contrary to your usual manner? You used to hunt down the lowly and the insignificant like a skilled hunter. Jesus, who is greater than all—by means of whom

did you intend to hunt him down? The taste of his arrows frightens you, the arrows he shot at you when you were tempting him. You and I, together with your soldiers—our assembled force is too small to fight the Son of Mary.
“But I advise this, if the Adversary allows us to do anything: go yourself and begin with that disciple of his, so that a chief may speak with chiefs. Unleash your entire camp; let it go
and stir up the Pharisees. Do not speak [?], as you usually do: ‘If you are God, fall from here!’ Kiss him lovingly and hand him over, and then envy and the sword of the Levites will torment him.”
Nisibis XXXVI
By the same author, to the same tune.
Our Lord restrained his power, and they seized him, so that his life-giving death might bring Adam to life. He gave his hands to be pierced by nails in place of the hand that plucked the fruit.
He received a blow on his cheek in the court, in place of the mouth that ate in Eden. Because Adam had stretched out his foot, they nailed his feet. Our Lord stripped himself
to put to shame [?]. With gall and vinegar he sweetened the serpent’s gall, which it had poured into humanity. Response: Blessed is he who defeated me and brought the dead to life to praise him!
“If you are God, show your power; if you are human, test our power. If it is Adam you seek, go away! He is imprisoned here for his debts. The cherubim and seraphim cannot
pay on his behalf. There is no mortal among them who could give his life for him. Who can open the mouth of Sheol, plunge in, and bring him up from it? It swallowed him and closed over him forever.
“I am the one who defeated all the wise, and look, they lie piled up for me in the corners of Sheol. Come in, son of Joseph, and see the horrors: the skulls of mighty men, Samson’s great skeleton,
and the bones of fierce Goliath. And Og, offspring of giants, who made himself an iron bed and lay on it—I toppled him from it and cast him down. I brought that cedar low at the gate of Sheol.

I alone have conquered many, yet one solitary man seeks to conquer me. Prophets and priests and the victorious warrior I have led away. I have conquered kings among their ranks and mighty men amid their slaughter.

And the righteous amid their victories. Rivers of corpses are cast into Sheol, and however much they pour into her, she remains thirsty. Whether someone is near or far, the end brings him to the gate of Sheol.
I have scorned the silver of the rich, and their offerings have not bribed me. Masters of slaves have never persuaded me to take a slave instead of his master, or a poor man instead of a rich man,
or an old man instead of a child. The wise who can persuade wild animals—their pleas do not enter my ears. Let everyone call me a hater of persuasion; I do what I have been commanded.
Who is this man, and whose son is he? What is the ancestry of the one who has conquered me? The record of the generations is with me. Look, I went in, labored, and read the names from Adam until now.
Not one of the dead is missing: generation after generation, they are written upon my limbs. For your sake, Jesus, I went in and made a reckoning, to show you that no one escapes my hands.
There are indeed two men—let me not lie—whose names are missing in Sheol. Enoch and Elijah have not come to me. I searched for them throughout creation, even where Jonah went down.
I went down and searched, but they were not there. And if I suppose that they entered Paradise and escaped, a fearsome cherub guards it. Jacob saw a ladder; perhaps they ascended on it to heaven?
Who has eaten the sand of the sea and scattered only two grains? This harvest, into which diseases cast their sickles every day like reapers—I alone carry

their sheaves and bury them. Those who bring them in drop handfuls when they hurry; grape-pickers leave clusters behind. Only two little grapes have escaped me in the great vintage that I gathered alone.
“It is I who have carried out,” says Death, “every slaughter on sea and dry land. The eagles in the air come to me, as do the dragons of the deep, creeping things, birds, and beasts; old men,

young men, and children. Let all these convince you, Son of Mary, that my dominion reigns over all. How has your cross conquered me? For it was through a tree that I triumphed and conquered in the beginning.
I wanted to speak and say much more, for I am not short of words. Yet words are not needed: here are deeds close at hand, crying out. I do not, as you do, give assurances
to simple people about hidden things, saying, ‘There will be a resurrection.’ When? When? But if you are so mighty, give a pledge close at hand, so that your distant promise may also be believed.”
Death finished uttering his mockery, and the voice of our Lord thundered in Sheol. He cried out and split the graves open one by one. Pangs
seized Death. In Sheol, which had never known light, rays flashed from the angels who had entered and brought out
the dead to meet that dead man who gave life to all. The dead came out, and the living were put to shame—those who thought they had conquered the giver of life to all.
“If only someone would give me the day of Moses!” said Death. “It made a feast for me. For that lamb in Egypt gave me the firstfruits from every household. Heaps upon heaps of firstborn

it piled up for me at the gate of Sheol. This Passover lamb has plundered Sheol, carried off the dead, and taken them away from me. That lamb filled graves for me, but this one empties graves that were full.”
The death of Jesus is torment to me. I would much rather have had his life than his death. Here is a dead man whose death I hate! In the death
of everyone else I rejoice; at his death I am distressed. I am waiting for him to return to life. While he was alive, three dead people
he brought to life and raised. But now, through his death, the dead who have come to life have trampled me at the gate of Sheol, where I had gone to hold them back.

I will run and shut the gates of Sheol against that dead man whose death has plundered me. Whoever hears should marvel at my humiliation: I have been defeated by a dead man outside! All the dead want to go out, but this one

presses to come in. The medicine of life has entered Sheol and brought her dead to life. Who, I wonder, brought in and hid within me a living fire, by which the cold, dark recesses of Sheol have melted?
Death saw Watchers in Sheol, immortals instead of mortals, and said, “Confusion has entered our dwelling! There is torment on both accounts: the dead have gone out of Sheol,

and Watchers who do not die have entered her. Look, one has entered and sat at the head of his tomb, and his other companion at his feet. I will ask him and plead with him to take his hostage up and go to his kingdom.
Good Jesus, do not hold against me the words my arrogance spoke before you. Who, on seeing your cross, would not have doubted that you were a man? Who could have seen your power and not believed

that you are also God? So now, through both, I have learned to confess that you are a man and are also God. Since the dead do not repent in Sheol, go up among the living, my Lord, and carry up my repentance.
King Jesus, accept my petition, and along with my petition take a hostage for yourself. Lead away Adam, the great hostage, in whom all the dead are hidden, just as, when I received him, hidden in him
were all the living. I have given you the first hostage, Adam’s body. Go up now and reign over all. Whenever I hear your trumpet, I myself will bring out the dead with my own hands at your coming.”
Our living King went forth in triumph and ascended from Sheol as a conqueror. Wailing swept over the left side: anguish for the spirits and demons, suffering for Satan and Death, and for Sin
and Sheol, mourning. Today there was joy for the right side, on this great day. Let us therefore give great glory to him who died and is alive, who will bring everyone to life and raise them.
Nisibis 37
3. By the same author, to the same tune.
Death was weeping over Sheol when he saw that her treasuries had been emptied. He said, “Who, I wonder, is plundering your wealth? Gehazi stole
and was exposed. But though I steal every day, no theft has ever been proved against me. I am sent against kings; in their illnesses they are surrounded
by their guards. While the guards are at the door, I carry off the kings’ souls and leave.” Refrain: Blessed is he who broke Sheol’s sting by his cross!
All barren women grieve, but Sheol rejoices in her barrenness. She became desolate when she gave birth. The Power that constrains all constrained her barren, cold womb, and it yielded back
despite its ruthlessness. Rebekah, whom two infants pressed, asked for death. How great, then, must Sheol’s pain be, struck by new labor pains! For those who [?] and came out of her were not dead.
Could this be the saying that I heard from Isaiah and scorned when he stood and said:
“Who has heard anything like this: that the earth should go into labor in a single day and give birth to a people in a single hour?” Is this what has happened, or perhaps—
It is still kept for us, even if this is only a shadow. I thought I was a king; I did not know that I was guarding something entrusted to me.
I heard two bewildering sayings from that Isaiah. For he said that a virgin would conceive and give birth, and he said
again that the earth would give birth. Look: the virgin gave birth to him, and barren Sheol gave birth to him—two wombs acting contrary to nature.
Both the virgin and Sheol were changed through him. He made the virgin rejoice at his birth, but he saddened and distressed Sheol at his resurrection.
I saw Ezekiel in the valley, raising the dead when he was questioned. I saw the bones stirring and moving. There was a tumult of bones in Sheol, each bone seeking its companion
and each joint its partner. There was no one there asking or being asked whether these bones could live, for without a question the voice of Jesus, the commander of creation, brought them to life.
Sheol was saddened when she saw the sorrowful dead rejoicing. She wept over Lazarus as he went out: “Go in peace, living dead man, cherished in two houses of mourning,

whose lamentations are both outside and inside! His sisters wept as he entered the tomb to come to me, and I wept over him as he went out. At his death there was weeping among the living, and at his resurrection there was great mourning in Sheol too.”
Now she has tasted the taste of the grief of someone who weeps over a loved one. If the dead are so dear to Sheol, how dearly their parents love them! “The limbs that she cut off and took—look,

they are being cut off from me and taken away! If I suffer so much at parting from that young man [who was raised], blessed is he who had compassion on the widow! Through her only son he brought peace to her bereaved home.
All this suffering that I cause human beings through their loved ones—he has finally gathered it all upon me. For when
the dead leave Sheol, everyone will have resurrection, and I alone will have torment. Who, then, will be able to endure me?”
All this he showed to Sheol alone: that the voice which splits open graves lays her waste and brings out the dead within her.
If anyone reads the prophets, he hears there of righteous battles. If anyone meditates on the story of Jesus, he learns compassion and mercy. And if anyone thinks that Jesus is a stranger,
that is blasphemy to me. Another, foreign key can never fit the gate of Sheol. There is only one key, the Creator’s: he who opened her will also open her at his coming.
Who can assemble the bones except the power that created them? Who can join together the broken pieces of the body except the Maker’s hand? Who can restore their forms except
the Creator’s finger? He who created and then destroyed is also able to renew and raise to life. No other god can enter and restore creatures that are not his.
“If there were another power, I would be very glad for it to come to me. If it descended into the depths of Sheol, it would learn that there is
only one God. The mortals who went astray and proclaimed that there are many gods—look, I hold them imprisoned in Sheol, and their gods
have never grieved over them. I know one God; I recognize his prophets and his apostles too.”
Nisibis 38
4. To the same tune.
My throne was established for me in Sheol, but one dead man arose and toppled me from it. Everyone feared me alone, while I did not fear anyone
Fear, terror, and worry among the living; peace and tranquility among the dead, through a slain man. Look, a captive has entered Sheol! As for me, everyone—

I used to take captive. The son of a captive whom I had captured has captured me. He led away those I had captured and went to Paradise.
Response: Blessed is he who brought the dead of Sheol to life through his cross.
Everyone has received much from me, but I have received from only one. Who among human beings is as just as I am? The time has come for my vindication. I love everyone,

and whoever hates me knows it himself. Never in my life have I known what a bribe is. I have shown no partiality to kings. Through me equality is proclaimed, for I make the slave and his master equal in Sheol.
I serve before God, with whom there is no partiality. Who else endures as I do? I am reviled while I do good; in return, injuries are paid back to me.
The good things that I heap up—though my deeds are good, my reputation is not good. My mind rests in its integrity. I take comfort in God, who, though he is good, is wronged every day and endures it.
I have spared the old all pains, and children all sins. I quiet hidden battles in Sheol. In our land no injustice occurs. Only Sheol and heaven

are spared all sins. This earth, which lies between them, is inhabited by injustice. Therefore, whoever is discerning should either ascend to heaven or, if that is difficult, descend to Sheol, which is easy.
Everyone runs to comfort a person over a single dead person. But as for me, whose many dead have come to life, no one comes in to comfort me.
As for Satan, who grumbled, seven woes to him too! Although the Son of Mary has thoroughly trampled him, his spirit is proud. He is a serpent, crushed yet insolent.
It is better for me to fall down and worship before this Jesus, who defeated me through his cross.

When he enters the gate of Sheol, I will proclaim before him in John's place and cry out, ‘Look, the one who gives life to the dead has arrived!’ From now on I am your servant, Jesus. Because of your body I treated you with contempt,

for you concealed your divinity. Do not be angry, Son of the King, with your treasurer. At your command I opened and shut. Although my wings are swift, it is at your signal that I run in every direction.
Not all who were raised were firstborn, for our Lord is the firstborn of Sheol. How can a dead person precede the power through which he was raised? There are last who are first,

and younger ones who became firstborn. For Manasseh was the firstborn: how was Ephraim able to take his birthright? And if a child born later preceded him, how much more will the Lord and Son take precedence in his resurrection!
Look, John, like a herald, declares that he comes afterward, although he is older. For he said, ‘Look, a man comes after me,’ and, he says, ‘he has come before me.’ For how could he have preceded

the power through which he was proclaiming? For everything that came into being for the sake of something else is later, even if it is earlier. For the cause that called it into being is older and takes precedence in everything.
The purpose for Adam existed before the creatures prepared for him. For the Creator was looking toward Adam all the time as he created. And if Adam, even before he came into being, was older

than the creatures, how much older, then, my Lord, must your humanity be through your divinity, which has existed eternally with the one who begot you! Glory to you, and through you to your Father, from us all.

Glory to you, for you come first in your divinity and in your humanity. For although Elijah went up before you, he could not precede the one for whose sake he was taken up, for his symbolic meaning depends
on your reality. Although the symbols visibly preceded your truth, it invisibly precedes them. The creatures preceded Adam, yet he preceded them, since they were prepared for his sake.
My Lord, grant me that resurrection,

not the one compelled by your power, but the one arising from your love. Your compelling power gives life even to sinners. Iscariot, too, would have wished to choose the death of Sheol rather than the life of Gehenna.
Grant me, then, the resurrection that comes from your compassion. If your justice does not permit it, your grace has a reason: remember for me this alone—that I was immersed in it.
Nisibis 39
5. By the same author, to the same tune.
I have had encounters with the righteous, but no one has shattered me like the Son of Mary. For Elijah brought a dead man to life, and although he himself escaped from
my hands, afterward I had this consolation: I carried off the dead man whom he had brought to life. From Elisha son of Shaphat I received blows, for he brought two dead people to life.
With one blow I struck back: I carried off the prophet, and also the dead people whom he had brought to life. Refrain: Blessed is he who tore open the graves of Sheol with his voice!
I was afraid of Gehazi when I saw him place the staff over the boy. The thief took up the staff and returned. Elisha came and bent down,
made himself small beside the boy, and rose up. Then he walked back and forth. I was bewildered by the new symbols I saw there, though they brought only one
boy to life. How fortunate I was when these were only symbols, unlike now, when the dead have rebelled and defeated me!
When I saw the great radiance on Moses’ face, I was afraid of him. Yet what happened to me was not what I had feared: he made spring bloom for me in Sheol, for I fed on a pasture of corpses—
six hundred thousand who had fallen. This despised and humble man, whom I scorned, healed the sick and the infirm. He multiplied bread for others, but snatches our own bread from our mouths.
There was a great wedding feast in Sheol when it swallowed Korah’s company. Satan made a great banquet for me by causing a division among the Levites. He made a fountain of milk and honey flow

for me in a thirsty land, for crowds of the wicked went down to Sheol. But now the righteous have come to life and gone out! Moses brought the living down into it, but Jesus raised the dead and brought them up.
How fortunate I was in the days of the zealous, when I feasted through their swords! The zealous Phinehas thrust and gave me delight on the tip
of his spear. He handed me Zimri and Cozbi together on the point of his lance. To whom, I wonder, have two fattened bulls ever
been offered on the point of a spear? But in exchange for Cozbi, the daughter of chiefs, Jesus snatched Jairus’s daughter from my hands.

Aaron’s censer frightened me when he stood between the dead and the living and defeated me. The cross frightens me more than it, for it tears open the graves of Sheol. The cross by which I used to kill—

now by that very thing I have been killed! The disgrace of someone defeated by an armed warrior is not so very great. My disgrace is worse for me than my torment, for my might was defeated by a crucified man.
Phinehas’s spear also frightened me, for with it, with his sword, he stopped the plague. The spear that guarded the tree of life both gladdened me and grieved me,
because it kept Adam from life, and kept death from the people. But the spear-thrust that Jesus received—I suffered from it. He was struck, and I wailed.
Water and blood flowed out of him. Adam bathed, came to life, and returned to Paradise.

The Sadducees became my mouthpieces and disputed with him as though expressing my own thoughts: “There is no resurrection of the dead at all.” Jesus repeated to them a saying whose significance I alone recognized. From

the bush he cried out and distressed me: “I am the God of Abraham,” and God is not the God of the dead. I would have been happy if these had only been words, and he had not shown me the resurrection of the dead in action.
Joshua son of Nun destroyed thirty kings and filled graves and pits for me. He devastated Jericho and filled Sheol. But this Jesus who has come emptied graves of their dead
and filled the cities above. Why, though they are alike in their names, are they not alike in their deeds? That one gave me Achan’s body, but this one took away Lazarus’s body.
Moses kicked that Egyptian; he mingled justice with his humility. Where has this new law sprung up against me: “If someone strikes you on your cheek,

offer him your other cheek, and take care not to hate him”? In place of the fierce, zealous man who kicked and killed, a new merciful one has dawned upon us. Samuel cut Agag to pieces, but Jesus healed the paralyzed man.

Compassion—how little there was at that time! Now it has grown abundant. There were even occasions when it was utterly hateful for someone to transgress the commandment. For without mercy they were killed—

Saul and Ahab—because they wished to have mercy on the wicked, and those who deserved punishment were not killed. Jesus has overturned my own age: “Let everyone live,” he says, “and spare his killer.”

Samson is remembered, the lion’s cub, who crushed the wild asses of Philistia and gave them to me. That mighty warrior too, Abner son of Ner, hunted a swift gazelle for me: Asahel son of Zeruiah, whom he struck
and threw to the ground. Benaiah too killed Joab in the holy temple, justly, as it is written. Now that justice has withheld her sword, let the repentant rejoice in grace.
David measured out the Edomites, cord by cord, and destroyed them. How merciful you are, Son of David! David’s justice was doubled: he killed two measured groups,
but let a full measured group live. Yet the Son of David teaches us: “Forgive your brother seventy times seven.” There, justice was measured out; here, kindness is beyond measure.
David possessed zeal and strength. He killed both the lion and the wolf. He left the mighty lion behind and ran against the fierce warrior. With a stone he scattered his light, and

his life left him, and he perished. But Jesus called to the dead man, “Young man, young man!” Even the dead are merely sleeping to him. He brought the young man to life and snatched him from me, while he drowned worthless pigs for me in the sea.
Because of the calf, the Levites killed their fathers and their brothers. Jephthah slaughtered his daughter with his own hands. The king of Moab, on the wall, sacrificed his firstborn son.
I rejoiced at his sword. But through Jesus the sword grew blunt, and fire, Sheol’s sister, was also rebuked. Simon’s mother-in-law was healed,
but through her healing the Good One made Sheol sick.

This Jesus, though he is the Son of the Just One, is proclaimed as wholly gracious. But for me, his very grace is torment through him. Envy is the cause of our delight, for from the beginning envy mixed

Blood was my beginning. Who can strike the son of Mary, who came and commanded, “Do not be angry with your brother”? He removed the sword from among brothers—the sword of Cain with which you were pleased to set me loose.
Samson found a honeycomb inside a carcass. Was this perhaps a symbol? This Jesus multiplied symbols for us among the waves.
I fell before his symbols, for he depicted for us the resurrection of the dead in all our mysteries and all our types. “Out of the eater came food,”
Samson said in his riddle. But the opposite happened to me: out of the food came an eater for me. For look—from Adam came the son of Adam who has brought me to an end.

The righteous, too, did much to break me, for through them the resurrection of the dead was proclaimed. Yet they mixed great comfort into my mourning: through the prayers of Asa and Hezekiah I feasted on the slain.

I also dined on corpses. Elijah slaughtered the prophets of Baal and gave them to me; they had been fattened on Jezebel’s bread. The righteous compelled me to gorge myself, but Jesus compelled me to give back to you what I had eaten.
I was afraid of that sprinkled blood which Moses sprinkled on every doorway, because, though it was slain, it protected the living. As for blood, from
the beginning I feared none except the blood on the doorways, and now this blood on the cross. The blood of the slain is a delight, and like a fragrance
that is pleasant. But the blood of Jesus is a terror to me, for whenever I went to smell his blood, the scent of life hidden within it terrified me.
Priests and high priests, anointed ones and kings, who displayed types of the resurrection of the dead, did not win their victories through their crosses.
They wore wreaths and crowns. When I entered their contests, I received blows and also dealt blows. But this carpenter’s son,
with his crown of thorns, humbled my arrogance and cast it down through lowliness and death. Sheol saw him and trembled before him.
The sea saw Moses and fled; it feared his staff and his glory. I saw his radiance, his staff, and his authority,
and also that rock which was split open. But Sheol, whose graves were torn open—what did she see in Jesus? Instead of radiance, the pallor of the dead
he wore, and he shook her. And if the appearance of his slayer [?] killed her, how will she be able to endure when he comes in his glory to raise the dead? [End.]
Nisibis XL
6. To the same tune.
The Evil One became aware of his great humiliation and boasted before his servants. He spoke grandly as he declared, “The knowledge I possess—
a little of it comes from nature, but most of it, indeed all of it, comes from learning. I was my own teacher, and I exercised my mind. Without a teacher I learned
everything. I equipped myself with everything, and through it I carried off the crown I desired among humanity.” Response: Blessed is he who came and put an end to the schemes of sin.
It was in the Pharisee that I put on my hateful qualities to fight against that son of Mary. Wrath rained arrows like a bow; insolence insulted him,
and wantonness assailed him. Injustice oppressed him; envy and jealousy angrily quarreled with him.
Blasphemy picked up stones. The physician entered and stood among the sick, and I stirred up the sick to fight against him.
Since he did not fall under accusation, I took refuge in questions. I kept stirring up pretexts, but I saw that my deceit had been exposed and my shamelessness had become known,

and my obstinacy was held in contempt. I hid behind the twists and turns of argument. Wherever I disputed with him, all my labor became like chaff, and the word of truth scattered it in every direction.
She saw that he was an athlete, a mighty warrior, skilled within a human being. [The crawling creature outside frightens her,] while his impulse is within.
He burns; his zeal constantly hisses like a snake. He produces deadly desires, yet he is terrified of fire. The commandment, in place of
a medicinal root, can restrain him, [the tormentor who strikes to destroy]. Love can break the tongue’s hidden and bitter sting.
