Who is more foolish than a human being, who cares for his dwelling more than for himself? Every day he inspects the vessels in his storage bag, while a moth lies hidden in his limbs. He sews up the tears in his clothes, while there is

a tear in his mind. His house is bright because of him, but his heart is dark. He plasters over his senses and washes his windows. His door is locked and his money guarded; his mouth is broken open and the treasure of his thought is stolen.

The fool values his livestock above himself, caring more for his possessions than for himself. He sows good seed in his land, but sows weeds in his heart. His mind lies broken down and abandoned, while over the fences
of his vineyards he labors. He selects and plants saplings, while his mind is a vine from the vines of Sodom. All his seed is [?], and the wild boar grazes on his thought.

I am a furnace for human beings, and their minds are tested through me. Therefore I am permitted to weave deception. I teach astrology, so that through true things I may gain acceptance and be trusted concerning
false things. In Egypt I bewitched their eyes: I showed them lice, and they thought they existed, although they did not. Through illusion I teach zodiac signs that do not exist in heaven.

Through my swiftness I flew and saw, and showed things beforehand to the diviner. Those whom I misled considered me a prophet. There are times, however, when I act boldly and ask that, for the space of

an hour, hidden things may be revealed to me, so that through me the faithful may be tested, like Job, and also the false, like Saul. One I exposed in his divination; another I refined in his truthfulness, and he was praised.
Nisibis 41
7. To the same tune.
The Evil One said: “I was afraid of him, of Jesus, lest he bring my activities to an end. For look, I am thousands of years old, and I have never been idle.
I have never seen anything being put in order and neglected it or left it alone. He has come, the one who puts the vile to shame. Now I will mourn, for he has torn down everything I built.
My labors multiplied along with my disciples, for I covered the whole creation with every kind of evil.” Response: Blessed is he who came and exposed the schemes of the cunning one.

“I matched my running against the swift and surpassed them. I fought, and the tumult of the multitude was my weapon. I rejoiced in the people’s tumult, because it gave an opportunity to the swift one, for fierce

is the assault of the multitude. With the strength of the multitude I raised a great mountain, a tower stretching up to heaven. If they fought against heaven, how much more will they defeat someone whose battle is on earth!
I fight skillfully, in step with the times and with their help. The people heard that God is one, and made themselves a multitude of gods. But when they saw the Son of God, they ran
to the one God, so that, while seeming to acknowledge God, they would deny him, and while seeming zealous, they would flee from him. Thus in every age they would prove contrary and be without God.
Look, I am many years old, and I have never looked down on a newborn. I have taken great trouble over children, so that habits
that are not good I might have them acquire from the beginning, so that their faults would grow up with them. There are also foolish fathers who do not
He weakens the seed that I sowed in their children. And there are some who, like good farmers, uprooted faults from their children's minds.
Instead of chains, I bound people with laziness, and they stopped working and sat idle. I deprived their senses of good things, their eyes of reading, their mouths of praise, their minds
of instruction. How diligent they are at destructive and idle tales, how unrestrained in empty talk! If a word of life comes up, they either push it away or get up and move away from it.
How many satans there are within a human being! Yet everyone curses only me. For a person's anger is a demon that torments him every day. Demons resemble guests,
who leave if they are forced to. But even if all the righteous adjure anger, it cannot be uprooted from its place. Instead of loathsome envy, everyone hates the contemptible and weak demon.
The sorcerer is put to shame, along with [?]. He subdues snakes every day, but the viper within him has rebelled against him, for his desire
within him he does not subdue. Hidden sin is like an asp: when it breathed on him, he went astray, when he approached it, the viper.
Through his craft, my deception struck him secretly. He holds the reptile spellbound with his incantations; with his incantations he rouses great wrath against himself.
I set out stings and sat waiting. Who is there whose mind is patient with everyone? [?] I sat beside the patient man, and step by step I wore him down, so that he would fall into despair.
As for the one who recoils from sins, habits subdued him. Little by little I trained him until he was under the yoke. He entered and grew accustomed to it, and did not even want to leave.

I realized and saw that it is the patient one who can subdue everyone. When I conquered Adam, he was alone. I left him while he was having children, and sought another occupation for myself, so that idleness would not taste

me. I became a counter of the sand of the sea, to practice patience with it and test whether my memory would suffice for human beings when they multiplied. Before they multiplied, I tested them in many ways.

The Evil One's workers argued with him and refuted his words with counterarguments: “Look,” they said, “Elisha raised the dead! The one who conquered death in the upper room and brought the widow's son to life—look,

he is now enslaved in Sheol!” But the Evil One was very astute in his thinking. He refuted their words with their own words: “How was Elisha defeated? Look, in Sheol he raised a dead man through his bones!
If Elisha, who was insignificant, had great power within Sheol—if he brought one dead man to life there—how many dead people will the mighty death of Jesus bring to life there?
From this, my companions, understand how much greater Jesus was! Look, he deceived you with his cunning, and you could not fathom his greatness, since you compared him to the prophets.
Your consolations are meager,” the Evil One says to those of his own ranks. “For how can death overpower the one who brought Lazarus to life when he was dead? And if death does conquer him,

it is he himself who has chosen to submit to it. And if he is willing to submit, be all the more afraid, for he does not die for nothing. He has brought great disaster upon us, for by dying he enters to bring Adam to life.”

Death peered out from within his cavern, and when he again saw our Lord crucified, he said, “You who bring the dead to life, where are you? You will become food for me in place of beloved Lazarus! For look,

Its taste is still in my mouth. Let Jairus’s daughter come and see. Here is your crucified one; the widow’s son is looking at you. The tree caught Adam for me. Blessed is the cross that caught the Son of David for me!

Death opened his mouth and said, “Have you not heard, Son of Mary, that Moses, who grew great and surpassed everyone, became a god and did what God does? He killed the firstborn and rescued the firstborn.

He held back the plague from the living. I went up the mountain with Moses, and he whose glory is blessed handed him directly over to me. However great a human being becomes, he is dust and returns to his dust, for he is from the earth.”
Satan came with his workers to see our Lord, who lay in Sheol, and to rejoice with Death, his royal kinsman. But he saw him
downcast and mourning over the dead who, at the Firstborn’s voice, had come to life and gone out of Sheol. The Evil One stood up to comfort
Death, his kinsman: “You have not lost as much as you thought. As long as Jesus is inside you, both those who have come to life and those who are living will come into your hands.”

“Open up for us to see him and mock him. Let us answer and say, ‘Where is your power? Look, it has already been three days for him!’ Let us say to him, ‘You who are on your third day, who raised Lazarus on his fourth day,

bring yourself to life!’” Death opened the gates of Sheol, and the radiance of our Lord’s face shone out from it. Like the people of Sodom, they were struck down; they groped about and searched for Sheol’s gate, which had vanished.
Nisibis 42
8. To the same tune.
The Evil One wailed: “Where can I now flee from the righteous? I incited Death so that I might kill the apostles and escape their
torments. Now, through their deaths, I am tormented even more severely! The apostle whom I killed in India has preceded me to Edessa. He is entirely here
and also there! I went there, and there he was! Here and there I found him, and I was distressed.” Refrain: Blessed is the power that dwells in the victorious bones!
That merchant was carrying bones.
“Or perhaps it was they that carried him! For they traded with one another. But what does it matter to me that they helped and were helped by one another? For me, in either case,
it is a loss! Who will show me that money box of Iscariot, from which I used to gain strength? Thomas’s casket has killed me, for the hidden power dwelling in it torments me!”
Moses, the chosen one, carried bones in faith, as something profitable. If that great prophet believed that help was to be found in bones, the merchant did well to believe.

And rightly was he called a merchant! This merchant traded, grew great, and became a king. “His treasure has greatly impoverished me!” His treasure was opened in Edessa and enriched the great city with its benefits.
I marveled at this store of treasures, for its treasury was small at first. As long as no one took from it, it was too poor for anyone to seek its riches. But when many surrounded it

and plundered it and seized its benefits, the more it was plundered, the more its wealth increased. For if someone stirs up a confined spring, it breaks forth all the more, swells, flows, and overflows.
It is clear that Elisha too was a spring among a thirsty people. Because the thirsty did not stir him up, his flow did not increase. But when Naaman stirred him up,

he overflowed and poured out healing. He took the spring and cast it into the spring, for in the river he cleansed the leprosy. Jesus, the sea of benefits, sent the blind man to Siloam, and his eyes were opened.

Gehazi could not raise the boy with the staff of the raiser of the dead. How, then, did the victorious one come up through a necromancer? It was we who mocked Saul: instead of the one demon he asked for, two
demons came up and mocked him. Learn from Elisha’s bones about Samuel’s too: if bones brought a dead man to life, a dead necromancer cannot bring up living and holy bones.
How often I asked for this request, but the Giver of all did not grant it to me! For if demons had been stirred by the bones of a pagan priest, or of a magus or sorcerer, of a Chaldean

or a diviner, I too would have known that it was a mockery. I would have led people astray in two ways: either I would have discredited the apostles, or I would have made my apostles resemble the apostles.
Look, the ranks of demons are being emptied; the ranks of devils are bearing lashes. Though no one visibly raises a rod, demons cry out in pain. Though no one has bound or fettered them,

the spirits hang suspended and fettered. This is a tranquil judgment, restful and quiet, which does not even toil at questioning. A single power, sufficient for this, has now taken up residence in the bones of the second Elisha.
He gave his twelve authority to judge, so that they might judge the twelve tribes. If the apostles are destined to judge the children of great Abraham, surely it is no great thing

for them to judge demons now. If the crucifiers do not acknowledge the Judge who is to come, let them consider our own judgment: they will cry out worse than we do before the apostles, the judges of the tribes.
For the apostle Saul was a wolf, and I raised him on the blood of sheep. He grew strong and became a lone wolf. But near Damascus the wolf was suddenly changed into a sheep. He used to say
that the apostles were destined to judge angels. For he called the priests angels, as it is written. If they have such authority, woe to the demons from the lashes dealt by their bones!
Nisibis 43
To the tune of “They Comforted with the Promise.”
Joseph was a wall for himself in a time of peace. Moses carried his bones so that they might be a wall for his camp in the wilderness. For he saw that people,
dead to its Creator through its idols. He carried dead bones so that, on behalf of the living, they might be a censer of atonement, an advocate for reconciliation. Refrain:
Let not the bodies of the righteous who believed in you be wronged.
In the bedroom Joseph saw the One who sees all, where a person supposed that no one could see him. In his youth he put on the restraints of chastity.
Moses carried his bones so that they might rebuke the people whom the daughters of Midian openly praised. He accused the sexually immoral through the bones of the victorious one.
Moses left the living and ran to the dead. They were his fellow workers. The breaches in the people multiplied: it was a vineyard whose fence had been broken down
for tramplers. But that blessed turtledove grew strong among its vines. She stole the blessing and brought it out from the place of ruins to the dwelling of the nations.
Elisha’s bones sowed hope in Sheol. The power hidden in the bones comforted the dead. Death saw the dead man move and was terrified.
Who has seen such a wondrous sight: a dead man snatched a corpse from Death’s mouth and brought it to life! The buried man was accompanying his buriers home.
Sheol inspected her treasury, the storehouses of all our bodies. She secured her gates and her bars and felt confident, for she had never seen a bone move.
Ezekiel’s voice had astonished her. The bones stirred, sought one another, and joined together. As they joined, Sheol herself grew faint and came undone.
At the sound of the bones, Death fled and hid in his caverns. He grew sick because of the dead; he thought his end had come. He summoned Sheol, gave her his instructions, and made her his heir.
He abandoned hope and drew up a will. In his terror he admitted that he was passing away, and put in writing that he was poor and that the deposit would have to return to its giver.
The dead rose to live, the buried to bury others, those lying down to walk, and the silent to speak. For Hezekiah, David guarded his city from his grave. And the bones
appealed to Josiah, and they did not approach that old man. Through bones they protected his bones. He deceived, killed, and buried; yet he believed, sought refuge, and escaped.

For that old man led the innocent man astray, yet believed that when the one who had strayed was killed, he himself would escape through him. It is a marvel that, although he killed him, he believed he could take refuge in him. Who has seen such a wonder in Sheol? A murdered man, over his murderer,
was keeping watch in the grave. How much more, my brothers, will those slain in Christ keep watch!
Again, Elisha laid his sick hands upon the healthy hands of the king who came down to visit him. They gained strength and shot the arrow of deliverance.
One should marvel at the sickness of the strong: he seeks healing for the bodies of those who visit him. Make me worthy of their visitation, you who visit those who visit you.
Their sickness, then, gave strength to kings. Their three names helped six hundred thousand. May they stop up my enemy Satan’s
mouth, for my advocates are good and bold, eloquent and numerous. They can delay the accuser in court and give relief to the guilty.
Let us marvel at them, my brothers, for their weapon is silence. Through silence they plead with the one who hears the silent. Discerning silence is prayer to the one who knows
everything. My advocates are hired for little, yet they labor greatly. They are bribed on my behalf with weeping, hired on my behalf with the tears I have poured over their graves.
Let us run to their graves so that we may live through their deaths. Elisha’s bones bear witness to their bones, for he gave life through them. Death grew afraid
and learned, and began to honor the bones of the righteous within Sheol, rebuking the unbelievers who paid no heed to the resurrection, which even Sheol perceives.
For nothing is dead to the one who gives life to all, except that death concerning which he swore and said that he had never desired the death
of the sinner. Although everything is easy for the Lord of all, it is difficult to reverse the death of free choice, when someone dies by his own will—the death that comes through sins.
For even the body is the vessel of free will’s life. Free will killed it in the beginning in Paradise, when, by its own authority, it broke down the barrier of the law.
For the Righteous One, who made free will sovereign, did not want to compel it by force. It had been given authority, yet it violated his will and died by its own choice.
Sleep is very dear to the weary, and death is a friend to the one who fasts and keeps vigil. Natural sleep does not kill those who sleep.
Nor has Sheol killed, nor does it kill. Sleep brings refreshment, and Sheol too leads to resurrection. As for that second death, there is no remedy for it.
Sleep in beds has never been angry with the one who slumbers and sleeps, for he will soon awaken again. Nor has Sheol been angry, nor is it angry, my brothers.
Look, sleep rebukes Sheol: morning awakens sleepers, and the voice raises the dead. It is the death of free choice that has cut off its hope with its own hands.
This, then, namely, what was difficult for his justice, he granted in his grace, since it is easy for our will: that we should live in spirit, and he should raise the body.
For when creeping things and wild animals eat it, both the eaten and the eaters return to the earth, and their dust is separated at the resurrection as in a furnace.
For if a craftsman should choose to grind up gold and scatter it again in the earth, he separates it and takes it out of the earth in a furnace.
How much more will the Creator refine the body at the resurrection! In his furnace he separates everything, removing and throwing away the dust of the animals.
For look: in the mind of our Maker himself, human dust was distinctly marked out. He separated and took Adam’s dust and fashioned him.
Thus the dust of humanity was distinct and marked out in his mind, and it alone he raises up. Look at the beginning, which bears witness to the end.
Copper, though it is perishable, is distinct within its ore, and before it is stripped out, it is visible to its craftsman. Even if it falls back into its earth, it rests within it
again. How much more, for the Knower of all, is everything distinct—every kind of dust according to its species! Greater to him than all of them is human dust, for it is the robe of his Beloved.
The Firstborn is wrapped in the body; it is the veil of his glory. The Bridegroom who does not die shines in that robe. Let the invited guests, in their robes, resemble that robe of his.
Let your bodies, your garments, shine, for they bound that man whose body was stained. Look upon my stains at your banquet with your rays.
See how many enclosing depths the body has torn open and left: the womb at its birth, the grave at its resurrection. It overcame the den of wild animals
and the furnace. The fish that swallowed it gave it back again. It walked in the sea, flew and soared in the air, and sat at the right hand, crowned with glory.
Who has confined it? Who has bound it? What enclosing depth can possibly contain it, if it did not spare even the womb that bore it?

With its birth pains it broke through and came out, leaving the womb behind. Now it is empty of it, for it never returned and entered it again. How thoroughly its departure and resurrection will lay waste to Sheol!
Elijah’s ascent teaches believers that both together ascended in the chariot—the body and the soul—to that dwelling above.
The men who went out and searched, but did not find him, taught that he had not taken off his body and thrown it away somewhere: he ascended whole, in the body, because he had been holy in the body.
Elijah’s very dust also teaches this: it was separated and left behind by him, borrowed and perishable. It was shaken off, separated, and fell, for it is a temporary garment,
to give assurance concerning the body that was caught up: that its nature is a true garment, which accompanied its wearer. The dust separated and fell, while the body flew and ascended.
The Jordan too set barriers in its course. The waters restrained themselves; its streams supported one another. It abandoned its free course,

which was natural to it, and flowed backward, contrary to its nature, to give assurance, as it gathered and rose at the command, that the body, in the victorious ones, flies and ascends to the height.
But if it is difficult for Noah’s decayed body to rise, far more difficult is the case of Enoch, whose body did not dissolve. Through the mystery of Enoch he taught us that the dead are alive
to him. Through Moses and Elijah, who appeared, he rebuked those who deny: those who are buried are alive, and those who are left behind fly upward. Make me worthy of your coming. [End.]
Nisibis 44
2. To the same tune.

The Good One fashioned the body to teach those who go astray how great the work of his hands is, and that it endures forever. The Just One breathed in the soul to teach how much greater it is than that.

of the animals, into which he did not breathe. For the one into which no breath was breathed has a silent and mute mouth, while the one into whose mouth he breathed has a mouth that also speaks. Refrain:
May soul and body, my Lord, rejoice in your resurrection.
Weigh the human being alongside the animals in the scales of understanding, and consider him in your mind: just as the beast is destined for destruction
and passes away entirely, in every form, so humanity is a treasure kept safe; in its entirety, at the resurrection, it is destined for life.
Look again at the constitution of the animals, and see that it is entirely consistent with itself. It is all alike in this: it is all without hope,
to refute those who have gone astray and divided human nature. Although it is a unified whole, they have placed half of it under hope and half of it without hope.
The beast that suffers injustice bears witness to our recompense: its labor is without hope, its running without reward, its suffering without a promise, and its entire being without resurrection,
to teach the human being, so that you may be convinced that, for the two under one yoke, their race leads to a crown, their labor to the promise, and their suffering to victory.

Now two arguments depend on this weak man: to explain the unrewarded race of the animals, and to explain the reward promised to the human being; and to explain that there is no injustice in the Creator, who promised the human being
the Garden and Gehenna, and gave the animals abundant comforts without obligations.
Look again at the animals: none has endured hardship and lent anything to God, so that we might say they are being wronged. The body has endured hardship, lending its fasting to righteousness.
And if it has no resurrection, it has been wronged. Louder than Abel’s blood, its silence within the earth cries out over what it has entrusted, before him who repays everyone.
Kill an animal and learn that no one puts you to death. Its soul passes away along with that body, and there is nothing in it that comes to resurrection.
This is a saying that resolves every dispute: just as the souls of animals are like their bodies, so our body is destined to live in the likeness of our soul.
The Scriptures teach the discerning, and nature teaches those who deny: what passes away is preserved for a full span of time, while what does not pass away is preserved forever.
Whoever kills it is killed. Its dissolution makes clear that his own imprisonment lasts forever. The serpent, who deceived it and brought about its dissolution, is cursed in every way by everyone.
For birds, fish, and animals are slaughtered with a blessing, and with it they are also eaten. With it grain is harvested; with it is picked
the fruit. No one who slaughters or picks is cursed. But if the human body is destined for destruction, why is a curse laid on the serpent or the murderer, or why are they accursed?
Grain that has withered and fallen, and fruit that has lost its flavor and spoiled, reproach the farmer who delayed and did not gather it, and did not strip and separate the grain from the straw.
According to their argument, it is right to blame anyone who does not kill an old man whose flavor has faded, to loosen the heavy bond from that soul.
And the whole reason why old men who are no longer useful are spared

is so that the Good One may teach liars the truth through them: even though the sword brings relief to an old man, the young man who strikes him is struck. He destroys the youth that destroyed old age, to teach us how dear the body is to its Maker.
An old man full of every infirmity is a bearer of troubles. Everyone waits for his death, but no one kills him. Although his death is welcome, there is great fear of
killing him, so that we may learn through his lowliness how glorious he is, how honored he was when he was in Paradise, and how great his glory will be when he rises and is raised to life.
Nisibis XLV
3. To the same tune.
If the soul eats and fasts and receives a reward, it is right that the body too should receive a reward, since it fasted with the soul. And if it is well known that it was the body that ate and also

fasted, rebuke those who go astray: how greatly they have erred, saying that the soul, which did not fast, should receive the reward, while the body, which fasted and toiled, should remain without a reward! Refrain:
At your resurrection, may the body receive its partner.

The soul too, they say, is afflicted by the body's fasts and sufferings. And if the borrowed sufferings that came to it from the body benefited it, how much more will the body live through the beatings
of its limbs! For this is an injustice even to hear: if the soul grew great through the force of the body's victories, how much more should the body grow great through the reward for its races!

It is shameful that the body should labor and the soul receive the reward. It is shameful that the body should receive fire and the soul recognition. It is foolish that the body should receive the sword and the soul, instead,
the crown of life. The body was killed for the sake of its Creator; it lost its life here and its resurrection in the world beyond. Oh, how twisted is the whole account of those who go astray!
For the body is hunger, wakefulness, and thirst—the resources without which the soul cannot grow rich. The soul has cheated the merchant of both principal and interest,
for look, it grows rich from the profit on the body's talents! Yet instead of its profits, fools have drawn up a certificate of debt against the body, declaring that it has no resurrection.

It is unjust that the body should go hungry while the soul boasts of its fasting. It is unjust that the body should be parched while the soul is praised for its thirst. The soul took the wages of the body's labors and left it the dregs.
And, as they say, it is set apart for fire. They have cheated the farmer who exhausted himself: they took his grain and left him chaff and straw in which to burn.

It is just that the body should be in glory and the soul too in praise. It is just that the body should have life and the soul too be alive. It is just that the body should be in Eden and the soul too
in Paradise. For what they say is unjust: that half of a human being should live in the kingdom, while the other half, which committed no wrong, should be thrown into torment.
The followers of error are blind when they look at the contest. If there is victory, they attribute it to the soul; but if there is disgrace, they attach it to the name
of the body. They do not even behave like spectators in this world, who sometimes acclaim the charioteer and sometimes acclaim the horses for winning.
If the soul's essence is pure and beautiful, then the body is ugly and labors to adorn itself. If it becomes ugly, woe to it; and if it becomes beautiful, a double
woe! Although the body bears the burden of desire, virginity belongs to the soul, along with the reward for chastity. The essence comes and raises its voice at the eleventh hour.

But if desire and greed belong to the soul, the body has a complaint against it, for it has been choked by the soul's vile deeds. If the soul is indeed unruly, reckless, and dissolute, why has the body been wronged through its desire?
Joseph is wronged and silent, while his mistress's voice is loud. Naboth received a heap of stones, and Jezebel the vineyard.
And how can the body be washed by any means if it is mixed from the four elements of its being? And how did it disturb the pure nature of that
soul? For the body cannot disturb it, since light is not disturbed by shadows; rather, by shining, it clears away the shadow.
Fools who turn things around have turned the story around: they say that darkness grew bold and disturbed the light. They can easily be refuted by the witnesses
they themselves have brought forward. For both walk among us, and light is never dyed by darkness; rather, by shining, it dyes what is black.
It is one of two things; let the followers of error choose: if the body cannot

So that it may become beautiful and be washed clean. The soul dwelling in it is choked by its filth, and it is rust that must be rubbed away for it to be polished. But if the body is a nature that can be purified, the Evil One has confused those who have declared it to be without resurrection.
Let us ask the deniers: Who supplied a cause of life to something that was dead? Through that cause of life it could live
by it. And if he brought it to life at our beginning [?], all the more will he raise it, since he has given it a taste of life. Let those who deny even easy things be put to shame by difficult ones.

He who gave it life for a little while is not too weak to give it much more. He who called it from the grave will not grow weary of calling it again. And he who was good in forming it—how just he will be
in raising it! For if he gave it life freely in the beginning, how much more will the Just One raise it to repay it! Be rebuked by grace, you who deny justice!
But if that body is a nature incapable of coming to resurrection, let us first ask how it was possible for it to live through
the soul. For how was that will which brought it to life sufficient to give life to something that was not alive? Be defeated by its life, you who deny its resurrection!
Even that robber who perceived your kindness became an advocate for your silence, which defeats everyone. He became rich on the right hand, having rebuked the left.
Have mercy, my Lord, on my sinfulness, for I have believed and rebuked the deniers who stand on the left. Let this be the reward for my words: do not exact my debt from me.
Nisibis 46
4. To the same tune.
Let the followers of error explain how the body is unclean to our Savior, who came down and dwelt in Mary and today dwells in the bodies of chaste men and women.
If a king dwells in a place, he grants it freedom and makes it great. And the Good One who dwelt in the body—did he really promise it this: that it should have no resurrection? Refrain:
Let the buried body that believed in you not be denied its due.
The Exalted One humbled himself even to the body and washed its feet. The heels that were honored teach how greatly he will exalt the head
at the resurrection. He carried it in the children and honored it; he lifted it onto his breast and cherished it in John. These things are enough to put Bardaisan to shame.
The coin, which resembles a dead person in its images, is fashioned from the earth and fell back into it and was lost. It is a stamped image that resembles the body, which comes from the earth.
And it is right that, according to the symbolism of the coin, there should be joy at the body's discovery for grace, which labored and found it, as the woman did for the coin.
He magnified the widow's small coin [?] and her mite. He also became for her an observer, a witness, and a guarantor, and showed that the treasury had accepted
her offering. Learn from the mite, which he did not deprive of its due: how could he deprive the body that traded and gained talents through the sword of persecutors?
An image without senses, a stamped figure without movement—the coin he brought up in a fish's mouth to his glory. How much more will he be glorified in his image
that can speak! He commanded the one that swallowed it; at the end, as with the coin, it will return and give him the image stamped in the likeness of its Maker.
The Good One, whose oath assures us that he will not withhold the reward for a cup of cold water given for his name's sake—how could he deny the body its virginity's due,
when it has struggled in the contest for a hundred years, and its enemy has not left it alone even in a dream? Who would not lament if this body were denied its due?
The three defeated that fire in a single day, but this one has defeated every day the fire dwelling within it: even as it was being quenched, it blazed, and as it lingered, it consumed.
Blessed is the one who thirsted and quenched it! If fire blazes up, it is quenched with water; but if this fire is quenched, it is set ablaze with wine.
But our Lord’s care assures us that he healed the whole human being in every respect: he baptized him in the Holy Spirit and nourished him with the medicine of life.
How hateful are Mani and Marcion and blind Bardaisan! They read but do not see that the whole human form is put back together at the resurrection.
For even the ear that Simon cut off and threw away—the Exalted One bent down, picked it up, and attached it so that it would not perish. How much more will he look after the whole body
at the resurrection, so that none of its dust is left behind! Not even in the furnace was any part of the head lost, to make known the care he will exercise at the resurrection.
If, concerning the bread, he gave orders and its fragments and leftovers were gathered up—he urged that they be collected and warned that none of his blessing should perish—
how much more does he care for the body, that its bones should be gathered, its joints fitted together, and its voices proclaim the glory of the one who raises it!
His bread bears indisputable witness to our resurrection: he who blessed the food—how much more will he bless those who eat it! With the twelve loaves that he blessed and multiplied,
he blessed his Twelve and multiplied them. Then he took and broke another loaf, a single one, a symbol of that unique body from Mary.
He gladdened the widow by bringing her beloved back to life. But if, as fools say, the body comes from the Evil One, then it was the Evil One he brought to life, and Satan whom he gladdened!
Again, when he brought Jairus’s daughter back to life, was it sin that he raised in her? By saying that she was asleep, he rebuked those who deny that our body will awaken again.
For when Jonah fell and sank into the sea, the passengers and sailors all gave up hope. Who was mighty enough to say that he would come up

again? And who was wise enough to argue the case? These things were impossible and difficult, but for One they were easy: he signaled to the sea, and it grew calm; he commanded the fish, and it vomited him out.

The seed in its dust is a witness to its resurrection. Even in its death it proclaims its return to life, and its rising is hidden within its fall. Through rain it comes to life and awakens. How much more, at the resurrection,
will the dew be sprinkled upon our dust, through which Adam was formed and brought to life!
Even the locust, which was planted within the earth and buried in the dust as though beyond hope, filled hollows like graves

and left them. But those who deny the resurrection were put to shame: they did not resemble even that locust, which covered and buried its offspring; it was buried and came to life at its appointed time, at the command.
And if a bird’s young are motionless corpses, her love gathers them, her wing cherishes them, and she imprints voice and life upon their dead state.
And the waters are adorned in every form, and she raises the buried ones from within their shells. How much more will graves be split open at the voice of the one who raises all!
Thus, from the very seed of humanity, a person can take an image of his resurrection. For it too, like the dead, is kept within
the womb. Through birth pangs it comes to life and awakens, and comes out into the light, into another world. His conception and birth are guarantees of his resurrection.
Nisibis 47
5. To the same tune.
Fire is hidden within wood, and our mind, through its skills, strikes with a [?] and makes it shine. And if our will brings created things to life, how much
more can the will of the Almighty command and make the soul shine within the body! Though it departed and abandoned the body, it shines within it again. Refrain:
Let body and soul, my Lord, sing praise in your paradise.
My Lord, demand redress for the house in which the soul lived as a tenant. For this is the rent she paid when she departed: she demolished it and left it in ruins. Let her enter and live in it.
Teaching hymn. Let her sing hallelujah within his dwelling and sing praise in his chambers. Let her voice be heard again from the dwelling that has fallen into desolation.
The portions of life that she pours into his limbs, the movements of her thoughts that move within his senses, the stores of her perfumes spread their fragrance

through his arteries. Return what he borrowed, so that he may repay her! Through him she acquires her wealth; through him she voices her praise, when their course and their labors are called to account there.
Through his mouth she offered prayer to the Hearer of all. Through his hands she lent alms to the Repayer of all. Through his eyes she read Scripture; through his ears,
the promise. With his feet she served at the gate of his house. See from experience that she depends entirely on him. Blessed is he who made the soul dependent, so that he might exalt her partner!
His Creator’s will gathers his dust, renews him, and makes him a temple of praise. He brings him in, and in his bridal chamber he comforts his spouse.
The one who was grieved in Sheol rejoices. The one whose hope was cut off shouts for joy at his promise. The one whom fools treated with contempt is overwhelmed with mercy.
His bound feet leap in paradise, and his hands, which had gone limp, gather every blessing. His eyes, which had closed, behold
the Enlightener of all. His mouth, which had fallen silent, opens. His stopped ears hear the trumpet, and his body, which had decayed, shines in glory.
And if, even while anger, lust, greed, and the rest of the hateful passions are barking from him—because he concealed them in the world of his free choice—
the deniers acknowledge that he is a temple, and the Spirit does not recoil from dwelling in his filth, nor is she distressed within him as Jeremiah was in the pit,
rebuke the deniers who have been trapped by their own words! They have condemned themselves by acknowledging that the Holy Spirit dwells within their body, wandering

and gluttonous as it is. While they think they have won, they have been defeated. For if, while filthy, it is a splendid dwelling place, how much more will it receive mercy when purified at its resurrection!
A demon dwells in the body, and although it is a hateful bed, he loves to live in it, though he is an accursed guest. Fasting uproots him, the greedy one who will not
leave. How much more will the soul love her dwelling! For if they came to an agreement together, they drove out the lodger and invited the Holy Spirit to dwell between them.

And if even an unclean spirit dwells in a basin, rests upon a corpse and is bound to it, and joins itself to carved wood that cannot hear, how much more will the Holy Spirit love the body that, in hope,
was sacrificed rather than offer sacrifice! It is clear that even its being killed bears witness to its resurrection.
For our Lord said that he is not the God of the dead—the dead who bury their dead without hope. They had gathered and disputed with him who gives life to human
beings. They were defeated by the very argument they had constructed. He recited Scripture to them and raised the dead for them. Through words and deeds he confirmed the resurrection.
He called Lazarus, and he came out and put them to shame. For if he had been dead to his Lord, he could not have answered him. In his death he was alive to the voice that raised him.
The dead man lived, while they grew envious and died. Our Lord wept over them, the living who were dead, who grieved at the resurrection that brought Lazarus joy.
The dead person in whom hidden life lies buried is alive to God even before being raised. So too the sinner.
He was dead before he died. The dead man was convincing the deniers that they themselves were dead, buried while still alive, puffed up in their clothes, corrupt in their sins.
My Lord, do not let them see me with them in Gehenna and jeer that I am no better than they are. Do not let me suffer injustice, for my tongue has contended for the truth.
My Lord, do not let them see me beside them. Let them know that you have shown me favor at the resurrection because I spoke about the resurrection as much as I could.
Nisibis 48
6. To the same tune.
The Levite’s staff sprouted and grew young again, for the will of the Most High revived it, though it had been cut down. In its silence it whispered to us the mystery of the resurrection.
It was clothed in fruit and leaves. Through its branches it proclaimed joyfully that the priestly garments rightfully belonged to Aaron,

the rightful privileges of ministry.
Refrain: My Lord, redress the wrong done to the body at your resurrection.
The staffs were brought in and laid down, all of them representing the body. When they came out and were separated, one alone was crowned, while all the others were stripped bare and disgrace
was what they bore. See in the staff a mystery of the end: the bodies of the sexually immoral rise in shame, while the bodies of the holy shine in glory.
That staff was placed in the ark, and as long as it was there, it blossomed and rejoiced. It is a symbol of paradise, where bodies rejoice.
The manna assures us about it that it does not decay: while it was inside the jar, it did not spoil, though it was liable to spoil. It is a symbol of mortals who do not die in Eden.
The staff of the son of Amram suddenly acquired eyes. If that which had no such nature acquired a form and life,

how much more beautiful will the body’s natural form become! The staff came alive and moved at a word. If, contrary to its customary state, it acquired what did not belong to it, how much more will the body return to what belongs to it at the resurrection!
Moses preserved the bones, but broke the tablets and threw them down. He honored a corpse more than the tablets. He carved tablets to replace the tablets, to teach
that they were not destined for resurrection. But it was not another body in place of Lazarus’s that came out, so that he might make known that this very body is the one raised.
If anyone touched bones in the wilderness, Moses declared him unclean in writing—Moses whom the bones did not make unclean. For forty years a dead man traveled
in the camp. There he depicted a mystery of the church, in which the death of the one who gives life to all is proclaimed every day. It was the life-giving cross that traveled in the camp.
By the painter’s finger and a wealth of pigments, the king’s image is painted. Because it wears out, craftsmen fashion an image that does not
wear out. Kings exalt their images. Who has ever seen a king become united with his image, put on his likeness, and dwell in it, so that through him his image might receive homage?
Another made an image sixty-six cubits tall. Though he himself was small, he wished to become great through the image. He gathered for that image of his worship
that was rebuked. Our Lord worked a wonder at his coming: though he is without limit, he became small in a despised image, and in that image gathered the worship that had been scattered.

Adam returned to his earth and made a testament. He wrote that he owed a great debt to death and sin. By transgressing the commandment, he sealed himself over as a pledge. Our Lord came, redeemed him, and raised him. Death, in turn, gave a written undertaking, and Sheol stood surety with it,
that they would return at the resurrection everything they had plundered and seized.
The rib of Eve, in turn, multiplied from itself and within itself. A bone brought forth bones, senses, and arteries. She is a shoot from Adam, in whom he himself is hidden.
The beauty of the house whose dust now lies within Sheol—how easy it is for the Architect of all to rebuild it from that dust and with it, at the signal of his coming!
Fish reproduce within the waters without wombs, and the sea, though deadly, keeps them alive in its depths; and although it is very bitter, within its bosom
it nurses them. All of them praise the Lord of all, for fish leap about within the sea in its deadliness, but if they rise into the air, they suffocate in what gives life.
Do not let voices without hope bewilder you, for there is One who, if he commands life, makes it kill you; and he is the one who, if he signals to death, makes it bring life
to you. In the treasury of his will everything is to be found. For the righteous, death is sleep in their graves; for sinners, life kills in Gehenna.
Nisibis 49
7. To the same tune.
Look, my son, at the fairness of the earth, into which people cast stripped wheat and a bare vine cutting. It loads them both with provisions and clothing, with clusters that it has not

borrowed. It repays principal and interest. It repays the farmer; how much more will it repay its Lord his seeds, without interest!
Refrain: May your truth within us be leaven that draws us onward.

For it is not one body that is sown and many that spring from it at the resurrection, as with wheat. One alone fell and raised up the ear of grain of our generations, to expose the deniers—how greatly they denied!
For if he did not put on our body, how did he taste our death? And if his body was not slain, he broke his bread in falsehood.
The earth, which at the command also brings forth creeping creatures, makes harmful stingers swarm with its vitality. How much it rejoices in its son, that he will live
and rise again! For his sake it was exalted when he was formed: the Creator’s hand honored its dust, and for his sake our Lord stooped down and walked upon it.
Barrenness is worse than Sheol by comparison: the seed of life is suffocated within its womb. For in Sheol no living person is ever buried
alive; it is a body that enters it when it has died. If even barrenness has given human beings back, how much more will the earth’s womb give back at the resurrection!
Fire too is harsher than Sheol when put to the test, for both the living and the dead

it swallows in its hunger. Yet it preserved the body within its bosom at the command. The oppressor gave back, and increased what it returned: it restored principal and interest to those watching, for instead of three it displayed four.
It was fire that had devoured many in its greed. Three had fallen into it, and they became more numerous within its bosom. The fire that had withheld everything it had consumed
repaid the man who wished to be defrauded, who had lent in order to destroy. Although he did not demand repayment, it repaid him. He received more and was ashamed; he was repaid and put to shame.
He resembles Satan, who lends and does not demand repayment. His money sinks the borrower down beside him. He lends and charges him the stipulated payment and interest.
Fire returned to one of its own kind something he had not demanded from it. How much more will the earth repay its debt at the resurrection to the Righteous One who demands it from her!
A dead body produces worms without mating. If deadness has brought forth life, how much more will the Giver of life to all bring deadness to life!
A dead body produces offspring within Sheol. If deadness has stirred with life, how much more will its bones stir at the voice of the Giver of life to all!
Let the prophet in the valley teach you how motionless bones stirred at the command. The house built itself when its Architect commanded it,
and Death, who had been king within Sheol, suddenly became a laborer, bringing the bones together and laboring to build that temple which he had cast down.
Merciless winter went out like a bandit. It strips the trees of their garments and leaves them gloomy and naked, taking away their clothing.
In everything it was an image of death. Nisan repays you and, as a symbol of the One who gives life to all, restores their clothing to the flowers and trees.
He revives the grasses and roots, the flowers and blossoms, in their beauty, and dyes them in their colors—the Good One, who cares for the flowers, though they have lent him
nothing. His goodness cares for them in everything. Far be it from his justice to wrong and forget the bodies of his beloved ones at his glorious coming!
Who can hide the sun in his lap? Who can cover a mountain with the folds of his garment? Who can conceal the truth with his arguments?
For he is the hope of those who sleep in death. Who can give the lie to the accumulated evidence? The Good One’s pledges bear witness to his raising of the dead.
If Sarah rejoices that she will welcome Abraham, and that both will be in the kingdom in purity, how much will the soul rejoice
to welcome its companion! Their separation bears witness to their love. Their tears convince you: when they part, they weep, because they long to see one another again at the resurrection.
Call the body to be a witness to its own resurrection. For when Adam was formed, who poured a fountain of discernment into that simple dust?
It was dust that was transformed into all these things: it spoke, saw, heard, smelled, touched, and tasted; it flourished, sinned, and fell; it received mercy, came to life, and rose.

The rock and flint were split open at the command. It swallowed without having done wrong, and payment was demanded of it though it had received nothing. Although it had borrowed from no one, it repaid everyone
with water. Death, which has grown greedy, is emptied by the sudden blast and the thunder of that horn, which [?] the dead to meet the King’s Son.
Just as, if suddenly in the middle of the night there comes very fierce thunder and a very powerful crash, it startles and awakens sleepers and rouses
those sunk in sleep, so it will be with that last horn. Its sound raises the dead, not because it is powerful, but because the command dwells in it at the resurrection.
When they suddenly awaken, they are astonished and alarmed: one remembers his wrongdoing, another his uncleanness. Blessed at that hour is the one who remembered
it! For there, at that hour, they quake and tremble, because pangs of wrath strike the wicked. Let all the righteous pray for me at that time.
Nisibis 50
To the tune of “You, My Lord, Wrote It.”

I will give thanks while I exist; I will not be as though I did not exist. I will give thanks during my life; I will not be dead while I live. For the idle person is doubly dead, and land that lies barren has cheated its farmer.
Refrain:
Through you, my Lord, may my mouth bear the fruit of acceptable praise.
Through you, my Lord, may my mouth bring praises out of silence. Let our mouth not be barren of praise, nor our lips deprived of thanksgiving. May your praise spring up within us.

Those who were formed shaped dust, and those of earth labored on the earth. The body that gave us life is dear to us, like a member of our family. For dust is our root, and our branches bear the fruits of its labors.

“Do not worry about a day”—yet we worry about years. Through the lilies, the One who clothes everyone put weavers to shame. Through greedy ravens, the One who feeds everyone, who gives everything to everyone, rebuked the greedy.

Our generation is like a leaf, and now its time to fall has come. Since the span of our lives is short, let us lengthen our praise. For however long the term of our debt may be, through it we gain life without measure.

For the root of our faith is grafted into our Lord. Though he is far away, he is near us through the mingling of love. May the roots of our love be bound to him, and may the streams of his compassion mingle with us.
My Lord, may the body be a temple for its builder, and may the soul be a glorious citadel for its architect. My Lord, let our body not become a swamp, nor our soul a harbor of ruin.

When the light flickered in this breath of time, the lamp that had gone out in the evening shone in the morning. The sun came with the heat of its rising, raising those who were cold and lighting those who had gone out.
It is right that we give thanks to that Light who enlightens all. In the morning the lamp goes out when the sun rises. The new Sun does something new: in Sheol he lights lamps that have gone out.
In place of death, which has spread the smell of its deadness everywhere, a living fragrance that gives life to all breathes through Sheol. From his life the dead draw new life, in which death dies.

It is a symbol that the fragrance of the buried man gives life to the dead man. The man newly dead drew life from the one long dead. A living fragrance breathed from the bones and entered the corpse: a mystery of the one who gives life to all.

Jesus explained to us the mysteries that took place in Sheol: from that extinguished lamp another lamp shone. While he himself lay there, he raised up one who had fallen. He remained and sent witnesses ahead of his coming.

However much I feel for you, my Lord, it is not you that I touch, for my mind has touched nothing of your hidden nature. I have seen in your mystery an image that is visible and gentle, while the searching out of you remains hidden.
Nisibis 51
To the tune: “O Giver of Discernment.”
My brothers, I encountered a weed that wore the appearance of wheat, to confuse the good seed. Though the farmers had been instructed, they did not remove it, nor did they

uproot it. Yet although the farmers were negligent, the seed grew stronger than the weeds. It grew, increased, covered the weed, and choked it.
Refrain: Glory to you, Giver of life to all.
A book by Bardaisan came my way, and I was compelled for a whole hour to defile my pure ears and make them a passageway for speech full of blasphemy.
Then I hurried and washed them again with the clear and pure reading of the divine Scriptures.
In that reading I heard him blaspheming against Justice and her companion, Grace. For if the body does not rise,
it is a wicked insult to Grace, who created it, as though she had done so for our decay; and it is blasphemy against Justice, who cast it away, as though for destruction.
That reading distressed soul and body equally, for it cast between these beloved companions a separation that cut off hope.
It deprived the body of its resurrection and the soul of her companion. The harm that the serpent inflicted, Bardaisan called a benefit.
If someone who dares to kill a single body deserves death, then someone whose tongue kills all human bodies—
even if he descends into the great sea, the sea cannot stand surety for him, to repay with its measure of water the slaughter his tongue has committed.
How many cruel murderers the frail body has had!
Cain killed it first, and the murderer handed his sword over to others, so that they might rival him. See how all his disciples labor at his craft, to resemble the master who taught himself.
Swords killed it openly, and tongues secretly. The cunning one killed it at the beginning, and the crafty one afterward.
The bitter serpent sweetened his tongue as he killed it. His bitter disciples likewise killed it with a sweet tongue.
Body, may the good compassion of your Maker stand up against the wrong done to you. The serpent cast you out of Paradise, and his offspring cast you out of the kingdom.
He deprived you of life, and these men deprive you of resurrection. The serpent hurried at the beginning, and his disciples at the end.
But the soul, which is clothed in the body, takes great care of it, lest they be separated from one another in this passing life.
And how could it bear to live without it in the end? For its love for the body does not let it hold back from the body's resurrection.
See how their claim is refuted and undone when they are terrified of the sword and of the biting reptile. The sons of
the serpent feared the serpent, the killer, on account of the body. They ought to have hated its life, just as they hated its resurrection.
For hateful desires are hateful when they are put into practice. It is these that the law condemns; it is these that the judge pursues.
It is for these that the penitent feels remorse. The body is honored in Scripture; it is also loved by nature, and human beings take care of it.
The Creator also calls the murderer to account for destroying the body. The Just One dissolves his bodily structure, so that he may learn how evil its destruction is.
For the image that grace fashioned, he makes him suffer in the body that he made suffer. In his own body the murderer learns that he destroyed the Maker's temple.
But if the murderer is called to account, it is not because he killed anyone's soul. According to their claim, he merely released it. And if the one who releases it is a murderer,
where will Bardaisan flee? He sharpens his tongue in controversy and has killed the body by excluding it from the life that is given at the resurrection.
The first one killed it by his counsel, and the dragon also by his teaching. That one killed it as though caring for it, and these men do so as though helping it.
Through their cunning, the disputants have become the serpent's partners. The serpent's sons are destined to be put to shame, like their first father.
Through the body's limbs and senses the soul learns everything good. And if the body is hateful, how can the soul do good through it?
And if it is deceitful by nature, how can the soul learn truth through it? For no one gives a craftsman a tool unsuited to his work.
For a scribe does not write a book with a farmer's blade, nor does a painter paint with a carpenter's saw. Nor does
a physician heal an eye with a scorpion's hateful sting, nor does he ever lance an abscess with the bone of a snake or a horned serpent.
For everything is properly accomplished, with discernment, through a tool suited to it and a sense that works with it. The body too,
if it belongs to sin, no one can become righteous through it. The righteous who triumphed through it threaten anyone who maligns it.
Nisibis 52
On Satan and Death. To the tune of “O Death, Do Not Exalt Yourself.”
I heard the voices of Death and Satan as they argued over which of them was stronger against humanity. Refrain:
Glory to you, Son of the Shepherd of all, who rescued his flock from the hidden wolves that swallowed it: the Evil One and Death.
Death displayed his power, by which he conquers everyone. Satan displayed his cunning, by which he leads everyone into sin.
“Only those who wish to obey you listen to you, Evil One. But to me they come, whether they wish to or not.”
You, Death, have only the coercive force of tyranny; I have the traps and snares of cunning.
Listen, evil one: anyone who is shrewd has broken your yoke, but no one can rebel against mine.
You, Death, have tested your strength against the sick; I, however, am even more powerful in dreams.
The evil one has no authority over everyone who reviles him. As for me, those who have cursed me and those who curse me come into my hands.
You, Death, received your power from God; but I alone lead people into sin, with no one helping me.
You, evil one, set traps like a weakling; I exercise authority like a king.
You are too foolish, Death, to know how great I am: I have managed to capture sovereign free will itself.
You, evil one, go about like a beggar; I crush like a lion, and I am not afraid.
You, Death, have no one who serves you or worships you; kings have served me with sacrifices as though I were God.
Many call upon Death as upon a benefactor; but no one has called upon you, evil one, or calls upon you now.
Are you not aware, Death, how many invoke me under all sorts of guises and offer sacrifices to me?
Your name is hateful, Satan. Do not dress up your name: everyone curses it. Hide your disgrace!
You are hard of hearing, Death: you do not hear that everyone howls against you. Hide yourself!

***
My face is uncovered throughout creation, for I have not practiced deceit like you: you do not pass a night without deceit.
You have gained no advantage by being honest, since human beings hate you too, just as they hate me.
Everyone fears me as a master; but they hate you as an evil one.
They hate both your name and your deeds, Death. My own name is hated, but my pleasures are greatly loved.
That sweetness of yours turns into gnashing of teeth; remorse always accompanies your pleasures.
Hateful is Sheol, where there is not even repentance—the abyss that swallows and stills every movement.
Dreadful is Sheol, but everyone who has fallen into it will be raised. It is sin that is hateful, for it has cut off humanity’s hope.
Although it grieves me, I have made room for those who repent; you have cut off the hope of the sinner who died in his sins.
Who ever came to you with his hope already cut off? For if you had not led him into sin, he would have departed well.

***
Blessed is he who set those accursed servants against one another, so that we might look upon them as they looked upon us and mocked us.
What we have seen happen to them, my brothers, is a pledge that we shall look upon them again when we are raised.
Nisibis LIII
2. To the same tune.
Come, let us listen as they fight over victory—the defeated ones who have never won and never will.
Death says to the Evil One, “In the end, victory is mine, for Death holds the final outcome as the victor.”
“True death is [?], if you can kill someone through lusts while he is still alive.”
“Look, I see both good and evil people dying. The righteous who despised you, Evil One, did not despise me.”
“This death of the body is a temporary sleep. Do not think, Death, that you are death, for you are like a shadow.”
“The righteous have defeated you, Evil One, and still defeat you. But look, I defeat those who defeated you.”
“Even when you kill the righteous, the victory is not yours. Because of Adam, whom I defeated, they drank the cup.”
“Look, Sheol is full of Sodomites and Assyrians, and the giants who perished in the flood. Who is like me?”
“All these, Death, were slain by me. I am the one who made them sin so that they would perish.”
“Joseph defeated you, Satan, but I defeated him. He defeated you in the bedroom, but I defeated him and laid him low in the grave.”
“Moses defeated you, Death, by sprinkling blood. He defeated you in Egypt, but who defeated him at the rock?”
“Elijah was not afraid of you, Satan, but he fled from Jezebel because he feared me.”
“Aaron stopped you, Death, with fragrant incense. I gave him gold earrings, and he fashioned a calf.”
“You entered the contest with Job, and he defeated you and came out victorious. But after he defeated you, I in turn defeated him.”
“David stopped that plague with his sackcloth. On the rooftop I defeated the one who defeated Goliath.”
“Jehu demolished the house of Baal, the Evil One’s temple. He could not demolish Sheol, the fortress of my kingdom.”
“Solomon snatched the child from your mouth through his judgment. In his old age I made him a worker at the high places.”
“Samuel despised you, Satan, when it came to gold. I defeated that victor who overcame bribery.”
“Samson despised you, Death, when he faced the young lion. Through Delilah, a frail vessel, I harnessed him to the mill.”
“Josiah despised you from his youth, Evil One. Yet even in his old age he could not overcome me.”
“Hezekiah overcame you, Death, defeating his appointed end. I confused him so that he disregarded the miracle and displayed his treasures.”
“John defeated you, Evil One, and forgave sins and baptized. I extinguished that lamp which was exposing you.”
“Simon defeated you when he brought the blessed woman back to life. He defeated you through a woman, and through a woman I defeated him and made him deny.”
“The apostles and prophets together cursed you, Death: ‘Where is Death’s victory, and where is Sheol’s sting?’”
You imprisoned your Lord in Sheol, you accursed slave! God hates you, and so do human beings. Be still!
His own will confined the one who gives life to all in Sheol. You were the one who summoned him to this, you who made Adam sin.
Companion of the deceitful one who insulted his Lord in the wilderness, accursed is your mouth, which said to him, “Fall down and worship me!”
Nisibis 54
3. To the same tune.
Listen, free will, to the dispute of two slaves, as they accuse each other of being weak. Refrain:
Glory to you! Through your humiliation Adam was exalted, and through your death he was brought back to life and returned to Eden.
If, then, the Evil One defeats you, great is your disgrace: Death, his companion, reproaches him for being weak.
And if Death in turn defeats you, here is your shame: the Evil One, his companion, despises him as a mere shadow.
Their dispute is a mirror for you, in which you can see that both of them are like chaff before your bellows.
The prophets and apostles too, through their promises, teach you that they wither like flowers when you rise.
You are Death, whom both the living and the dead hate. You dissolve and destroy everything that is joined together.
It is not visible death that kills, Satan; it is your hidden death that kills human beings.
Look, my name is not hated like yours, for the angel presented himself as an adversary on the road to Balaam.
How does this name of yours resemble me, Satan? You strayed from the path and also led the innocent Adam astray.
Do not ramble like an ignorant man and lose the thread of your argument. Debate, Death, if you are capable of answering back.
You know that you are clever, Satan, at making a noose out of sand.
Finish your argument, Death! Whoever is losing, once he has finished and exhausted his words, begins to insult.
I am victorious over everyone, yet am I defeated by you? Let Adam, whom you conquered, convince you, Satan!
I am the one who bound Adam and threw him down before you. I came and triumphed over the mighty man whom my tricks had bound.
I am the one who newly bound on a crown in the world, for I imprisoned Adam, the foremost of the mighty, in Sheol.
I killed Adam, who sinned, with a hidden death. You, Death, put to death a dead man whom I had already killed.
In your desire to win, Evil One, you have made yourself hateful: you are both Death and Satan, and even that is too little for you.
Then keep quiet, Death, like a weakling, since neither in words nor in deeds have you been strong enough to stand your ground.
You have won to your own harm, Evil One, if you understand. Your whole crown is disgrace, if you realize it.
Let me lose and you win, Satan! It is better for me to be ignorant than wicked.
Blessed is the Just One who divided those who were so closely united! Blessed is the Good One who unites us who are divided!
May I overcome the Evil One through your forgiveness, you who show mercy to all! May I overcome Death through your resurrection, you who give life to all!
Nisibis 55
4. To the same tune.

See, the Evil One insults Death and is himself insulted. Their insults come from them, pass between them, and fall upon them.
Refrain:
Glory to you, Son of the Lord of all, who died for all and rose again to give life to all on the day of his coming!
Jonah, who defeated you and returned from Sheol, became my advocate, asking why sinners were allowed to live.
Do not wrong that son of Amittai, Evil One! He showed an angry face so that they would give thanks all the more.
All your persuasion is utterly feeble, Death, you tyrant! Nothing you have said has pleased me.
When has a truthful word ever pleased you? Your dwelling is a pit for truth, you liar!
I have been righteous all my days, not a penitent. I am the one who takes human beings away from you.
What repentance, Death! Welcome indeed! A mighty cry: “Is Saul also among the prophets?”
If you, Death, can be declared righteous, then I do not give up hope even for myself, though I do not repent.
I have not set up an idol alongside my Lord, you hater of your Lord! With dead idols you kill the living.
I know that you are my other half, Death, and I am yours. It is my other half that repents—if it does repent! Yet I am amazed.
Your partner [?] in the spoils, but not in sin. The slain are mine; the murderers whom you led into sin are yours.
Let my cunning weep over itself because I debated with you! Let my tricks mourn over me because I came to you!
Divination, omens, and necromancers, together with every sin—the fire you built up in the world has gone out in Sheol.
You penitent who strained out gnats and swallowed the righteous! May the chaste who cry out from inside your belly tear you apart!
All the righteous are kept safe for me in a treasury. Their resurrection threatens you, who persecuted them.
The glutton who has packed all creation into his bowels now mocks me because I have been stripped of my possessions.
Do not complain before the scourging, for it has not yet reached you. The day will come when you will groan, and I will hear and rejoice.
Fire will come and strip even your skin from you, just as you scraped Job’s skin with a potsherd.
The smell of humiliation has begun, as it were, to waft over me. Is it really a dream that I have come to nothing—a little mountain [?]?
It was not because I lacked words that I kept silent about that; I grieved over the time that had passed in vain.
The deceit in your speech—I dearly wish I had not heard it, for my whole attention was on my affairs.
This humanity that was lost—distraction corrupted it; idleness and contempt yoked it together.
Mammon the broker bought her, the [?] of lust; strife and pride became the guarantors.
I fight through persistence rather than strength; if I become even slightly careless, my power is gone.
With persistent drops I have pierced rocks, for a persistent persuader can even dismantle a mountain.
Habit becomes master even of nature itself; it teaches and leads even a lion like a beast of burden.
Pleasant habit, advantage, and persistence—by these free will, the hardest of all, is overcome.
If its will grows strong, it breaks bars of steel; but if it grows careless, a weak snare can catch it.
If free will roars, we scatter; but if it grows careless, we gather together to mock it.
Let us not talk too much, lest we waste too much time. Let us attack the wall with love, and look—it is breached!
You go and attend to diseases, and I to snares; for sins are a great comfort to me, and pestilence to you.
Even when I am idle, I do not stop scheming, for my will has never rested: it stands ready.
Nisibis 56
5. To the same tune.

Your struggle is with free will, Evil One; it can lay the blame on you if it pleases.
Refrain:
Glory to you, through whose victory we have been strengthened, and through whose resurrection we have dared to challenge even death.
Look, they themselves have again exposed their weakness: Death reminded the Evil One of your strength.
Fire is in your nest, Death, and you do not notice! The faith of the departed is your destruction.
Look, Death and the Evil One have proclaimed your strength; the Evil One too reminded him of your faith.
If those who oppose you become your advocates, this is a great thing: persecutors have become heralds.
I acknowledge, Evil One, that like a household steward I guard the King's treasures until his coming.
I, Death, firmly reject this treasure of deceit gathered for me, since it does not belong to God.
Your coin, then, Satan, is counterfeit, for it is not accepted in God's treasury.
I mint a new coin in the King's likeness; look, my merchants bring counterfeit goods into the world.
God created everything out of nothing, and I created great wickedness out of nothing.
Let your evil mouth be shut and sealed—how insolent it is! Look, you are bringing yourself into comparison with the Creator.
I am Death; I have the right to speak boldly. Your own tongue is a slave kept under fear.
There is now a chasm between us, Satan, for you are shamelessly attacking your Lord.
Death, why have you broken with our partnership? Be my companion and ally, and we shall reign.
Come, let us draw a pair of swords against humanity, I in secret and you openly, and we shall finish it off.
The king gave sin and Sheol, the two to the two of us, saying, “If you become divided, you are lost.”
Look at water: if it is scattered, it also sinks low; but if it is gathered together, it becomes strong. The same is true of you.
When you were divided, you came to nothing like weaklings; when you joined together, you reigned like mighty men.
Love melts the many together as in a crucible and makes one great body that overcomes everything.
In it are wisdom and skills, strength and might; it is far greater than the statue sixty cubits tall.
They resolved, “Let us gather and go against the one who has chosen [?], for as long as he remains united, there is no way he can ever be defeated.”
The terrors said these things, gathered together, and came. May your day, my Lord, gather them to Gehenna.
By your mercy, my Lord, may I worship you when I am raised; at your trumpet blast, may I praise your Son when I am forgiven.
Nisibis 57
Also by the same author, to the same tune.
Listen, my brothers, as Death mocks the Evil One because he caused the forefather of our race and its mother to sin. Refrain:
Glory to you, through whose humiliation Satan was defeated! Your lowliness raised up Adam, who had been brought low.
Let Adam’s children see your great disgrace, just as you mocked his disgrace when you caused him to sin.
Let Eve leave that serpent alone and contend with you, for you were the one who deceived her in her innocence, O dragon.
Let Abel see Cain, who has come to join you. Along with his apostate master, the disciple of wrath is reproached.
Noah had overcome the flood as though overcoming death. Through Ham’s mouth you laughed at him because wine had overcome him.
It was not Noah who was harmed, but your own instrument. The one you had clothed yourself in was clothed with curses and became a slave.
Lot overcame wrath, which is your likeness, Death. You gave his daughters advice that pleased me.
Lot’s wife listened to your advice, for she was your instrument. May half of you dry up, since your whole instrument dried up.
May Gehenna be overturned over your head, for it was your wickedness that overturned Sodom upon its inhabitants.
Waves of fire will assail you at the resurrection, for you incited the people against Moses and Elijah.
The righteous will mock you at the end, and Joseph will rejoice—he whose brothers mocked him when you stirred them up.
A cloud of smoke will enter and choke your senses, just as the waters of the sea choked the senses of the wicked.
Chaste women, too, will mock you, for through your counsel the daughters of Midian mocked the foolish people.
A flame will consume your head because of Samson, for through a woman you shaved off the hair of that fearsome lion.
Saul, whom you defeated through jealousy, defeated you through divination, when he inquired and brought Samuel up from his grave.
Do not insult the dead man, for he did not come up alive. It was you who came up through the medium, for he was at rest.
The decree will hang you over a flame, evil one, for it was through you that they hung Absalom on a tree.
In the fire you will see your humiliation among unclean women, for through you Solomon was brought low among pagan women.
Justice will rage against you, just as you inflamed Jezebel, who devoured the prophets; you brought her to ruin.
You will justly burn in fire, for you made the two whom Elijah burned up drunk, and they threatened him and went up.
Burning coals will also be heaped upon you, and Naboth will see and rejoice—he over whom you heaped a mound of stones.
You will wear disgrace on the day of judgment before the seers, for through your thievery you clothed Gehazi with leprosy.
You will be struck by lightning instead of an arrow, Satan, for you lodged arrows in Josiah’s heart.
You will sink in the smoke of Gehenna, Satan, for you sank Jeremiah in the mud of the pit.
Daniel came up from the pit into which you threw him. He will be comforted when he sees you forever in [?].
May your wrongdoing return upon your head, hater of humanity, just as the wrongdoing of your companion Haman returned upon his head.
The King’s bride will mock you as Esther did. On the day of judgment you will ask her to intercede for you.
The fire released those righteous men whom you bound. The blazing fire will be a mighty bond for you.
You will be torn to pieces, and the seven brothers will see your humiliation. The sons of Shamuni were torn to pieces by your wolves.
Fire will mock your skull, just as you toyed with the two heads of the Nazirites, sons of barren women.
Fire will toy with your head, for a mother and her daughter mocked John’s head when you drove them mad.
A flame will mock your head, evil one, for you mocked John’s head on a platter.
Nisibis LVIII
7. To the same tune.

Look, Death was up early and took the lead in mocking Satan, who is destined to become a mockery at the end.
Response:
Glory to you, who defeated the Evil One through your crucifixion, and through your resurrection won victory over Death as well.
He spoke on our Lord’s behalf, cursing the one who had caused his humiliation and crucifixion:
“Now the grave will be yours, Satan, because you blasphemed against the buried voice that splits graves open.
“I acknowledge my Lord and my Lord’s Son, Satan. You denied your Lord and crucified your Lord’s Son.
“This is the name that suits you: ‘Killer of his Lord.’ The one you killed when he appeared has killed you.
“Let everyone shake their head at you, because through you the rulers shook their heads at the Lord of life.
“You will be a crushed reed beneath the feet of the righteous, because through you they put a reed in the hand of the one who sustains everything.
“He was crowned with a crown of thorns to show that he had taken the royal crown away from the house of David.
“The King of kings was crowned with a crown of thorns, and because they dishonored him, he took the crown away from their kings.
“Through the mocking clothes they gave him, he mocked them, for he took away the glorious robe of priests and kings.
“We consign your memory to rust, Satan, because you offered vinegar to quench the thirst of the fountain of life.
