“Let everyone raise a hand against you, because a hand dared to strike the one by whose hand created things stand.
“He received a blow from a hand and cut off the hand of Caiaphas. The hand of the priesthood ceased, because the anointing ceased.
“Again, they stretched him out against a pillar to scourge him—the one whose pillar had gone before their tribes.
“The Pillar was being scourged against a pillar. He withdrew himself from within Zion, and she fell down.
“Because they fitted two pieces of wood together for him as a cross, he broke the two staffs that guarded them.
“Ezekiel joined two pieces of wood together in unity. Through the two pieces of wood of the cross, their staffs came to an end.
“Two pieces of wood carried the people like wings. Look, its two staffs have been broken, like its wings.
“He spread out the wings and pinions of the cross in compassion. His feathers bent down and carried the nations, so that he might go to Eden.
“For he is a relative of the tree [?] of life, and he leads his friends to his kinsman, so that they may feed on its fruits upon its branches.
“Go, lament and weep, Evil One, over me and over you all, because not one of us enters the garden of life.”
“Now that you have admitted it, Death, come, let me tell you: all this exposition is useless to me.
“I will go and inspect the snares I have set. You too, Death, fly off and visit all who are sick.”
Our Lord brought both of them to nothing in two places: let the evil one be brought to nothing here, and Death there.
Nisibis LIX
8. To the same melody.

Look, Death is demanding vengeance for us from Satan. Come, let us hear his humiliation and rejoice, for he rejoiced in our humiliation.
Refrain:
Glory to you from your flock, beneath whose feet both Death and Satan have been subjected through you.
Let the wicked be hung upright, but you upside down, for you crucified Simon upside down on the wood.
You kept silent about everything, Death, when my time [?]. Simon himself swore, “Crucify me this way.”
If the righteous had cursed me, I would not have grieved. Death’s outcry is worse for me than Gehenna.
I have not spoken of our Lord’s humiliation. It is too great for my mouth to weigh and compare his suffering with your torment.
He has prepared twelve thrones for his twelve, and by the twelve tribes you yourself will be condemned.
A rope will hang you for nothing, O Satan, for that disciple of yours hanged himself with a rope at a high price.
Perhaps that Gehenna will be emptied through mercy, and you alone will remain in it with your servants.
Your curses are many; how many can I count? Look, the sum of all your curses is upon your limbs.
The wicked whom you harmed will stab you in the fire. They will reproach you: “Why did you bring us here?”
Sinners will attack you, and perhaps their threats will hurt you more than the torment of that Gehenna.
There they will all be satans to you, just as here you were one Satan to them.
The Watchers will take you and throw you down, remembering that through you they threw their Lord from the height into the depth.
Everyone will run to stone you, not forgetting that through you the unruly people ran to stone the Son.
For you, evil one, there is angry spittle from every mouth, because through you they spat on him who opened the blind man’s eyes with his spittle.
For you, evil one, from [?] tongue, every curse as well, because through you they blasphemed against him who opened mouths that were shut.
Blessed is he who avenged our humiliation, though it was silent, and stirred up the evil one against Death, through whom he himself fell.
Let us raise a shout with hosannas, my brothers, like Gideon, for when he raised a shout, the pursuers fell upon one another.
Nisibis LX
9. To the same melody.

Oh, the wonder that suddenly befell the evil one, my brothers: sin was rebuked and came to its senses.
Refrain:
Praise to the one alone who conquered the Evil One, and to him himself also thanksgiving, because he overcame Death.
Again, the Evil One: Where is her laughter, and where is her pleasure? Where is her dancing, her outward finery, and her hidden wickedness?
Instead of that shameless laughter of hers, she is occupied with weeping. She loosened her hair to wipe the dirt off Jesus.
Nothing of my teaching stands firm in her; nothing remains in her. She escaped our instruction and threw away everything I taught her.
She renounced us and our company. As though she had never even seen me, she erased our image from her mind.
The living leaven of Jesus spread within her. Jesus was silent, but she boldly pressed forward and entered, although they had not invited her.
She forgot our love of many years, and in the blink of an eye she took death and placed it between me and her.
For weeping pleased her instead of laughter; instead of eye paint, a shower of tears; and instead of adornment, a sorrowful appearance.
I made Zacchaeus the chief of oppressors, and I made this woman the chief of unclean women. Jesus broke both my wings.
If Zacchaeus has become his disciple, and if this woman has obeyed him, then shut down our trade from now on.
From now on, carved images become objects of mockery, their carvers objects of contempt, and their makers a laughingstock.
I closed people's eyes so that they would not perceive that these were carved images. Jesus opened their eyes so that they would see that these were manufactured things.
If Jesus has chosen a herald for himself, our proclamation, which fills the world, will be silenced.
Look, the astrologers and diviners, the necromancers and soothsayers, are defeated, along with the priests and all our evils.
Priests, you have eaten and [?]. Now go, diviners, become farmers! Let the astrologer roll up his books too.
If the Hebrews have become his disciples, though they were not subdued by all the signs, who among the nations will not obey him?
If he has begun to set the wayward right, our cause is undone. Let us have no doubt: from now on everyone rebukes us.
I used to be worshiped in every temple. Our disgrace exceeds our honor, for everyone spits on our burnt offerings.
Sacrificial meat becomes something loathsome, and idols are chopped up. They burn carved images beneath their cooking pots.
All our work becomes a mockery; everything we build is overthrown, and everything we have taught is ruined.
The hidden mysteries that I solemnly taught them are destined to be proclaimed on the rooftops.
You boast about the Egyptians more than any other nation, to the point that they even worshiped onions and garlic.
Look, I am afraid that truth may flourish where my deception abounded, and that Jesus may reign there all the more.
When he was a child and fled and went down, Egypt was amazed and even protected him. She who had strangled infants loved the infant.
For he had gone down and given her a pledge, like a bridegroom. He gave assurance that when he grew up, he would also marry her.
Pharaoh cannot gain a foothold, for he is no fool whom he can deceive, nor a slave to whom he can lie.
Moses struck when the Egyptians rebelled, and he led the people. The Hebrews rebelled; Jesus received blows and struck everyone.
This is difficult: if not by force, with what can we yoke him? Because they rebel, he is scourged, and someone else learns.
He accepted the spittle from his mouth and took away Adam’s shame. Through the blows to his cheeks, he uprooted our anger from his disciples.
With the nails he received, he was hurting me. I rejoiced that I had crucified him, not knowing that I had crucified myself by crucifying him.
Nisibis 61
10. To the same tune.
Let us listen thoughtfully to Death, my beloved, as he accuses us over our weeping and our lamentations. Response:
Glory to you, who descended after Adam! He had found Adam, and in him Adam’s children as well.
And perhaps he rightly said: “You killed without mercy, yet here are your tears, as though you were merciful!
You have made me out to be a criminal, you murderers! For you kill one another without me.
While Death is still preparing to come, the sword goes before him. Let us see against whom the blood of the slain cries out.
Those who were strangled in their distress cry out against you. For I have been put to shame by the violence of their strangling.
They pass judgment against me and heap disgrace on me. How did the strangled and the slain enter Sheol without me?
Look, your infants are thrown away, as in Egypt! You sacrificed your children to demons, you demon-possessed people!
While Death was still preparing to taste your corpses, Cain was the first to lavish human blood on me.
While I was preparing to wait patiently for Adam to die, you gave me power over your bodies before my rule began.
Cain broke down Sheol’s gate with his sword. It had been shut, but he went ahead and opened it before its time.
Toil has trodden the road to Sheol without me. For look, I travel along the road you have trodden for me.
For nine hundred years I sat waiting for Adam to die, but Cain did not leave his brother even a day.
The robbers along the roads are worse than I am. I am asleep, but they stay awake to kill.
Look at those of you struck down by the sword in the graves, your murdered people along the roads, and your strangled people on your stakes.
If, as you say, I rebelled against my Lord and killed him, tell me, then: who is killing these people?
And if I, Death, carried off your departed, who kills those who are strangled, murdered, and struck down by the sword?
You are Satan to one another, yet the Evil One is despised. You are a plague to one another, yet Death is blamed.”
Your own will is your Satan, and it is also your murderer. Yet everyone complains about Death and Satan.
You also give one another deadly poison to drink. Look how many deaths you have apart from me!
Schemes, ambushes, traps, the sword, and poison—look how many deaths arise from you and among you!
The judge inside the courthouse is death to two. He kills for a secret payment, while I do it for nothing.
I saw bribery and marveled at it, for it ran ahead of me. How many killings bribery commits, without anyone noticing!
I was ashamed that I conduct myself like an amateur: if I carry away a single corpse, everyone notices.
There is weeping in the houses and dancing in the streets, until they howl against me at the very gates of Sheol.
Howl against yourselves, for how hateful you are! Yet you hate me. From now on, let Sheol howl against you, you murderers!
With the comb, the scourge, fire, and stoning, you put people to death, and you boast about it.
I am ashamed before you, though I am compassionate and respectful, for I carry away your departed with honor.
On their beds I gently coax those who are sick, and peacefully I lay them down to sleep for a time.
Nisibis 62
11. To the same tune.
Look, my brothers, Death, the king of silence, complained that his land was filled with the wailing of those who had lost hope. Refrain:
Great glory to you, who descended to those below, suffered, and rose to life, and through your body raised our bodies to life!
Since we weep like madmen at the gates of Sheol, listen to what Death said as he rebuked us.
“I am ashamed,” said Death, “for you have defeated me. Half of Sheol is not enough to hold those you have killed.
For corpses that are not mine are piled up in Sheol. Two portions are there: the dead and the murdered.
Instead of my complaining that you have outdone me, here you are weeping! You have worn down Sheol’s gate and harassed me.”
For you resemble a baby who, while still crying, laughs again—just as you do over your dead.
There is no sense in your mourning and no understanding in your laughter, for you seem to me like fools.
One moment there is weeping and lamentation, and a little later there is play and frivolity, as with children.
For you cannot be mature people, without either weeping or laughter, like sensible people.
We feel sorry for your scribes, who have worn out the books of divinity by reading them to you.
The readers cry out loudly, for you are parrots. Their very shouting proves that you are wild asses.
For both the reader and the interpreter cry aloud. Are your ears dull, then, or your hearts?
For if there were a receptive ear, it would be right to hear little and do much.
But when the hearing is blocked, the voice that strikes it turns back to the one who sent it.
There is no need for shouting with me: I am not deaf. Neither reader nor interpreter is needed: I am not idle.
The God of truth commanded me to hurry, and the deed went along with the command.
There is no delay with me, nor any detours. I think that not even an arrow can get ahead of me.
But I despise your voices when you weep without hope over the graves of your departed.
If I had the authority or permission, when you weep I would come out to strike you in the face.
For I am laboring to give an account of the dead, and your voices confuse me, making me lose count.
You nations, do not let your understanding be childish, like that people whose understanding never grew up.
Understanding has not awakened in it, as with a fool, for its thinking is dark, without discernment.
For at the resurrection your infants and your children will come out first, like firstfruits.
After them come the righteous, like the victorious; last come the sinners, like people put to shame.
For although they come to life in the blink of an eye, their ranks come out of Sheol in order.
The prophets come out, and the apostles and the fathers after them, group by group, as commanded.
Those who are now sown all mixed together will return in great order, like seeds.
For when someone mixes and sows all kinds of seeds, whichever ripens earlier than its companion comes before it.
Their coming up from the earth is not confused like their mixed descent into it; it has been put in order.
Look, I have turned against myself by what I have said, for you have learned from me hidden things that you had not understood.
Instead of shedding useless tears beside the grave, pour them out in prayers within the churches.
Through them there is benefit for the dead and also for the living. Do not weep with a weeping that distresses both the dead and the living.
Nisibis 63
12. To the same tune.
Who can weigh the reward of that Abraham, at whom I marveled when he bound his only son? Refrain:
Glory to you, the voice that brought the dead of Sheol to life! They came up and became heralds of the Son who gives life to all.
At that time I broke through and went out to see the wonder: his knife was drawn against his beloved.
I gathered and multiplied my recollections from every quarter, and collected myself to marvel at that champion.
How, then, do you read his great story? You have dishonored the account read in your hearing.
Jephthah’s sword put the mourner to shame; his daughter became for him a mirror of the resurrection of the dead.
She gave herself to her father; you too must entrust your lives to the Father of all when the end comes.
Did you not experience the mystery of Sheol in the womb? For you are far more at rest in Sheol than in the womb.
It is hard for you to stand against my great will, for look, it has led your departed away for their benefit.
Let anyone who laments the departed be rebuked by the king of Moab, who slaughtered his son with his own hands.
He was a pagan, as you yourselves read, while you are teachers and well instructed, as you suppose.
He endured, but you rage in your mourning, weeping over the will of the Lord of all.
For I am afraid to let the story of Job pass through this feeble mouth of mine, since I am unworthy.
Therefore I rejoice so over their bones, giving thanks to the one who granted that they should come to me.
Do not dishonor your bodies with your sins, for in Sheol the bones of those who acted wickedly are despised.
Wherever I see the body of one of the wicked, I trample on it and curse even his memory.
And wherever I see the bones of one of the righteous, I step aside and show honor, bowing down.
You weak ones do not perceive all my arrangements. It is to you that the order of things seems confused, because you are blind.
Moses alone, I know, honored as I do the bones of Joseph, whom I exalt.
Moses honored one pure body, but I honor the bodies and bones of all the righteous.
The bones of the prophets and apostles shine; all the righteous have been a lamp for me in the darkness.
I bow down to the one who illuminated the darkness of Sheol for me. The radiance of Moses, such as it was, was a sun to me.
Nisibis LXIV
13. To the same tune.
You weak ones, why do you weep over your dead, who through death have escaped afflictions and sins? Refrain:
Glory to the one who endured everything for everyone, and even tasted death for all, to raise all to life.
I will reveal to you that even Satan, though he groans greatly, laughs greatly at your tears and your mourning.
He pinched me mockingly and winked at me like a jester: “Come, let us laugh at the sinners—look how they are raving!
“They have abandoned all thought of that fire stored up for them, and look, the fools are getting drunk at the mourning gatherings for their departed.
“Instead of weeping over how I stripped their dead and carried them away without provisions, look, they are raving.
“The souls of the wicked are tormented until the day of judgment, while these people weep over graves like madmen.
“They do not worry about their sins, or that perhaps tomorrow they will come shamefaced to join their dead.
“Then they will indeed be ashamed, all alike, family after family. In Sheol the wretched repent to no avail.
“Let them get drunk and rave on until that day when the wine wears off for the one who was raving.
“I am going to amuse them like children, so that they may play and rave until they come to their end.”
Look, I have also revealed to you my companion’s hidden secret. Go out, then, and devote yourselves to repentance.
Leave me alone, so that I too may go and attend to my affairs, that I may give my account to my Lord without shame.
I know that a wind has blown and carried away my words, for you are the very people I have tested so often.
Jeremiah is remembered for comparing insolence to an Ethiopian who does not change, although it is a matter of free will.
For this too belongs to that free will: it has bound itself by choice as though by nature.
For the will is sovereign, since it is freeborn, and through its conduct it can even resemble nature.
Nisibis 65
14. By the same author. To the same tune.
O Death, do not mock the image of Adam, which is entrusted to the earth like seed until the resurrection. Response:
Glory to you who descended and plunged down after Adam, drew him up from the depths of Sheol, and brought him into Eden.
I marvel at this seed, as you call it: look, five thousand years have passed, and it has still not sprouted.
This age will come to an end like winter, and at the resurrection the sheaf will come into the storehouse of life.
I know that it is a vintage, for I have never seen the dead being sown or reaped.
A harvest is coming, O Death, that will empty you, and the watchers will come out as reapers to mow you down.
And when did I become a farmer instead of a grape-picker? Who made Sheol, the winepress, into a field?
Does the seed not teach you? It decays and perishes, and its hope is cut off, yet from the rain it gains its hope.
You have dreamed, weaklings, that the dead have come to life, for when you are awake you see no resurrection.
Your own nature has deprived you of seeing the assemblies of symbols as they cry out about the resurrection.
I know that seeds come to life, but I have not seen bones sprout in Sheol, send out shoots, and rise up.
All your talk is just like you! Look, Ezekiel taught you in the valley how the dead come to life.
I have seen trees put on their clothing in summer, but bones lie naked in Sheol.
Moses broke your heart with his radiance, Death; a son of Adam adorned himself with Adam’s glory and wore it.
Our rule in Sheol is this: to keep silence. Words belong to you, but deeds belong to me, you weaklings!
Why are old men spared if you are a reaper? The one who has kept you from their lives is the one who raises everyone.
The infant buried there in the womb rebukes you. It proclaims to us the resurrection of the dead, and to you that you will be emptied.
The lowly blossom mocks you: it closes and opens. Even when it has perished, it has not perished, for it blooms again.
The buried chick cries out from inside its fortress that graves are split open by a voice and the body rises.
For the chick inside its fortress is also a body. Its body proclaims to our body the resurrection of the dead.
With the locust your argument ends and is finished, Death, for it comes out of the dust, teaching the resurrection of the dead.
I would have been glad if the resurrection had already happened, so that on the day of resurrection I could have had relief from your judges.
The Son of the Most High is merciful, good, and just. He will not unjustly hold me accountable for Adam’s death.
Is there really no one with sense among you to recognize this: that your father brought this ruin upon you?
Nisibis LXVI
15. To the same tune.

“Be quiet for a little while, mortals,” said Death, “and be like me: how quiet I am inside Sheol!”
Refrain:
Glory to you, Wakeful One, who went down after the sleepers, cried out on the cross, and awakened them.
You wear yourselves out and weep for the one who has departed, as though he had come to grind at a mill for me in Sheol.
I give great quiet to those who toil. Unlike you, I neither toil nor make others toil.
I hear every curse from wrongdoers. Adam’s children resemble Adam, who wronged his Lord.
Your voices and your deeds are all in turmoil. In speech one weeps, but in action one fights every day.
I heard weeping and thought that no one was toiling. I saw the bustle and thought that no one was dying.
A person’s toil makes me think that he is not mortal. His great weeping makes me think that tomorrow he will be gone.
Listen, and I will be your counselor, if you wish, for both these burdens are very bitter.
Rest a little from that toil and from weeping. Toil and weep like mortals whose lives will end tomorrow.
You are driven mad by weeping for your departed, and you wear yourselves out with [?] your possessions.
It is well that children die, and blessed are they, for they escape the misery in which you lie.
Let me go to Sheol and say there, “Blessed are you, silent dead! How restful you are!”
Listen to the conclusion of your own words: if there is a resurrection, do not weep, and do not toil like permanent residents.
You wear yourselves out like someone who will live here forever, and you weep like someone who will never rise again.
Listen to my words, if you have room within you to listen, and prepare provisions so that you may answer when I call.
For I too listen to the one who calls me, and I give back your bodies along with your treasures.
Let there be peace between us until that day, and when you depart, I will cry out and say, “Go in peace!”
Come, you and I, let us now give glory to the one who puts to death and also gives life, so that he may help us.
May the thanksgiving of us all, my Lord, be a sacrifice of life, for through the sacrifice of your body you gave life to the living and the dead.
Thanks to the one who put on our body, died, and rose again! He died in us, and we live in him. Blessed is the one who sent him!
Nisibis 67
16. To the same tune.
Come, let us listen as Death rebukes the people, whose sword against the righteous is harsher than death. Refrain:
Glory to you, who through his sacrifice made amends for our disgrace! His death stands in place of every death, so that he may raise everyone.
“It was not Death,” he says, “who crucified Jesus, but the people. How hateful, then, are the people, who are even more hateful than I!
They threw Jeremiah, whom they hated, into a pit, but I bestowed honor on his bones in Sheol.
They pelted Naboth with stones as though he were a dog. How good I am, who have never even stoned a dog!
The Hebrew women ate their children in the famine. Good Sheol released them and gave them back without difficulty.
I gave the widow her son through Elijah, and the Shunammite woman her beloved through Elisha.
The ravenous Hebrew women ate their children. Sheol gave back the dead and learned a chaste fast.
Sheol is not the real Sheol, but only Death’s. Jezebel is the true Sheol, who swallowed the righteous.
She slaughtered the sons of the prophets and the prophets and cast them aside. Elijah fled to heaven from her wantonness.
How many deaths there were among the people in place of one death, and how many Sheols there were there in place of one!
Samaria and Jezreel her daughter—the house of Israel; and Zion and Jerusalem her sister—the house of Judah.
In these two pits they strangled the prophets and the righteous who were in Judah and Israel.
Why, then, is Sheol alone hated, when there are many more hateful than she?
The dead of the Jews are very hateful to me; even their bones are repulsive to me within Sheol.
If only there were a way for me to remove them—their bones—from Sheol, for they make her stink!

❦
I marvel at the Holy Spirit: how long it dwelt among a people whose smell was as foul as their conduct!
Onions and garlic proclaim their deeds; the foul people's thinking is like their food.
Through the prayer of everyone who has knelt and worshiped your Father, have mercy on your worshiper who has wronged your love.
From the Hebrews and the Arameans, and also from the Watchers, glory to you, and through you praise also to your Father!
In return for my becoming a mouth for Death, who has no mouth, may the Son, who is all mouths, carry my request to his Father.
Nisibis 68
17. To the same tune.

O Death, do not exalt yourself over the righteous, the children of your Lord, who come to you at his command.
Refrain:
Glory to you, at whose command Death became king, and at whose resurrection he is brought low like a pauper!
By this I am all the greater, according to your own words: though I am a slave, I trample the freeborn.

Adam was chosen and given authority, and beneath his yoke you, Death, and the Evil One your companion were slaves.
❦
For this is our boast: look, slaves have become masters! Death and Satan his companion have trampled Adam.
Look at your abasement and your companion's, you renegade slaves! For Enoch trampled you both, flew away, and became king.
Even if Enoch has grieved us, I am comforted, for look, I trample Noah's dust in Sheol.
Tremble, Death, before the human being, who, even though he is a servant, establishes the yoke of his dominion over the creatures.
I rejoice, then, that those I have conquered are not insignificant, for the greater the vanquished, the greater the one who conquered him.
Your voice is very shrill, Death, against the righteous, for Enoch and Elijah have broken your pair of wings.
I know that my sorrows are balanced by my consolations: in place of two, look how many have come and are coming!
Everyone who has come and is coming to you lodges as a temporary resident and departs from your dwelling, like Lazarus.
This voice did not break me as much as it pained me, for I enslaved Lazarus again after he had rebelled against me.

* * *
Death, submit to questioning and argue: [?] compelled him to rise, unless his resurrection portrayed a mystery?
You are eager for debate, like people with nothing to do. But I labor at my work, separating people and leading them away.
You have prepared yourself for much debate—who has restrained you? The truth of our resurrection presses you with its counterarguments.
You have made me hateful to you, though I do not hate. I am the one who gives rest to your elderly and your afflicted.
You have treated me like a criminal, you mortals! Adam killed you, yet I am the one reproached.
I can easily expose you, for I was a servant, and you yourselves made me king through your sins.
[?] Adam awakened me, for I had been resting. I was dead, and you brought me to life so that you might die through me.
I put up with liars who killed and denied it. For Adam killed himself, yet I am blamed.
The source of the quarrel is the accursed serpent, well and truly crippled. Crawling on [?], he sowed discord between me and you.
Satan is left alone, while you attack me! Go and fight the Evil One, for he is the one who condemned you.
He is my partner—I do not deny it—but since he is so hated, rather than be reproached on his account, I disown him from now on.
Listen to my words, you mortals, and I will comfort you. I have caused distress, but I acknowledge the resurrection of the dead.
For the sound of the trumpet's preparations has begun to trickle into my ears, as it readies itself to sound its cry.
Listen to my words and gather plenty of oil for your lamps, for you will meet no hindrance from me.
Know that, even though I have said all this, your company is dear to the desolation of Sheol.
For the human being is precious to me, and great is the peace he brings: crawling creatures, fish, and birds come to meet him.
It is astonishing that his company is dear even to the Watchers. Even the Evil One wants his companionship in Gehenna.
May you have the resurrection of the dead, you mortals! And may I, who have cut others off, be cut off within Sheol.

Let thanksgiving rise from everyone to you, who give life to all, for you gather Adam's dust from every place.
* * *
Nisibis LXIX
To the tune of “The Ordinary Messenger.”

You are the one who fashioned the dust in mercy from the beginning, and you are the one who brings your gift to completion for it in love.
Refrain: Praises to your lordship!
You, the Good One, created Adam, though it was clear to you that he would wrong you and go astray. You fashioned him so that you might acquit him.
You looked upon the body as it mourned, upon the soul as it grieved, for you had joined them in love, but they departed and parted in sorrow.

Judge the body and the soul:
which made its companion sin?
The fault belongs to both,
for freedom belongs to both.

It is yours, Blessed One,
to show mercy yet again.
Let your hand fashion anew;
let your finger shape Adam.

For look, my Lord, from the beginning
your compassion has never left him.
You began with him in love;
finish with him in mercy.

For if, when he did not exist,
you created him so that he might exist,
now that his dust exists,
let his temple be renewed through you.

It is fitting for a king,
when he sees that his image has grown old,
to brighten the faded image
with choice pigments.

It was a wondrous sight:
your glorious majesty stooped
toward lowly dust
to fashion a splendid image.

This latter deed is better
than what happened in the beginning:
for you did not create him,
but clothed yourself in him.

The Most High knew that Adam
wanted to become God.
He sent his Son and clothed him in Adam,
to grant Adam his desire.

The Evil One was dismayed when he saw
that the more he cast Adam down,
the higher Adam rose in rank,
bringing shame on the one who cast him down.

Gladden the body with the soul;
return the soul to the body.
Let them yearn for one another,
those who parted, returned, and were joined again.

Bring back the soul,
and let it enter its home.
Let its dwelling be at peace,
and let its lamp shine within it.

Let light dwell in his eyes;
let sound pass through his ears.
Let his senses, ruined and deserted,
be filled with companionship and peace.

Hateful old age
will not oppress them,
nor will the pains and sufferings
that they cast off at death.

For death has become
a new opportunity for the dead:
through it they take off suffering,
and through it they put on glory.

The dead man's mouth in Eden
speaks with the soul:
“From where, and to where,
and how have you come here?”

The light there dyes
the body with its colors.
He sees himself
wrapped, as it were, in rays of light.

The light there is intense;
its radiance flashes upon those
who had marked its great symbol
upon themselves here.

The fiery Watchers approach
human beings of flesh.
They yearn lovingly for those
who labored and found rest for their souls.

The Watchers approach to recount
to the righteous the race they ran.
They recall their victories
and honor them for their own deeds.

The firstfruits of the praise
of our feast rise
from sealed mouths
that are now imprisoned in Sheol.

Death heard the ringing sound
and inclined his ear in fear.
Trembling seized him,
for the dead had begun to speak.

His prisoners abandon him,
for his captives have rebelled against him.
The jailer is imprisoned:
they have imprisoned him in his own prison.

May our Lord make us worthy
to offer thanksgiving with you,
O blessed righteous ones,
whose voice never ceases.

Thanks to him who makes
springs flow in a sealed mouth,
so that it may offer unceasing glory
through the Son to the Father who is worshiped.
Nisibis 70
2. To the same tune.

Oh, how bitter, my brothers, is this cup of death! It makes even the chaste drunk, so that they lose their composure in tears.
Response: Blessed is he who gives life to the dead!
At the departure of the dead, even a dignified person is overcome, so that he loses his restraint and wails over his beloved who has departed.
For the member that remains cries out in its love over its partner who has been cut off, whose familiar presence and companionship have ended.
Few indeed are those who resemble Abraham, who dared to give the fruit of his love over to death for his Lord’s sake.
This is the pillar of truth that bore the burden among the people: the waves of suffering battered it, but its steadfastness was not shaken.
Here is the farmer who, when he saw fruit in his barren old wife—a cluster that had appeared after a long delay—offered it as firstfruits.

Jephthah’s deed, too, is astonishing: the farmer who plucked the young shoot that had blossomed offered it to the Lord of the vineyard.
***
His struggle overcame his affections; he constrained his love and offered her up. He did not lose his composure in his suffering, for his faith sustained him.
For death’s wine is new wine stirred up with grief. It makes its drinkers drunk with tears, and its guests with weeping.
Very comforting, then, is the great example of Jephthah, who with the sword offered the treasure of his life to her Lord.
Jephthah stretched out his right hand and offered up the sacrifice. The dove saw that he was grieving and encouraged him with her voice.
He was a fitting priest, serving as priest with blood that came from himself, to become a figure of his Lord, who served as priest with his own blood.
Everyone who is drunk with love, yet triumphs through love of the truth, sees his departed beloved as though in a dream.

***
For someone may happen to see his companion dying in his dream; then morning comes and comforts him after the sorrow of the dream.
How like a sleeping person the departed one is! Death resembles a dream, and resurrection resembles the morning.
Let truth dawn within us like light in the eye, and behold, we see that death is like the terror of a dream.
For someone is foolish if he sees that sleep is gone by morning, yet supposes that death’s sleep will last forever.
If he possesses the eye of hope, he can see in secret that this sleep of death comes to an end on that morning.
The wondrous fragrance of that treasury of life spread through the body, the soul’s house, which was deserted when she went out from it.

Its ornaments and its beauties are many.
***
For it is the Spirit’s temple of love. Though it lay desolate, it is restored to peace and becomes a dwelling of peace.
The trumpet’s voice cries out to the silent assemblies: “Rise, sing, and give praise aloud before the bridegroom!”
There was a tumult at the mouths of the opening graves. Each spoke to the other with his limbs and gave praise with his voices.
Glory to you, who exalted Adam when he was pure! Glory to you, who humbled him in Sheol when he exalted himself!
Give thanks to him who humbled, and give thanks to him who raised the dead. Let my harp also praise its Lord for its resurrection.
Nisibis 71
On the resurrection. To the tune of “Abel is alive, and Cain is slain.”
The Spirit said through David, “I will repay them for their deeds”—Moses, Aaron, and Samuel. She did not say that she had repaid them,
but rather, “I will repay them.” Blessed is he who revealed in a few words the glory of their resurrection! Refrain:
Blessed is he who, through the upright and also through the prophets, depicted the mystery of the resurrection of the dead.

The prophet showed that Noah, Job, and Daniel are alive, if the listener understands. If they are righteous and can rescue their own souls, they are also delivered from death and rescued from Sheol itself.
For what benefit would their righteousness bring the persecuted if the dead do not live? It would be foolish
for them to be killed for the sake of a God who does not give life, and for the Just One to deny them recompense for their sufferings, so that they ended up in Sheol like everyone else.

“Even if Moses and Samuel stood before me”: by this he showed that they are alive, according to the meaning of the reading. Why trouble himself over sinners if the righteous do not live? Why trouble himself over the corrupt if the chaste person is not raised?
Enoch lived for Adam’s sake, so that he would not lose hope after hearing, “You are from dust, and to it you will return,” and to show
that the body can live forever with the soul. Blessed is he who, through Enoch, gave abundant comfort to our father Adam!

He rewarded Elijah in heaven, so that the greedy people would not suppose that recompense is only on earth. He withheld Jeremiah’s reward in the pit, so that they would ponder where he would reward him. He stirred them to take their stand upon the certainty of recompense.

If there is no resurrection, what benefit did Abel’s blood gain by crying out against his murderer? The offering he presented brought about his death, though he could have lived nine hundred years. If there is no new life, why did he lose the life that was at hand?

He did not first give greedy Death a sinful dead person, so that Death would not have a rightful claim against him. Death swallowed the upright man at the beginning, so that resurrection might roar within it, and so that, when the first upright man is drawn out, Death will be emptied of everyone.
Blessed is he who gave the female donkey plain speech like a goad, so that she could strike her master for striking her—
the foolish mule who saw a heap of silver and lusted for it! Let us not resemble the beast and abandon hope in our resurrection.
The seven brothers who were slaughtered like lambs in a slaughterhouse—where are they to seek their lives? On what
condition did they reject both gifts and promises? Blessed is he who gives Shmuni [?] the crown of her sons!

If the old prophet believed that Josiah would distinguish between one set of bones and another like a judge, here, my brothers, is a great mystery: our Lord comes and raises the dead, and distinguishes the deeds of the departed along with their bones.

If there is no resurrection, what benefit did Josiah bring by honoring the prophet’s bones? The lion crushed him while he could feel, and he was honored when he could no longer feel. The prophet’s preserved bones proclaimed the resurrection in a mystery.
The lion that killed the prophet did not kill the female donkey, because she had not despised the commandment. From that donkey who was preserved,
let Eve, who was killed, learn that the commandment she despised killed her, for the Judge did not act unjustly.

He who permitted the ravenous lion to crush the hungry prophet, who had been enticed by food, commanded Death, which had grown hungry, and it swallowed Adam, who had become greedy. Death and the lion will be brought to an end; the prophet and Adam will be raised.
And if that deaf thing without ears—the altar that Jeroboam made—heard the prophet’s voice and split open its belly
and poured out the ashes, graves are split open in the mystery it represents. For if stones listened to the prophet, bones will listen to the Son.
Look, my brothers, at the mystery in the fish: Jonah was alive to God while he was dead to human beings. The dead too
are dead to us while they are alive to the Godhead. And our Beloved, who was immersed in Sheol, sprang out of it like Jonah.

A living man fell into the lifeless sea, a speaking man into the sealed pit, and bound men into the unrestrained fire. The sea, the pit, and the furnace are pledges for the dead: this is how they will answer from every place when the resurrection calls us.

The pit of the beloved man has comforted us: instead of one ravenous death, hungry mouths surrounded him. The pit was opened like the graves, and the beasts were defeated like death. The victorious man came up and proclaimed life for the dead to those who are buried.
Nisibis 72
2. By the same author, to the same tune.
Listen and be comforted, you mortals: the fish became a steward. It received him, kept him, and returned and gave him back. In the same way he will give
an account—Death, the steward of Sheol. For when our Lord brought the dead to life, he demanded even their eyelashes from him. Refrain:
Glory to you, Christ the King, who rouses the sleepers with the sound of his trumpet.

If Zipporah circumcised her son with the temporary circumcision, and death was stopped by circumcision, how much more is death stopped by the true baptism! For whoever has been baptized into Christ has put on the Living One who gives life to all.
How could God wrong Abraham after his death, disregarding either his love or his righteous deeds? And how could he wrong
Isaac, disregarding the bonds on his hands and feet and the knife that his eye saw suddenly drawn over him?
How could he wrong the prophets, who, like lambs cut to pieces, were silenced in their folds? For Jezebel,
the she-wolf of the prophets, silenced the prophets, and the hundred prophets who escaped were tormented by hunger and thirst.
And how could he wrong Lot, who offered both his daughters in exchange for the holy ones who came to him? From
the mouth of fire he rescued him, only to throw him into the mouth of Sheol! What benefit is rescue if there is no resurrection?

Look at the infants who were drowned, and also the prophets who were slaughtered, Job’s children who were buried, and the seven brothers who were flayed, together with the many who were stoned. How could God wrong all these victors?
Judge for yourself how your mouth prays to God: is he one who rewards, or one who cheats? If he is one who cheats,
do not trouble yourself; but if he rewards, do not stop. Does he demand wages for a hired worker, yet withhold the reward for prayer?

And if he rewards you only here, he has prepared a bad end for you, since he will not raise you to life. Nor does he reward you here, since your whole life is misery, and you count for nothing more before God than sinners do.

The robber is more vigorous than you, the thief freer than you, the fornicator more at ease than you, the sinner healthier than you, and the wicked man more prosperous than you. If there is no resurrection, your running is in vain, weak man.

And if you boast of this life, a snake has far more life than you, and a dragon more than you. The beasts are healthier than you, eagles are swifter than you, and lions are stronger. What are you boasting about, fool?

Tell us, weak man: what is the reward for your prayer, and what is the recompense for your fasting? Your vow is an additional burden, and your offering is a loss. If there is no resurrection, you are on the same footing as everyone else in Sheol.

And if you fear the sword, so that you do not kill lest you perish, and do not steal lest you be burned—look, your judge is a human being, and for a bribe he can put you to death, just as he has killed the innocent and, instead, acquitted the guilty.
Yet the question still stands: if the law and just judgment come from God, how could justice that lasts for a time please God more than everlasting justice, if he denies our resurrection?
For if he is just, how could he deny us our alms and prayers after our death? And if he does not love justice—which we must never believe—how and from whom did just laws originate on earth?

If we say, “From humanity,” is a human being then more just than his Creator? We are forbidden to say this! For an unjust person sets laws aside for a bribe. And if the law comes from fate, the two cancel each other out.
But if God is just, he cannot establish a horoscope from which injustices arise. And because God
is good, he cannot hate the resurrection, for it would be very wrong for the righteous, for whose sake he died, to be defrauded.

It has been established from every side, investigated, and demonstrated that there will be a resurrection for the dead. What will you lose, fool, if there is a resurrection? Believe that through these just requirements that you observe, you will reign.

For those things you observe without reward, because of the sword and the torture combs, observe because of hope. And let whatever you do for praise be done for the resurrection. Instead of dying a death that cuts off hope, die a death filled with hope.
They burned the victorious in fire, drowned the upright in water, slaughtered the mourners with swords, and stoned
the prophets; and they hung the apostles on crosses. How, then, could the Just One withhold ten thousand times ten thousand things entrusted to him?
Nisibis 63
3. By the same author, to the same tune.
Look, my beloved, beneath the earth are the corpses and bodies of the buried, and look, in heaven are the righteous. For look, they bear—
both of them—the things entrusted by humanity. Earth and heaven cry out if the righteous are defrauded. Refrain:
Glory to the Son, who at the sound of his horn splits open the graves and raises the dead.

If an honest merchant borrows money under a contract, its interest silently accumulates. And if the owner of the contract dies, the interest lives on after him. Who can set a limit to the interest on the offering that Abel offered?
Who would not lend to God, since the interest on his prayers lives on after his departure? A contract produces interest, and the earth [?] and [?], and God's treasury increases our alms and prayers.
There is one road for us all, my brothers, from birth to death, and from death to resurrection; and from there,
two roads: one to the fire and one to Eden. Let everyone pray for his dead, that he may be found worthy of the road to Eden.
He cast the corpses of the Indians and Assyrians into the wilderness, and brought the bones in the valley to life. It is not by some other power,
my brothers, that we are driven by force. It is the will that rules over everything that brings to birth, puts to death, and raises to life.

Good news for the children! Pharaoh drowned the newborns, but the deliverance of the people drowned him. So death will die at the resurrection that brings joy to everyone, and death will cease to trouble little children, as Pharaoh ceased to trouble the newborns.
How could he defraud the newborns? Like dead locusts floating on the water, the babies floated in the river, while their fathers,
watching, wept and cried out to heaven. Blessed is he who showed them in blood an image of their newborns' resurrection.
One of the Watchers was commanded to mark the sign of salvation on the foreheads of the righteous. Circumcision was put to shame
when it saw the hidden seal that triumphed. Mark your dead with the cross, so that they may overcome the second death.

That wise Maker did not employ evil, nor did he fashion and destroy in vain. If a mortal craftsman does not work without understanding, far be it from us to say that God put things together and took them apart without discernment.

If a human being endowed with speech prizes speechless gold and guards it lest it be lost, and a painter who has painted an image preserves it from damage, how much more does the Good One preserve the image he established for his glory!
If there is no resurrection, life has distressed the righteous man: he passed through it and became an object of contempt; he fell to the ground and reached
his end. His story ended, and he was entirely finished. Far be this from the just Rewarder, for he does not defraud his righteous ones. [End.]
Nisibis XXXIV
To the tune of “O my Lord, in your gardens.”

Oh, how great Adam was, and glorious in his creation! Oh, how great his abasement at the time of his death! May your resurrection make him great.
Response: May your resurrection renew him.
In his formation the wisdom of his Creator is portrayed; in his corruption the wickedness of his deceiver is marked. May the deceiver be put to shame by his renewal.
He was chosen and great when he was made, but he is despised at his departure. In life he is like something; in death, like nothing. My Lord, make him great again.
He judges and condemns; he examines and acquits. His likeness is God's, but his death is that of the animals. May your image become great through you.
See, his speech is mighty and is proclaimed everywhere. In the world he speaks, but in Sheol he is silenced. Renew his songs.
He dives into the sea and brings up its treasures, but when he dives into Sheol, death closes over him. Through you, my Lord, may he be drawn up.
The mighty one who subdues sea and dry land is brought low in the grave and becomes a crawling thing. May your mercies roll it away, my Lord.
His mighty yoke subdues the animals, but death's yoke brings his freedom low. Through you, my Lord, may he be set free.
With bits he controls the rush of the chariot. Death bridles him and binds him in Sheol. May the one who releases all release him.
He sits on a throne with a diadem and a crown, but death brings down his rank and breaks him. Through you, my Lord, may he be honored.
He writes and reads, studies and interprets, but cannot persuade death with his wisdom. Through you, my Lord, may he be delivered.
Though he confines the lion and binds the dragon, [?] death confines him in the pit of Sheol. May the sound of the horn bring him out.
He cuts down a tree, and it sprouts again and grows; but death separates him from all his loved ones. May he see them in your glory.
He heals wounds with the medicines he has discovered, but no medicine has proved effective against death's wound. May the medicine of life heal him.
His oil, his perfumes, and his many spices cannot dispel his odor when he dies. May he be made sweet with your salt.
He apportions the heavenly lights to hours and seasons, but does not know when the hour of his departure will be. Glory to the one who knows all!
He busies himself with earthly things and investigates heavenly things, but when death reaches him, he loses his way and is bewildered. Through you, my Lord, may he be delivered.
He accumulated interest and added to his capital; he demanded payment and gathered it, then scattered it by leaving it to others. May your grace enrich him.
He makes dwellings for summer and winter, but one grave is enough for him for summer and winter. May he delight in Eden.
He divided things up, and after taking his share, asked for more. Death measured out and gave him three cubits in Sheol. May he fly to meet you, my Lord.
He clarified wines and multiplied pleasures. Death shuts his mouth against his will. May your table comfort him.
The greedy man hoarded and amassed treasures without tiring. Death brings him out and confines him in Sheol. May your resurrection bring him out.
He travels along paths and turns onto roads. He went down one road on which he never turned back. May he return to your paradise.
They bring pallbearers and summon carriers, and in place of his beds there is the bier of the dead. May the resurrection make him fly.
He toiled over spacious mansions that would suit him, yet his body filled a grave, and his dust filled a handful. Renew him once again.
Nisibis 75
2. To the same tune.
The day of departure is a bitter day, a day of anguish, a day of weeping.
Be our comfort, our Lord. Refrain: Be our comfort, my Lord.
It is a day that cuts off and takes away a limb from the united body of his brothers and relatives. May he be joined together in you, my Lord.
It is a day that grieves the elderly over their children, for death breaks the staff of their old age. May they lean on you, my Lord.
It is also a day that takes an only son away from his mother and cuts off the arm that supported her. You, my Lord, support her.
It is a day on which fathers have departed and gone away, leaving their children orphaned and bereft. You, my Lord, raise them.
It is also a day when a brother parts from his brother, the number is diminished, and the fingers are fewer. May they be made complete in you, my Lord.
It is a day when an old man's daughter parts from him, and the eye through which he used to see grows blind. May your light comfort him.
It is a day on which a man parts from his rib, and the earth is bereft because the head of the body is no longer there. In Eden she will see him again.
It is also a day when a woman parts from her household, and it is overturned and scattered because its order has perished. May your kingdom comfort her.
It is a day that suddenly brings news, entering and disturbing an ear accustomed to hearing good things. May it be calmed by your voice.
It is a day that stirs the eyes to weeping, the hands to beating in grief, and the mouth to lamentation. May we be quieted in you, my Lord.
It is a day that calls for much weeping. Whoever enters and whoever leaves has a mouth full of lamentation. May he be comforted by your blessedness.
It is a day on which a friend parts from his companion: two oxen separated from the yoke of companionship. May they be united in your love.
It is a day on which bridegrooms and brides are separated, and in place of that dancing there is beating in grief. May they reach your wedding feast.
It is the day that annuls the pledge of the betrothed and prepares a grave for her instead of a bridal chamber. Make her worthy of your bridal chamber.
It is the day that also separates daughter and sister, making them depart like doves from their dwelling. May they be settled in your paradise.
It is the day that also separates the little girl from her mother. Her grandmother grieves because the little one is no more. May she grow up in Eden.
It is the day that separates many little children, and the vine stripped of its fruit mourns and is desolate. May they be kept in your treasury.
When an only child dies, the branches bend down to mourn over him, over the fruit that has fallen. May he be offered to you, my Lord.
Glory to him who strangled death, placing it in the middle, between life and life, to teach you that he has abolished your death.
Take examples from the body itself, whose stages and developments come in order. May the Perfecter of all bring it to perfection.
A person cries out in his suffering and mourning. Give him room, my Lord, to soothe his sorrow, so that you may be praised in everything.
He is troubled and agitated, wanting to be raised soon. The Good One is not so troubled and impatient. Blessed is he who bears with everyone.
Disrupt the order, then, and put fruit before shoots and children before pregnancies! And rightly do you weep because the Giver of life to all has delayed!
Let our sorrow believe that we shall see our departed and, together with all our loved ones, give thanks to the Perfecter of all, who raises and gives life to all.
Nisibis 76
3. To the same tune.

Who will long for your adornment, O body? Who will serve your beauty as a slave? In you, my Lord, may we be set free.
Refrain: In you, my Lord, may we be set free.
The one whom your beauty captivated among the living sees you among the dead and recoils from you in Sheol. May we long for you, my Lord.
Foolish is the wise man who labors to please you and polishes his speech to receive praise from you. See our bondage, my Lord.
The one who serves you is without God. At your passing, he will be ashamed of the one he was trying to please. Through you may we please your Father.
Death has broken your swift wing, which labored and never settled except beside gold. May we fly toward you, my Lord.
Eagles flock to flesh, and people to silver. Blessed is he who made it impossible for anyone to eat gold. Your body is the medicine of life.
Though no one eats it, no one has had enough of it. Though it is not food, everyone hungers for it. May we long for your bread.
The world calls to you, “Come out and toil!” The grave calls to you, “Come, weary one, and rest!” May we rest in your harbor.
It is the day that adorns young men for the grave, crowns virgins, and sends them to Sheol. May they rejoice with your everlasting ones.
It is the day that darkens the house with weeping and spreads darkness and sorrow over its walls. May your consolation drive it away.
Rebuke death, my Lord, the glutton that devours us. It has swallowed us alive and buried us in its belly. May your trumpet split it open.
It is the day that strips the beds of their finery, and instead of their adornments they are shrouded in sackcloth. May your day bring us joy.
He brings a woman out of the chamber where she lives. Overturned, poured out, and disordered, its arrangements are lost. May he set our souls in order.
It is a day that bends and bows down tall forms. Cedars bend over cedars that have fallen. In you, my Lord, may we flourish again.
The body decays because the soul has departed—the pilot and life of the senses and the limbs. May it be adorned with her again.
It is a day when the rich man looks at his treasures and sees that possessions do not accompany their owner. May your treasury enrich us.
It is a day in which only the righteous rejoice, those who acquire and store up provisions of almsgiving. May your encouragement provide for us.
The skin covering the face is stripped away, and the face becomes naked and ugly. May your resurrection adorn it.
The ears have become holes for the crawling creatures of Sheol, and the eyes have become nests for the worms in the graves. See our humiliation, my Lord.
Those fashioned from clay have collapsed and become a heap of mud in Sheol—the lowly remains of the beautiful. See our decay, my Lord.
It is a day on which kings have departed in sorrow, taken off their crowns, and gone down to Sheol. Our King is in heaven.
Death brings everyone low. Death impoverishes everyone. Death lays everything waste. Death devours everyone. May your resurrection drive it away.
The day of departure is a bitter day. It is a day that makes everyone weep, a day that saddens everyone. May your day overcome it, my Lord.
The day of resurrection is what brings everyone together, what comforts everyone, what gladdens everyone. May your day reach us, my Lord.
It is a day when fathers see their children, a day also when brothers see their brothers. Glory to the one who gives life to all.
Nisibis 77
4. To the same tune.
In the departed man let us see our life, which is like a dream. For if the owner himself has vanished like a vision, how much more his possessions! Response: You, my Lord, raise him to life.
On this very day, when our bodily frame ceases to function, come, let us pause and look at the world that has ceased for him. Come, let us serve our Lord.
It is a day that silences the mouth so that it makes no sound, for the source of its words and the spring of its utterances have dried up. May it be comforted by your word.
It is a day that shuts the open ears: death seals them, and they become deaf. May they be opened by your voice.
It is a day that closes the beautiful eyes, the lamps and torches of the temple of souls. May they see your light.
It has shut the eyes like windows and darkens the house that the soul, its lodger, has left. May it receive her at the resurrection.
It is a day that binds the hands and makes them still. He began but did not finish, and left the [?]. May he be strengthened by your power.
It brings walking to a halt and wipes away the footprints. His steps are no more, for it has cut off his journeys. May they dance at your wedding feast.
It is a day that forbids the breath to enter. It presses it from within and drives it out. May you drive it away at the resurrection.
His thought, which is the wheel of every movement, it has bound in stupor and stilled in silence. May you make it worthy of your kingdom.
This is the day when one color changes into another; instead of the color of the living, it clothes itself in that of the dead. May we shine in your light.
Weigh the waves against bodies, and consider the Good One: if he revives the waves, how much more will he bring your bodies to life for his glory!
The hours are arranged, each one at its appointed time. So too the seasons are arranged for the Lord of all. Glory to the one who sets everything in order!
The tenth hour does not come before the sixth. Likewise, do not demand times before their appointed times. Blessed is the one who orders everything!
The months, too, are beautifully set in order, and no month comes before the months preceding it in the count. Blessed is he in his arrangements!
It would be disorder for Nisan to come before Tishri. And disordered is anyone who says, “Where is the resurrection?” Blessed is the one who arranges everything!
It would be disorder for harvest to come before sowing, and likewise for resurrection to precede death. Glory to our farmer!
For the sowing of the departed is coming to completion and reaching its full measure, while the time for the Watchers to go out to harvest is delayed. Glory to our sower!
It is indeed fitting that birth proceeds before death, and fitting that resurrection brings death to an end. Glory to the one who knows everything!
Here ends the volume of the Nisibene hymns of the blessed Mar Ephrem, which number seventy
and seven. Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit, now and at all times and forever and ever. Amen.
